[p. 314]

﴿A revelation of the Book from God, the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, so worship God, making your religion sincerely His.﴾ This is an elegant opening in praise of the Qur'an, placed at the head of this surah because the Qur'an comprises what this surah contains and more, namely the foundations of the religion.

The word ﴿tanzil﴾ (revelation) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) intended in its verbal sense, not as a passive participle (maf'ūl), especially since it is annexed to "the Book," and the basic principle of an annexation is that it should not be an explicative annexation (idāfah bayāniyyah).

"Tanzil" is the verbal noun of the doubled (mudaʿʿaf) verb "nazzala," and it implies that He sent it down in installments. The choice of this form here is a rebuttal of the critics, for they were among those who raised as an objection their statement: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. The difference between the doubled and the hamzated (mahmūz) verb in such forms was already explained in the First Introduction.

The definite article in "al-Kitab" (the Book) is for prior reference (ʿahd), referring to the Qur'an that they already knew of, at every reminder and every dispute. The description "the Almighty, the All-Wise" follows the divine name (Allah) to indicate that what is sent down from Him comes in a manner suited to these two attributes. Thus it is ʿazīz (mighty). God says: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾; that is, the Qur'an is mighty and dominant through its proof over whoever denies it, dominant through its excellence over all other books, insofar as dominance entails superiority and preeminence, and dominant over the eloquent Arabs, since it rendered them incapable of producing the like of even a single surah. It is also ḥakīm (wise), like the attribute of the One who sent it down.

As for "ḥakīm": it may mean "one who judges" (ḥākim). In that case the Qur'an also judges over its opponents by means of proof, and it judges over the other heavenly scriptures by what it contains of detailed explanation and clarification. God says: ﴿confirming what came before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

It may also mean "firm and perfected" (muḥkam mutqan), in which case the Qur'an comprises clear explanation that admits no error. Or it may mean "characterized by wisdom" (ḥikmah), in which case the Qur'an comprises wisdom, just as its Sender is characterized by it.

In our view these meanings are all intended by the verse, and moreover these two attributes contain an indication that the Qur'an is inimitable (muʿjiz) both in the eloquence of its wording and in its scientific inimitability, since it contains sciences of which people had no knowledge, as we explained in the Tenth Introduction.

In the description "the Wise" there is an indication that He sent it down with wisdom, and this wisdom is the Sharia: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

[p. 315]

In this there is guidance toward the obligation of contemplating the meanings of this Book, so that through such contemplation one may reach knowledge that it is the truth from God. God says: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

The meaning of "the Almighty, the All-Wise" as attributes of God was already explained in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And if you slip after clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is Almighty, All-Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The opening of the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ with the particle (inna) takes into account what the statement is used for, namely reminding of favor (imtinān). So the particle (inna) is understood as expressing attentiveness to the statement. It is also intended to allude to those who denied that it was sent down from God, so the particle (inna) is understood as emphasis, using a term that is shared between its two meanings. And because this verse contains greater proclamation of the truthfulness of the Prophet, to whom the Book was sent down, it is fitting for emphasis, since the proof of his truthfulness does not lie in his person alone; rather it rests upon the inimitability of the Qur'an and other miracles. Thus the requirement for emphasis exists, unlike the requirement of the situation in His saying ﴿A revelation of the Book from God﴾.

So the sentence ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book﴾ stands in the position of an explanation (bayān) of the sentence ﴿A revelation of the Book from God﴾.

The repetition of the word "Book" serves to honor its status, departing from what the apparent situation would require, namely the use of a pronoun, by using the explicit noun in a place where a pronoun would be expected.

The transitive use of "anzalna" with the preposition of termination (ilā) was already discussed in His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

The "bi" in "bil-ḥaqq" (in truth) is for accompaniment (mulābasah), and it is a stationary adverbial phrase functioning as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "the Book." That is: We sent down the Qur'an to you accompanied by truth in all its meanings: ﴿Falsehood cannot come at it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42].

From the explicit meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ follows the command that he should worship God, making the worship sincerely His. In this consequence there is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to what fits the allusive meaning of the premise, namely that those alluded to are to worship God, making religion sincerely His, and that they must reflect upon the meaning alluded to.

[p. 316]

This is an indication that the sending down of the Book upon him is a great blessing, which requires that the Messenger ﷺ respond with thankfulness by devoting worship to Him alone. It is also an indication that associating others with God in worship is ingratitude for His blessings which He has bestowed. Thankfulness is the servant's directing of all that God has bestowed upon him toward the purpose for which it was created, and worship realizes this meaning. God said: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

Therefore the purpose of the command to worship is to prepare for restricting worship to the state of sincerity in His saying ﴿making your religion sincerely His﴾. The commanded act is thus a specific worship, and for this reason the command to worship is not used to mean a command to persist in it.

For the same reason it is not expressed in this construction with a form of restriction (qaṣr), unlike His saying: ﴿Rather, worship God﴾ [al-Zumar: 66], because what is intended here is the additional explicit declaration of sincerity, and the Messenger ﷺ is too exalted to worship other than God. Ibn al-Hajib (Ibn al-Ḥājib) imagined from the non-fronting of the object here that the fronting of the object in His saying ﴿Rather, God, worship Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 66], at the end of this surah, does not convey restriction, and this is a slip of a scholar.

Sincerity (ikhlāṣ) means purification and freedom from admixture with anything else, and it includes singling out. The surah in which God's oneness is affirmed was called "the Surah of Sincerity," that is, the singling out of God in divinity. Sincerity is mentioned here to convey monotheism and something more specific than it, namely that the worship of the Prophet ﷺ toward his Lord should be unmixed with any worldly interest, as God said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾ [al-Furqan: 57].

Religion (dīn) means dealing (muʿāmalah). What is meant here is the creature's dealing with its Lord, which is worshipping Him. So the meaning is: sincerely devoting worship to Him, without mixing His worship with the worship of another.

"Mukhlisan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the hidden pronoun in "aʿbud" (I worship).

Since His saying ﴿making your religion sincerely His﴾ conveys the meaning of singling Him out in worship, there was no requirement here for fronting the object of "worship God" before its governing verb, because the exclusivity has already been derived from the state in His saying ﴿making your religion sincerely His﴾. By this, the argument of Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib from this verse is refuted, namely his reasoning in favor of his opinion that fronting the object before its verb does not indicate restriction, and his weakening of the argument of the masters of rhetoric (aʾimmat al-maʿānī) from His saying ﴿Rather, God, worship Him﴾ at the end of the surah, which they took as fronting merely for the sake of emphasis because of the occurrence of ﴿worship God﴾.

[p. 317]

He said, in Īḍāḥ al-Mufaṣṣal (Ibn al-Ḥājib's commentary on al-Zamakhsharī's al-Mufaṣṣal), explaining the words of the author of al-Mufaṣṣal in the preface, "God I praise, for He made me one of the scholars of Arabic": "God I praise" follows the pattern of ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], fronting the more important element. As for those who say that it is for restriction, there is no evidence for this, and holding to it by means of something like ﴿Rather, God, worship Him﴾ is weak, because ﴿worship God﴾ also occurs. End of quotation. It is reported from him that he wrote in his marginal notes on the Īḍāḥ at that place the words: "There is no evidence for restriction in it, for worshipfulness is one of His exclusive attributes, so the exclusivity is derived from the state, not from the fronting." End of quotation.

This is a mixing of one thing into another, for he did not limit himself to denying a proof that sound taste attested among the masters of usage. He also based his denial on the supposition that the fronting which is observed in one context must be observed in every context, as if speech were cast into fixed molds to be used in every situation. That conflicts with the variety of rhetorical contexts, to the point that he made the exclusivity of worship derived from the context rather than from fronting, as if the context, even if its existence were granted, would prevent reliance on the indication of the explicit wording.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Surely, to God belongs sincere religion (al-din al-khalis).﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) leading to the affirmation of His exclusive right to worship, which is the aim of the surah. It also conveys the reason (ta'lil) for the command to worship God sincerely, because if sincere religion is due to God and belongs exclusively to Him, then commanding sincerity toward Him hits its proper target. Thus the Prophet's ﷺ command to devote worship to Him is grounded in the blessing of the revelation of the Book to him, and it requires that He alone deserves sincerity in worship, the way a universal principle requires its particulars. By this generality the sentence also carries the sense of a concluding summary (tadhyil), so it bears three functions, all of which call for separation (fasl).

The sentence opens with the particle of alerting (ada't al-tanbih), to draw attention to its content so that the soul receives it wholeheartedly. This is what favored considering it a resumptive statement, and it made the sense of causation arise secondarily from the mention of general sincerity after specific sincerity, both having the same subject.

The lam in ﴿lillahi al-din al-khalis﴾ is the lam of ownership which carries the meaning of entitlement, i.e., sincere religion, meaning obedience unmixed with anything else, is only due to Him, in the manner of "al-hamdu lillah" (praise belongs to God). Page 318.

Fronting the predicate serves to express exclusivity; so His words ﴿lillahi al-din al-khalis﴾ indicate that He alone is entitled to it and that it is exclusively His.

Religion (al-din) means obedience, as mentioned earlier. Sincere (al-khalis) means free from any admixture of associating others in one's worship. This is the intended meaning of the verse.

Among the implications of the meaning of the verse is the sincerity of the believing monotheist in worshipping his Lord, i.e., that he worships God for His sake, meaning seeking His pleasure and complying with His command. This relates to the states of intention (ahwal al-niyyah) in worship, referred to by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Actions are but by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. Whoever's migration was for worldly gain he would obtain or for a woman he would marry, his migration is for what he migrated for." Actions are but by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. Whoever's migration was for worldly gain he would obtain or for a woman he would marry, his migration is for what he migrated for.

Al-Ghazali (al-Ghazali) defined sincerity as isolating the intention of drawing near to God from all impurities.

Sincerity in worship is that the motive for performing what is commanded and abandoning what is forbidden is seeking God's pleasure, which is the meaning of the saying "for the face of God" (li-wajh Allah), i.e., for the intention of compliance, such that worldly interest is not the driving motive for worship, like worshipping God so that people will praise him, such that if praise were absent he would abandon worship. Hence it is said: showing off (riya') is minor shirk, i.e., when it is the motive behind the deed. Similarly, one who fights for the sake of booty, and if he despairs of it he abandons fighting. But if there is an immediate personal benefit that is incidental to the worship and not its goal, it is excused, especially if such things are not free from souls or if it helps one to increase in worship.

In the Jami' al-'Utbiyya, regarding what has come that correct intention is not invalidated by a passing thought that is not within one's control: al-'Utbi related from 'Isa ibn Dinar, from Ibn Wahb, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that Mu'adh ibn Jabal said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "There is not a man from the Banu Salama but he is a fighter; some of them fight by natural disposition, some fight for show, and some fight seeking reward. Which of these is the martyr among the people of Paradise?" He said: "O Mu'adh ibn Jabal, whoever fights for any of these qualities, the fundamental matter of his affair being that the Word of God is supreme, and he is killed, he is a martyr among the people of Paradise."

Ibn Rushd said in his commentary: This hadith contains a clear text that whoever's fundamental deed is for God, and upon that he sets his intention, the passing thoughts that occur in the heart and are not controllable do not harm him, according to what Malik said, contrary to what Rabi'a held. They were asked about a man who loves to be seen on the path to the mosque and dislikes to be seen on the path to the market, and Rabi'a rejected this and did not approve that anyone should love to be seen doing good deeds.

Malik said: If the beginning and origin of that is for God, there is no harm in it, God willing; God said ﴿And I bestowed upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39] and said ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 84].

Malik said: This is only something that occurs in the heart and is not controllable, and it is the whispering of Satan to prevent him from acting. Whoever experiences that should not let it make him lazy from persisting in doing good, nor make him despair of reward, and he should repel Satan from himself as much as he can; i.e., when he wants to discourage him from acting, and renew the intention, for this is not held against him, God willing. End quote.

Before that, it was mentioned from Malik that he saw a man from the people of Egypt asking Rabi'a about this. It was mentioned that Rabi'a denied it. Malik said: I said to him, "What do you think of going early to the mosque before noon?" He said: "The righteous have always gone early."

In the Jami' al-Mi'yar: Malik was asked about a man who goes to raiding with surplus wealth to obtain from the surplus of the spoils, i.e., (to buy from people what is valid for them of the spoils). He answered: There is no harm in it, and he cited the verse about trade during the Hajj: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 198], and that this is not a hindrance nor a detriment to the validity of worship if his intention in the worship is the face of God, and this is not considered associating partners in worship, because God is the One who permitted that and lifted the burden from its doer, together with His saying ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110]; this shows that such association is not included, either in its wording or meaning, under the verse of al-Kahf. End quote.

I say: If one intends worship in order to draw near to God, so that he asks Him for what is good for him in this world as well, there is no harm in it, because that worship was made a means to supplication and the like, and all of that is drawing near to God Most High. Prayers have been prescribed to remove harm and fulfill needs, such as the prayer of istikhara and the prayer of distress and need. It is also excusable for the worker to intend from his deed
Page 320.
that the Muslims pray for him and mention him well. In this sense 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha, may God be pleased with him, said upon his departure for the Battle of Mu'ta, when the Muslims bade him farewell and prayed for him and those with him that God return them safe:

"But I ask the Merciful for forgiveness and a strike with a branching wound that spews foam,
or a thrust from the hand of one who finishes with a spear that pierces the entrails and the liver,
so that when they pass by my grave they say: May God guide you, O raider, for you have been rightly guided."

You have known from our restriction of the stake that it is a worldly stake that hoping for reward and seeking protection from punishment is included in the meaning of sincerity, because it refers back to drawing near for the pleasure of God Most High.

You should know that the excellence of sincerity in worship is a matter more specific than the matter of the validity and sufficiency of worship in itself, since worship may be devoid of the excellence of sincerity and yet be valid and sufficient. So sincerity has an effect on obtaining the reward of the deed and increasing it, and it has no connection to the validity of the deed.

In Mafatih al-Ghayb: As for sincerity, it is that the motive for performing the act or abandoning it is purely submission. If another motive is present along with it, then either the motive toward submission is stronger than the opposing motive, or equal to it, or weaker. They agreed that the equal and the weaker are invalid; as for when the motive toward obedience is stronger than the other motive, they differed as to whether it is effective or not. End quote.

Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi mentioned that al-Ghazali (i.e., in the Book of Intention from the Fourth Quarter of the Ihya) holds that whatever has a motive other than obedience that is weaker negates sincerity. Its sign is that obedience becomes lighter for the servant because of the purpose in it, and that Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi (i.e., in the book Siraj al-Muridin as transmitted by him in al-Mi'yar) holds that this does not detract from sincerity.

Al-Shatibi said: The scope of inquiry in this question turns on whether the two intentions can be separated or not. Al-Ghazali considers merely the existence of the two intentions together, whether or not the two intentions can be separated, while Ibn al-'Arabi considers the aspect of separation.
Page 321.

This is a subtle matter which we have appended to the tafsir of the verse because of its connection to the sincerity intended in the verse, and to draw attention to the apparent similarity between the aims that accompany the intention of worship and the association of another with the object of worship.

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him, [saying]: "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in position." Indeed, God will judge between them concerning that in which they differ.﴾ This is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿Surely, to God belongs sincere religion﴾, to increase the verification of the meaning of sincerity to God in worship, and that it is complete purity not mixed with any association; and not the association of those who claimed that they took protectors and worshipped them out of eagerness for nearness to God, which they claim as an excuse for themselves. So their saying is from corruption of the premise and inversion of the reality of worship, by making the worship of other than God a means to nearness to God; thus by this means they defeated its purpose and sought nearness through what distances them. A means that leads to nullifying its aim is a form of folly.

The relative pronoun is intended to refer to the polytheists; it is in the position of nominative as subject, and its predicate is the sentence "﴿Indeed, God will judge between them﴾".

The clause "we only worship them" is a quoted statement of an omitted saying, because its structure requires that, since there is nothing in the speech that could be referred to by the first-person plural with others; so it is determined that it is a pronoun referring to the subject, i.e., they are the speakers of it and of what follows it, and the verb of saying is omitted; it is "kathir" (commonly). This omitted saying may be construed with the form of the active participle, making it a circumstantial clause from "those who took": i.e., saying: "We only worship them"; and it may be construed in the verbal form. The construction: they said "We only worship them", and then the sentence would be a substitution of part (badal ishtimal) for the sentence "took", since their taking protectors included this statement.

His saying ﴿Indeed, God will judge between them﴾ is a threat against them for their saying that, so it is known from it that their pretext in their saying ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God﴾ is nullified, because in reality they worshipped idols more than they worshipped God.

So the pronoun in "between them" refers to those who took protectors. What is meant by "concerning that in which they differ"
Page 322.
is the disagreement of their paths in worshipping idols and in its kinds, from altars and angels and jinn, according to the disagreement of the polytheists in the lands of the Arabs.

The meaning of judging between them is that He will show them their error, all of them, on the Day of Resurrection; for judging between them does not necessarily mean judging in favor of one group over another, but rather the judgment between disputants may be by nullifying the claim of all of them.

It is also possible that it is a conjunction with an understood counterpart to "between them", similar to it, indicated by the sentence it is conjoined with, namely ﴿Surely, to God belongs sincere religion﴾, since it implies that those who made religion sincere to God have agreed with the truth; so the construction is: He will judge between them and between the sincere ones, on the pattern of the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Had Abu Hujr come safe, there would have been between the good and me only a few nights."

Its construction: between the good and between me, by the indication of the context of lamentation and yearning.

The exception in His words "except that they bring us nearer to God" (illa li-yuqarribunā) is an exception from omitted causes. That is: "We do not worship them for any reason except the cause that they bring us near to God." This yields a restriction upon this cause, a restriction of correction (qaṣr qalb idafi), i.e., rather than what you have censured us for, namely that we have denied the blessing of our Creator by worshipping other than Him. We have already mentioned earlier that they intended by this an excuse. In the exception particle there is istikhdam (a double usage), because the lam presumed before the exception is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), not the lam of cause (lam al-'illah), since denial of the Creator cannot be a cause for any rational person, but it is a result leading to it. So the restriction does not contradict that they designated them for other things, when they regarded them as intercessors and sought their help in calamities, and cast lots with their arrows for success, as is established in reality.

Al-zulfa: the station of nearness. That is, "that they may bring us near to God in the station of nearness." What is meant by it is the station of honour and favour in this world, because they do not believe in the stations of the Hereafter. It is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "li-yuqarribūnā," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), i.e., "that they may bring our station near to God."

It is also permissible that zulfa be a noun of verbal action (ism masdar), in which case it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), i.e., "a very great nearness."

The construction "they in it are disputing" (hum fihi yakhtalifun) conveys two matters: that the disagreement is established for them, and that it is recurrent and renewed. The first comes from the fronting of the subject (taqdim al-musnad ilayhi) over the verbal predicate, and the second from the predicate being a present-tense verb (fi'l mudari').

* * *
Page 323

"Indeed God does not guide one who is a liar, a disbeliever" (inna Allaha la yahdi man huwa kadhibun kaffar). It is permissible that this be a second predicate concerning "And those who took protectors other than Him" (wa-alladhina attakhadhu min dunihi awliya'). It is a metonymy (kinaya) for their being liars in their saying "We do not worship them except that they bring us near to God," and for their being disbelievers because of that, and a metonymy for their being astray.

It is also permissible that it be an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because His words "Indeed God will judge between them in that about which they differ" arouse in the minds of the listeners a question about the outcome of their state in this world as a result of taking protectors other than Him. It is answered that God does not guide one who is a liar, a disbeliever; that is, He leaves them in their error and gives them respite until the Day of Recompense, after He has made the religion clear to them and they opposed it.

What is meant by "one who is a liar, a disbeliever" are those who took protectors other than Him, that is, the polytheists. So the apparent course would have been to use their pronoun, but it is turned away from to the (noun) form because of the description of them as liars and the intensity of disbelief contained in the relative clause.

The guidance of God that is negated for them is this: that God overtake them with His gentleness by creating guidance in their souls. Thus the negated guidance is the creational guidance (al-hidaya al-takwiniyya), not guidance in the sense of instruction and conveying the message, which is evident. So what is meant is the negation of God's care for them, i.e., the care by which guidance is made easy for them so that they are guided; that is, God does not grant them success but leaves them to their own opinion, in anger toward them.

The expression of them by way of the relative construction (al-mawsuliyya) is because of what the relative clause has of suitability for indicating the allusion to the cause of the act, in order to convey that the reason for their being deprived of success is their lying and the severity of their disbelief.

For when God sends His messenger to people and he conveys to them, they, at the moment the Messenger conveys to them the message of his Lord, are at a level that is equal before God, in that they are all servants being nurtured. Then they become categories in receiving the call. Among them is one who seeks guidance, accepting what he understood and asking about what he did not know, reflecting, looking and asking. This one is in the place of his Lord's good pleasure, so He helps him and expands his breast for goodness, until his breast is made eager for goodness, until his inner self is illumined with the light of faith, as the Exalted said: ﴿Whomever God wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast constricted and tight﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. And He said: ﴿But God has endeared to you the faith and made it beautiful in your hearts, and made disliked to you disbelief, defiance and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. ﴿A bounty from God and a favour, and God is Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Hujurat: 8].
Page 324

There is no doubt that whenever a servant goes deep into lying against God and into disbelief in Him, the anger of God against him increases, and the distance of divine guidance from him increases, as the Exalted said: ﴿How would God guide a people who disbelieved after their faith, and had testified that the Messenger is true and clear proofs had come to them? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 86].

Tawfiq: the creation of the capacity for obedience. So the negation of God's guidance from them is a metonymy for the negation of His success and gentleness, because guidance is caused by success, so the negation of the effect is expressed by the negation of the cause.

Their lying is what they fabricated of disbelief by deifying idols, and what arises from that of fabricating imaginary attributes for the idols and laws by which they follow them.

Kaffar: one of intense disbelief, the eloquent in it. This is their disbelief in God, in the Messenger ﷺ, and in the Qur'an, by turning away from receiving it and being free from the impediments to reflecting upon it.

And it is known from comparing their description as liars with their description with eloquence in disbelief that they also exaggerate in lying, because their blameworthy lying is only their lying in their disbelieving utterances. So exaggeration in disbelief necessitates exaggeration in lying regarding it.

[Page 325]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 4:

﴿Had God wished to take a son, He would have chosen whatever He willed from what He creates. Glory be to Him! He is God, the One, the Subduer.﴾ The position of this verse is that of argument: that the polytheists are liars and ungrateful in taking guardians (awliya', sing. wali) besides God, and in their saying, ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and that God has deprived them of guidance. This is what His words before it contain: ﴿Indeed God does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. Thus the verse aims to nullify their polytheism by nullifying its strongest basis, namely their counting among His associates those whom they claimed as God's offspring, when they said, "God has taken a son." The polytheists claimed that al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat were the daughters of God: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza? And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19–20] ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21].

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "At that time they used to say: the angels and these idols, meaning these three, are the daughters of God." Al-Baghawi reported from al-Kalbi: "The polytheists in Mecca used to say: the idols and the angels are the daughters of God." Thus the belief is specified to the people of Mecca. It is apparent that they did not say this of anything other than al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, because their names are feminine. Otherwise, many of the names of their idols are masculine, such as Dhu al-Khalasa. Al-Zamakhshari also mentioned, when discussing the basmala, that when they began their actions they used to say: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-'Uzza."

Therefore, the purpose of this verse is to nullify the divinity of the idols of the polytheists by way of the method of kalam (scholastic theology).

Know that this verse and the verses after it contain arguments for God's singularity (infiradih).

The meaning of the verse is: if God were to take a son, He would choose from His creatures whatever He willed to choose; that is, He would choose what is most worthy of being chosen, and He would not choose stones for His sonship as you claim. This is because choosing naturally relates to the best of things from among those chosen. Thus it is invalid that al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are the daughters of God. If this is invalid concerning them, it is invalid concerning all the other idols by the principle of equality or a fortiori. So the (law) "lau" here is the one called (law) "al-suhaybiyya", i.e., the conditional whose condition is assumed on the furthest possible supposition. This is the one they illustrate with the well-known example: "Suhayb is an excellent servant; if he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." Thus this is a nullification of what is contained in His words, ﴿And those who take guardians besides Him, [saying] "We only worship them…"﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], up to His words, "ungrateful."

It is not a refutation of the saying of some Arabs that the angels are the daughters of God, because this was not part of the belief of the polytheists of Mecca to whom the address was directed. Nor is it a refutation of the sonship of Christ according to the Christians, because this was not believed by the addressed polytheists and they had no awareness of it. The aim is not to argue against the Christians, and the Meccan Qur'an did not address arguing with the Christians.

Know that the proof was built on the principle of the impossibility of a son for God, the Exalted. The conditional syllogism was built on the assumption of taking a son, not on the assumption of begetting. Therefore it implies that what is meant by taking a son is adoption (tabanni), because the refutation of adoption by this argument necessarily entails the refutation of begetting a son, all the more so.

The purpose was reinforced by mentioning the act of taking (ittikhadh) and following it with the act of choosing (istifa'), in the manner of accommodating the erring opponent in order to lead him into the pit of his error. That is: if anyone had a relation of sonship to God, that relation would be adoption and nothing else. For the sonship of God cannot be conceived except as adoption. And if God were an adopter, He would choose from His creatures what is most fitting for adoption, not the stones which you claim to be daughters of God. And when the sonship of those three alleged idols is invalidated, the divinity of all the other idols is invalidated, which they acknowledged to be in a rank below al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, by way of a fortiori and by agreement of the two opponents. Thus the discourse implies two proofs: one of them is omitted, namely the proof of the impossibility of a son in the literal sense for God, the Exalted; and the proof of the invalidity of adoption is mentioned, since it is not fitting that the Wise would adopt such things.

This is the way to interpret this verse and to explain its relation to what precedes it. By it, one escapes the confusion into which the exegetes (mufassirun) fell, so they took forced paths regarding its meaning, its construction and its position. None of them achieved a complete account of the necessary connection (mulazama) between the condition of "lau" and its consequent, and some of them remained silent about its interpretation.

In al-Kashshaf there occurs what indicates that the aim is to negate the polytheists' claim of the sonship of the angels, and that the consequent of "lau" is omitted, and that what is mentioned in the place of the consequent is a guidance to the correct belief regarding the angels. He said: "That is, if God had wished to take a son, He would have been unable to, and it would not have been valid, because that taking (i.e., that adoption) would be impossible, and it could not have come about except that He choose some of His creation and specially favour them and bring them near, as a man favours his son. He has done this with the angels, and their special status deceived you, so you claimed that they are His children, out of ignorance of His reality, which differs from the realities of bodies and accidents."

Thus what is apparently the consequent of "lau" was made to convey the meaning of istidrak (correction/qualification), which generally follows the antecedent and the consequent. Therefore he explained it with its synonym, which is the exception (istithna'), which is of the type of affirming a thing by means resembling its opposite.

Al-Taftazani has a discussion which implies that al-Kashshaf's exposition of the proof of the condition of "lau" and its consequent is not sound, and he inclined to hold that "lau" is "suhaybiyya", following an exposition mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf. Furthermore, the discourse of the author of al-Kashshaf makes this verse disconnected from the verses preceding it, placing it as a new topic, even though the construction of the verse is the construction of argument, not of information. Hence al-Kashshaf's interpretation of it is far-fetched. Setting this aside, there is obscurity and forced reasoning in the articulation of the necessary connection in the argument, as al-Shaqqar indicated in his book "al-Taqrib, Mukhtasar al-Kashshaf."

[Page 326]

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of taking a son is taking for honour and adoption. On this interpretation His words 'would have chosen' (lastafa) are consistent. But the taking familiar in the witnessed world (i.e., taking offspring) is impossible to attribute to God, and His words 'would have chosen' are not consistent with it. Something that indicates that the meaning of 'to take' here is choosing and adoption is His words, 'from what He creates,' i.e., from His originated creatures." End of quotation. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) followed him in this.

Upon this, the author of al-Taqrib built, and after criticizing the discourse of al-Kashshaf he said: "The better view is what has been said: If He had wished to take a son as you claim, He would have chosen the more excellent (i.e., males), not the lesser, who are females." Al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Kashshaf: "This is the meaning of the verse according to its apparent sense," and he mentioned that the author of al-Kashshaf did not adopt it for the reason al-Taftazani mentioned there.

What Ibn 'Atiyya adopted, though closer and clearer than the approach of al-Kashshaf in articulating the proof, nevertheless shares with it the fact that it does not link the verse to the verses before it, and what should not be cut off from its connections. How often has the first left for the last!

The phrase "Glory be to Him" (subhanahu) is a declaration of His transcendence above what they attributed to Him of associates, after He nullified it by the proof of impossibility. It returns to the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, which had been interrupted since His words, ﴿So worship God, making the religion sincerely His﴾ [al-Zumar: 2].

The phrase ﴿He is God, the One, the Subduer﴾ is a proof for the transcendence derived from "Glory be to Him." The phrase "He is God" is a preparation for the two attributes. His proper name was mentioned in order to bring Him to mind by the name specific to Him. For this reason it does not say "He is the One, the Subduer," as it says after ﴿Is He not the Mighty, the Forgiving?﴾ [al-Zumar: 5].

Affirming oneness (wahdaniyya) for Him nullifies any partner in divinity, despite the differing ranks of such partners. Affirming "al-Qahhar" (the Subduer) nullifies what they claimed: that their guardians bring them near to God in nearness and intercede for them.

Al-qahr is domination, i.e., He is intensely dominant over everything; nothing overcomes Him, and nothing turns Him away from His will.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 5:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a term appointed.﴾ This sentence is an explanation of the sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [al-Zumar: 4]. The creation of these worlds, and the governance of them in their intensity and greatness, makes clear the meaning of oneness (al-wahdaniyya) and the meaning of subduing (al-qahhariyya). Thus the sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [al-Zumar: 4] has two connections: a connection with the sentence ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son﴾ [al-Zumar: 4], as a connection of tadhyil (appended conclusion), and a connection with the sentence ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ as a connection of tamhid (preparatory introduction).

He has moved from reasoning by the requirement of the reality of divinity to the negation of a partner, to reasoning by the creation of the heavens and the earth that He alone is the one who creates, since their partners are unable to create worlds.

The ba' in "bil-haqq" (with truth) is for accompaniment (al-mula'abah). That is, He created them in a creation accompanied by truth, and here truth is the opposite of futility (al-'abath); that is, He created both in a creation accompanied by wisdom, rightness and benefit, with no futility or disorder mixing into their creation. God Most High said: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39].

The sentence "﴿yukawwiru al-layl﴾" (He wraps the night) is a second explanation, like the enumeration of sentences in a context of argument or of favour. The present tense is preferred in this sentence to indicate the renewal and recurrence of that, or to bring to mind the state of wrapping, following the bringing to mind of its effects, for the state of God's wrapping the night over the day is not witnessed; what is witnessed is its effect, and the renewal of the effect indicates the renewal of the influence.

The root meaning of takwir is wrapping and coiling. It is said: kawwara al-'imamah 'ala ra'sihi, when he coiled and wound it. Here the form of the night's covering the day over a part of the surface of the earth is represented by it, and the reverse of that in succession, in the form of the folds of a turban, as the night covers the night that preceded it.

This is a wondrous metaphor, capable of being divided into parts: the earth is likened to the head, and the alternation of night and day over it is likened to the winding of the folds of a turban. What further adds to its inventiveness is the choice of the root takwir, which is a scientific miracle among the miracles of the Qur'an, referred to in the fourth introduction and explained in the tenth introduction. The root takwir derives from the name al-kurah (the sphere), which is a body that is round from all its directions equally. The earth is in reality spherical in shape, and this the Arabs and most of mankind at that time were ignorant of. So the Qur'an pointed to it by describing the two accidents that alternate over the earth in succession, namely light and darkness, or night and day, since it made their alternation a takwir, because the accident of a sphere is spherical following its essence. Since the context of this verse is argument for the true divinity by the bringing into being of the heavens and the earth, the root takwir was chosen, rather than others, to argue for what follows that bringing into being, namely the creation of the two great accidents of the earth, in preference to other expressions such as the covering (ghashayan) expressed in His saying ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in Surat al-A'raf, because that verse is directed to indicate the breadth of disposal over created things, since its beginning is ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. So depicting that by the covering of night and day in particular was because it indicated the strength of power to change the accidents of His creatures; and for this reason it limited itself to changing the greatest accident, which is light, by imposing darkness upon it, so that this verse would be a miracle for those Muslims who come later and who acquire knowledge of astronomy.

The conjunction of the sentence "﴿wa-yukawwiru al-nahar 'ala al-layl﴾" (and He wraps the day over the night) is conjunction of the part intended from the report, like His saying ﴿thayyibat wa-abkaran﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The subjecting of the sun and the moon is their being made submissive to work according to the order of motion that God has set for them, the motion of the followed and the follower, and this has been mentioned earlier in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere.

The sentence ﴿wa-sakhkhara al-shamsa wa-al-qamar﴾ (and He has subjected the sun and the moon) is conjoined to the sentence ﴿yukawwiru al-layl 'ala al-nahar﴾ because that subjecting is appropriate to the wrapping of night over day and its reverse, for that wrapping is among the effects of that subjecting; this appropriateness required conjoining the sentence which includes it to the sentence before it.

The sentence ﴿kullun yajri li-ajalin musamma﴾ (each runs for a term appointed) is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the sentence "subjected the sun and the moon," and this is the clearest of the states of subjection.

The tanwin of "kull" is for compensation, meaning each one. Al-jary is swift motion. The lam is for cause.

The ajal is the term of their passing away, for since their running includes bringing their passing away near, their running is made as if it were for the sake of the term; that is, for the sake of what the term of remaining seeks and requires. This is like His saying ﴿and the sun runs to a station for it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38]. So the indefiniteness in "ajal" is for singularity.

It is possible that the intended meaning of ajal is the term of people's lives, which ends with the ending of the various lifespans. Lifespan is nothing but limited times and counted breaths, and the times and breaths are reckoned by the running of the sun and the moon, so their running became as if for a term.

The bishop of Najran said:
"The turning of the sun and its rising from where it never sets prevented remaining."
Their statements on this meaning are numerous.
So the indefiniteness in "ajal" is for the category, which has the sense of "for terms named."

Perhaps its following with the attribute "al-Ghaffar" favours this interpretation, as will come.

Al-musamma: that which is given a name (mawsum), i.e. that by which it is specified, and it is what God has specified for it to reach.

It has come in other verses: ﴿each runs to a term﴾ [Luqman: 29], with the particle of ending of the goal, and the lam of cause and the particle of goal are close in original meaning, and I suppose that the difference of expression with both is merely variety in speech.

* * *
﴿Surely He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ is an initiating resumption, in the sense of warning and promise. The attribute "the Mighty" is a metonymy that He does what He wills, with none to overpower Him, so the worship of their protectors does not benefit the polytheists. The attribute "the Forgiving" indicates an invitation to them to repentance by following Islam. In the attribute "the Forgiving" there is a suitability to the mention of the term, because forgiveness's effect appears after resurrection, which comes after death and the ending of the term, as an exhortation to hasten to repentance before death, when making amends is no longer possible.
The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting indicates the importance of its explicit and implicit meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

Page 331

﴿He created you from a single soul; then He made from it its mate﴾. This is a transition to the argument from the creation of humankind, which is the wondrous creation. Included in it is the argument from the creation of their origin, which is a single soul from which a great multitude spread, and from the creation of Adam's mate, so that the law of reproduction (namus al-tanasul) may be established.

The sentence may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun of majesty (Allah), and it may be a fresh, independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i) repeating the argument.

The address is to the polytheists, as shown by His words after it, "So how are you turned away?" This is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person. Its purpose is that when He had informed His Messenger ﷺ about them by way of the third person, He turned to address them, so as to combine in directing the argument at them both the indirect (ta'ridh) and the direct (tasrih) methods.

A parallel to this sentence occurred in Surah al-A'raf, except that in this sentence His words "made from it its mate" are conjoined with the particle "thumma" (then), which denotes a gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because its context is the argument for oneness and the refutation of a partner through its various levels. The creation of Adam was thus a proof of the greatness of His power, and the creation of his mate from his own self was another proof, independent in its indication of the greatness of His power. So the particle "thumma," which in the conjoining of sentences denotes a gradation in rank, was used to indicate that the conjoined sentence is independent in its indication, like the sentence it is conjoined to. Therefore the creation of Adam's mate from him is more indicative of the greatness of power than the creation of humankind from that single soul and from its mate, because it is a creation for which no custom has been established, and that creation is more apt to astonish the hearer than the creation of humankind. So the particle of gradation was used for it, which is employed for a gradation in rank and not for a gradation in time, because the time of the creation of Adam's mate precedes the creation of humankind.

As for the verse of al-A'raf, its context is that of bestowing favour upon people with the blessing of existence. So the two origins of humankind are mentioned, one conjoined to the other by a particle of joint participation in the ruling, which is that each is the origin of the creation of humankind.

The verse contains three indications of the greatness of power in the creation of humankind as male and female: the creation of the male and female directly, and the creation of the first male by way of incidental inclusion, and the creation of the female also directly.

* * *

Page 332

﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾. This is an argument from what Allah Most High created of the livestock, conjoined to the argument from the creation of man, because the addressees of the Qur'an at that time depended for the sustenance of their lives on livestock; nor were peoples at that time free of need for livestock, and the need for livestock has never ceased to surround mankind in the sustenance of their lives.

This is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the clause "He created you from a single soul" [al-Nisa: 1] and "He creates you in the wombs of your mothers," because of the connection between the pairs of livestock and the mate of the single soul.

Included in this argument is a bestowal of favour through the benefits they provide to people, as indicated by His word "for you" (lakum), because the livestock contain great materials for the sustenance of humankind. These are what is in His words, "And the livestock — He created them for you; in them is warmth" [al-Nahl: 5], down to His words, "except with great hardship to yourselves" [al-Nahl: 7], and His words, "and from their wool and their hair" [al-Nahl: 80], etc., in Surah al-Nahl.

Inzal (sending down) is the transfer of a body from a height to a lower place, and it is also used for the subduing of a difficult matter, as one says, "They submitted to the judgment of so-and-so," because a difficult matter is imagined as hard to reach, like one who holds fast to mountain peaks. Khassab ibn al-Mu'alla, one of the poets of the Hamasa, said:

"Time brought me down to its judgment from a lofty height to a low place."

So the use of inzal here means subjugation and enablement, in the manner of His words, "And We sent down iron" [al-Hadid: 25], i.e., We made it subservient to people, and We inspired them to know its smelting, so that they make from it swords, coats of mail, spears and weapons, despite its hardness and solidity. It is also possible that the sending down of the livestock is its literal sending down, i.e., the sending down of their origins from Noah's Ark, in the manner of His words, "And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam'" [al-A'raf: 11], i.e., We created your origin, who is Adam. He said, "We said: Carry in it of every kind two of each pair" [Hud: 40]. Then inzal would be ihbat (descending). He said, "It was said: O Noah, descend in peace from Us and with blessings upon you and upon nations from among those with you" [Hud: 48]. These are two good meanings for the use of inzal, and they are better than the exegetes' interpretation of sending down the livestock as meaning creation, i.e., because their creation by the command of origination descends from the Presence of Holiness to the angels.

Page 333

The "azwaj" (pairs) are the kinds, as in His words, "And from every fruit He made in it two pairs" [al-Ra'd: 3]. The intended meaning is the kinds of camels, sheep, cattle and goats.

The name "zawj" (pair), which is one of two, was applied to a kind because each kind's existence is constituted of male and female, and these are two mates. Or the term "azwaj" was applied to them because He indicated by it what was sent down from Noah's Ark, of them, male and female of each kind, as has been mentioned just above.

﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses﴾. This is a substitute (badal) for the clause "He created you from a single soul," and the pronoun of the addressees here refers to humankind only. It is an argument from the gradual development of human creation, indicating the greatness of Allah's power, His wisdom, and the subtleties of His workmanship.

The expression in the present tense serves to convey the renewal and repetition of creation, together with calling to mind the image of this wondrous development, called to mind in its general outline, according to the varying levels of people's understanding; its details are known to the scholars of medicine and the natural sciences. The Hadith from the Prophet ﷺ has explained it: "Indeed, each of you is gathered in creation in his mother's belly for forty days as a drop, then he becomes a clinging clot likewise, then he becomes a lump of flesh likewise, then the angel is sent to him and he breathes the spirit into him."

His words "creation after creation" mean a stage of creation after another stage that differs from it. These stages are ten:

First: the stage of the drop (nutfah), which is a mucous, round, white body devoid of organs, resembling a worm, about five millimetres long.

Second: the stage of the clot ('alaqah), which forms after thirty-three days from the time the drop settles in the womb, and is the size of a large ant; its length is about thirteen millimetres, in which the head appears and outlines of the forms of the organs.

Page 334

Third: the stage of the lump of flesh (mudghah), which is a red piece the size of a bee.

Fourth: upon completing two months, its length becomes three centimetres, its head is half its remaining size, and its neck and face are not distinguished, and its redness continues.

Fifth: in the third month its length is fifteen centimetres and its weight is one hundred grams, the outline of its forehead, nose, eyebrows and fingernails appears, and the redness of its skin continues.

Sixth: in the fourth month its length becomes twenty centimetres and its weight 240 grams; down appears on the head, its abdominal organs exceed its chest organs, and its fingernails become clear towards the end of that month.

Seventh: in the sixth month its length becomes about thirty centimetres and its weight five hundred grams, and it appears to be closed (?) and its nails harden.

Eighth: in the seventh month its length becomes thirty-eight centimetres, the redness of its skin decreases, its skin thickens, a greasy, thick, adhering oily substance appears on the skin, the hair of its head lengthens and tends toward a light reddish-blond, and its skull arches from the middle.

Ninth: in the eighth month its thickness increases more than its length grows, its length is about forty centimetres, its weight about four pounds or more, and its movement grows strong.

Tenth: in the ninth month its length becomes from fifty to sixty centimetres and its weight from six to eight pounds. Its bones are completed, its head enlarges, its hair thickens, the vital functions begin in it in the digestive system, the lungs and the heart, its growth becomes by nourishment, and the circulation of the blood appears in it, known as the fetal circulation.

"The three darknesses" are: the darkness of the mother's belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (mashimah), which is a membrane of skin created together with the fetus, enveloping it to protect it, and by means of which it becomes independent from what reaches it of nourishment through its own separate circulatory system, apart from its mother.

In mentioning these darknesses there is an alert to the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah Most High regarding things, and to the penetration of His power into them in the state of their greatest concealment.

Page 335

"Khalqan" (creation) is in the position of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the type, in view of its being qualified by "from after creation." The phrase "in three darknesses" is connected to "yakhluqukum" (He creates you).

The majority of readers read "ummahatikum" with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the mim, both in pause and in continuation. Hamza read it in continuous recitation with a kasra on the hamza, following the kasra of the nun of "buTun" (bellies), and with a kasra on the mim, following the kasra of the hamza. Al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the mim in continuous recitation with a fatha on the hamza.
