﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. There is no deity except Him; so how are you turned away?﴾ After Allah Most High's names were applied to the reports and attributes indicating that He is the one who disposes of all existents, their substances and accidents, their apparent and hidden aspects, beginning from His words, "He created the heavens and the earth in truth" [al-Zumar: 5], which guides the rational person to the fact that He alone has the disposal that deserves worship, and who alone is divine, He followed that with the demonstrative pronoun to alert to the fact that He is worthy of what follows after it on account of those acts of disposal and attributes.

The sentence is a summary and a conclusion produced by the preceding proofs, and for this reason it is separated (by no conjunction).

The demonstrative pronoun is used to distinguish the possessor of those attributes from others, in a manner that leads to what follows the demonstrative, in the manner established in His words, "Those are upon guidance from their Lord" [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: That One who created, subjected, originated people and livestock, and created man in stages, is Allah; so do not associate with Him anything else, since no doubt remains that could excuse the people of association for their association. That is, His affair does not resemble the state of your other gods. He said, "Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?" [al-Ra'd: 16].

The use of His proper name is to bring the named object to mind in people's minds by a particular name, as an added clarification, because the state of the addressees was treated as the state of one who does not know that the doer of those great acts is Allah Most High.

The proper name of Allah is the predicate of the demonstrative pronoun, and His words "your Lord" are an attribute of the name of Allah.

Page 336

Describing Him with lordship (rububiyyah) is a reminder to them of the blessing of existence and sustenance, which is the meaning of lordship, and a preparation for the record against them of ingratitude for His blessing, which comes in His words, "If you are ungrateful, then indeed Allah is free of need of you, and He does not approve for His servants disbelief" [al-Zumar: 7].

The sentence "to Him belongs dominion" is a second predicate of the demonstrative pronoun.

Mulk (dominion): its origin is the verbal noun of malaka, and it may be read with any of the three vowels on the mim, but the Arabic usage has restricted the mim with a damma to the sovereignty over lands and the governance of people, and in this sense came His words, "You give dominion to whom You will, and You strip dominion from whom You will" [Al 'Imran: 26]. Its possessor is malik, with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, and its plural is muluk.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to convey a claimed restriction (hasr ida'i): dominion belongs to Allah and not to other than Him. As for the dominion of kings, it is deficient and exposed to extinction, so it is like non-existence, as has been mentioned in His words, "Praise be to Allah," and in the Hadith of the Resurrection: "Then He will say, 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?'" Divinity is therefore the true dominion, and for this reason their claim of partners to the true God was an error, so the claimed restriction serves to refute the claim of the polytheists.

The sentence "There is no deity except Him" is an explanation of the restrictive sentence in His words, "to Him belongs dominion."

Hence, on this basis, comes a rhetorical question of denunciation regarding their turning away from the Tawhid (Oneness) of God, the Exalted. Since turning away (al-inṣirāf) is a state, it is questioned with the word "anná," which here carries the meaning of "how," as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [al-An'am: 101].

Al-ṣarf means to turn something away from something. The object from which they are turned here is omitted; its estimated form is "from His Tawhid," by the indication of His saying ﴿There is no god but Him﴾.

He made them turned away from Tawhid without mentioning any agent turning them away. Thus He used the passive verb and did not say "so where do you turn yourselves?" This is a reproach against them, that they are like those led toward disbelief, not independent in their affairs, whom the turners-away turn aside, meaning the leaders of disbelief or the devils who whisper to them. This is a stirring of their souls, so that they would refrain from following their leaders, who say to them ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat: 26], in hope that they would reflect on their own the evidences of Oneness mentioned to them.

Page 337

The meaning: How then can any turner-away turn you from His Tawhid after you have known the evidences that have just preceded?

The present tense here is intended to indicate the time of the future, by the indication of its being made a consequence of the evidences that came before it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you. And He does not approve disbelief for His servants; and if you are grateful, He approves it for you.﴾ This follows the denunciation of their turning away from the Tawhid of Allah after the proofs of its establishment had become manifest to them, by informing them that their disbelief, if they persist in it, does not harm Allah but only harms themselves.

This is the beginning of warning and threat to the disbelievers, set against encouragement and glad tidings for the believers. The sentence is therefore a fresh (mustanaf'a) statement that stands in the position of a conclusion to what preceded concerning the establishment of Allah's Oneness in divinity.

The clause ﴿If you disbelieve﴾ explains the denunciation of their turning away from Tawhid. That is: if you disbelieve after this time, then know that Allah is free of need of you. Its meaning is that He is free of need of your affirmation of His Oneness, that is, He is not dependent upon it. This is a kinaya (an allusive expression) indicating that the demand for Tawhid from them is for their own benefit and for averting harm from them, not for Allah's benefit. They are reminded of this so that they will turn to reflect on the proofs of Tawhid. The statement is used in the sense of a kinaya to alert the addressee to the error of his action.

His saying ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) between the two conditionals, intended as a safeguard lest the hearers suppose that Allah takes no notice of their disbelief and pays it no heed, so that they might imagine that disbelief and gratitude are equal in His sight. Through this, the meaning of using the statement to alert the addressee to his error is further emphasized.

From this it becomes determined that what is meant by His saying "for His servants" (li-'ibadihi) is the servants to whom the address was directed in His saying ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾. This accords with the usual linguistic usage of the word 'ibad, as in His saying ﴿And on the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah, and He says: "Did you lead these My servants astray, or did they themselves stray from the path?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 17], and so on. Although in the Qur'an the word 'ibad, when attributed to the Name of Allah or to His pronoun, generally refers to the specific believers and those brought near (to Him), the contextual indication here is manifest, more manifest than its indication in His saying ﴿Did you lead these My servants astray?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17].

The root meaning of riḍā (approval) is a psychological state that follows the attainment of something agreeable, accompanied by delight in it. In reality, it has a meaning that is not the same as that of irada (will), because it involves approbation and delight, and it is expressed by abstaining from objection. For this reason, approval is contrasted with anger (sukhṭ), and will is contrasted with compulsion (ikrah). Approval ultimately tends toward the meaning of love (maḥabba).

Approval entails that the approved object is precious in the eyes of the one who approves, and that he prefers and chooses it. When approval is attributed to Allah, the intended meaning must be the necessary consequence of its literal meaning, because Allah is exalted above emotional states, just as is the case with the attribution to Him of verbs and attributes that in language indicate emotional states, such as al-Raḥmān (the Most Merciful) and al-Ra'ūf (the Compassionate), and the attribution of anger, joy and love. Thus, approval is interpreted by its consequence: honour, care and recompense if it is related to people, and preciousness and excellence if it is related to abstract qualities. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) interpreted it as choice, in his commentary on the saying of the Exalted ﴿And I have approved Islam for you as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], in the Surah of al-'Uqud (Surah al-Ma'idah).

The verb riḍā is commonly transitive with the particle "'an" (from), and so it governs a concrete noun, but on account of a meaning in it which is the cause of approval. It may also be transitive with the particle "bi" (with), in which case it commonly governs an abstract noun, as in: "I approved of the judgment of So-and-so." It may govern a concrete noun on account of a meaning indicated by a specification (tamyiz) following it, as in: "I approved of Allah as Lord," or similar expressions, such as His saying ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]; or by a contextual indication, as in the saying of the Quraysh regarding the placing of the Black Stone: "This is Muhammad, we are content with him," meaning, we are content with him as an arbiter, since they had agreed to make the first person to enter the arbiter.

It may also be transitive without a preposition, and perhaps this is understood through implication (tadmin) or through omission and attachment (al-hadhf wa al-iṣal). In this case it commonly governs an abstract noun, as in: "I approved of the judgment of So-and-so," meaning: "I loved his judgment." In this case it may be transitive to a second object by means of the prepositional lam (for), as in His saying ﴿And I have approved Islam for you as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], meaning: I approved it for your sake and loved it for you, that is, for your benefit and advantage.

In this construction there is an intensification in extolling the approved thing to the hearer, to the extent that the speaker seems to approve it for the sake of the hearer.

Now, if His saying "for His servants" is general and not specific, and it is among the forms of generality, a problem has arisen in this verse among the theologians concerning the relation of Allah's will to the actions of the servants. For it is necessarily known that among the servants of Allah there are many disbelievers, and Allah the Exalted has informed that He does not approve disbelief for His servants, and it has been established by proof that everything that occurs is willed by Allah the Exalted, since nothing occurs in His dominion except what He wills. From this, by the third figure of syllogism (al-shakl al-thalith), the following results: the disbelief of the disbeliever is willed by Allah the Exalted, by His saying ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ [al-An'am: 112]; and no part of disbelief is approved by Allah the Exalted, by His saying ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants.﴾ The conclusion of the syllogism is: some of what Allah wills is not approved by Him.

Therefore it is necessary that will and approval be two distinct realities, and that their two terms not be synonymous. For this reason Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said: will is other than approval, and approval is other than will and volition (mashi'a). Will and volition have one meaning, and approval, love and choice have one meaning. This is an interpretation of these Qur'anic terms in meanings with which the verses can be reconciled. Al-Taftazani said: this is the position of the people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq).

On this is built the discussion of the relation of the divine attributes to the actions of the servants. His saying ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾ refers to the address of the legal obligations (khiṭab al-takalif al-shar'iyya), and His saying ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ [al-An'am: 112] refers to the relation of will to bringing into existence and creation. From the combination of these two, and from the combination of their counterparts, arises the belief that the servants have acquisition (kasb) in their voluntary actions, and that Allah's will relates to the creation of those voluntary actions at the moment the servant's acquisition is directed toward them. Thus Allah is the creator of the servant's actions without acquiring them, and the servant is an acquirer without being a creator. For acquisition, according to al-Ash'ari, is the capacity (istita'a), explained by him as the soundness of the causes and instruments of the act. It is an intermediate position between capacity (qudra) and compulsion (jabr): that is, it falls short of the relation of capacity and exceeds the subjugation of compulsion. This reconciles the religious proofs which declare that Allah is over all things powerful, and that He is the creator of all things, with the evidence of necessity which distinguishes between the movement of one who trembles and the movement of one who walks. It also reconciles the proofs of the general scope of power with the Sharia's addressing servants with commands to faith and righteous deeds, and prohibitions against disbelief and evil deeds, and with the establishment of reward and punishment.

As for those who saw the identity of the meanings of will, volition and approval, which is the view of many of the followers of al-Ash'ari and of all the Maturidis, they followed in interpreting the verse the reading of the word "for His servants" as general with a specific sense (al-'amm al-makhsus), that is, for His believing servants. They found support for this reading in the fact that it accords with the usual usage of the Qur'an in the word 'ibad when attributed to the Name of Allah or to His pronoun, as in His saying ﴿A spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6]. They said: whoever disbelieves, Allah has willed his disbelief, and whoever believes, Allah has willed his belief. Both groups, the Ash'aris and the Maturidis, upheld the principle regarding the relation of Allah's will and power to the voluntary actions of the servants, called acquisition, and they differed only regarding the attribution of the actions to the servants: whether it is real or metaphorical. The disagreement over the analogy of the actions between the two groups has been counted as merely verbal.

It is remarkable that al-Zamakhshari exaggerated this view, saying: "Some deviants have strained to establish for Allah what He has negated of Himself, namely approval of disbelief, and said: this is of the general that is intended to be specific, etc." Thus the end of his statement contradicts its beginning. Is interpretation to be considered misguidance, or is a general statement specified by evidence among the rare exceptions?

As for the Mu'tazila, they are far removed from all of this, because they affirm capacity for the servants over their actions, and hold that the actions of the servants are not within Allah's power. They interpret what is reported in the Book concerning the attribution of actions of the servants to Allah or to His power as meaning that He is the creator of their roots and causes. They take what is reported of the negation of this, as in His saying ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾, in its literal sense. For this reason they cited this verse as evidence. Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) cited it in al-Irshad, in a section in which he gathered what the Mu'tazila used as evidence from the apparent meanings of the Book.

His saying ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿If you disbelieve﴾. The meaning is: and if you are grateful after this admonition, so that you desist from disbelief and thank Allah by acknowledging His Oneness and His transcendence, He approves gratitude for you, that is, He recompenses you with the necessary consequences of approval. Gratitude is constituted of belief, speech and action, in return for a blessing received by the grateful person from the one thanked.

The pronoun in the accusative in His saying "yarḍahu" (He approves it) refers to the gratitude derived from the verb "in tashkurū" (if you are grateful).

* * *

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾. The occasion of this verse appears to be that when the previous verse mentioned that among those addressed there are a disbeliever and a grateful one, and they were in the same city, with ties of kinship and allegiance between them, the believers might have feared to be touched by sin on account of the disbelief of their relatives and allies. Or they feared that Allah might afflict the disbelievers with punishment in this world, and that it would reach those residing with them in Mecca. So Allah informed them that the disbelief of those does not diminish the faith of these, and He intended to reassure them concerning themselves.

The root of wizr, with a kasra on the waw, is weight, and it is applied to sin because the one who bears it suffers fatigue like that of one who carries a load. It is said: "wazira" in the sense of carrying a burden, and in the sense of earning sin.

The feminine forms of "wāzira" and "ukhrā" are based on considering the meaning of soul (nafs), as in His saying ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

The meaning is: no soul bears the burden of another soul, that is, no soul relieves another soul of any part of its sin. Therefore no soul should hope for help from its own kin and relatives. Likewise, a righteous soul should not fear being held to account for the consequence of another soul from among its kin or relatives. In this there is an allusion to disengagement and to ending contention with the polytheists, and that the utmost duty of the believers is to guide the misguided, not to compel them to faith, as was stated earlier at the end of Surah al-An'am.

* * *

﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts.﴾ The particle "thumma" (then) here indicates sequence in rank and temporal delay: that is, and greater than Allah's being free of need of you is that He has prepared for you the recompense for your disbelief, and you will return to Him. A parallel to it occurred at the end of Surah al-An'am.

In the verse of al-An'am it came as ﴿of that wherein you used to differ﴾ [al-An'am: 164], because it came after many verses that contained the differing between the states of the believers and the states of the polytheists, and nothing like that has come here. Therefore it is said here ﴿of what you used to do﴾, that is, of the disbelief of the one who disbelieved and the gratitude of the one who was grateful.

The word "al-anbā'" (to inform) is used figuratively for manifestation by which knowledge is attained. It may also be used in the literal sense of informing, by making known to them their deeds through the angels. The meaning is: He manifests the truth to you without doubt, or informs you of it directly. Its explanation has preceded at the end of al-An'am, and in it there is an allusion to promise and threat.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of the contents of the breasts﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ [al-An'am: 60], because one who knows the contents of the breasts leaves nothing unknown to Him. So when He informs them of their deeds, His informing is complete.

Wa-dhat (feminine of *dhū*, meaning "possessor of"), a *ṣifah* (qualifying adjective) for a *maḥdhūf* (elided word). Its estimated sense is: "the deeds," i.e., "with deeds possessing the breasts," meaning those that are lodged in intentions. He used "*al-ṣudūr*" (breasts) to express what dwells in them. By *al-ṣudūr* is meant the hearts, which are used to express that by which perception and resolve occur. This was already mentioned in His words, ﴿But God has spared [you]; indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Anfal: 43], in Surat al-Anfal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 8:

﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to Allah, to lead (others) astray from His way.﴾ This is an example of the vacillation of the polytheists between their associating others with Allah in worship, and their showing their need of Him; and this is a sign of the extent and utmost limit of their disbelief.

The sentence is joined (grammatically) to the sentence ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion﴾ [az-Zumar: 6] and what follows it, because both sentences share the indication that Allah alone is the one who disposes of affairs and deserves thanks, and that disbelief in Him is ugly. It also includes an argument for the Oneness of His divinity from the state of the polytheists who associate others with Him: when harm touches them, they turn to Him alone, and when a favor reaches them, they turn away from giving Him thanks and make for Him partners.

The definite article in "al-insan" (the man) is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), but its generality here is a customary generality (ʿumum ʿurfi) referring to a group of mankind, namely the people of polytheism specifically, because His saying ﴿and set up rivals to Allah﴾ does not agree with the state of the believers.

The view that the intended referent is a specific individual, namely ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a or Abu Jahl, departs from the course of the discourse; rather, these two and their like are among this category. The mention of "al-insan" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, because the intended addressees are those mentioned in His saying ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾ [az-Zumar: 6] up to His saying ﴿then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ [az-Zumar: 7]. So the apparent form would have been to say, "And when harm touches you, you call upon your Lord," etc. He shifted to the explicit noun because of what the meaning of "man" (insan) carries of taking into account the human nature's fluctuation and instability, except for whomever Allah protects with success, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And man says, "When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66] and His saying ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3], and other than that. Also, because in the name "insan" there is a correspondence with the forgetting mentioned in His saying ﴿he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before﴾.

A parallel to this verse has already occurred in His saying ﴿And when harm touches the people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [ar-Rum: 33] in Surat ar-Rum.

Al-takhwil (التخويل): giving and granting ownership without seeking a return. Its middle radical is necessarily a waw. It is derived from al-khawal, with two fathas, which is the name for servants and attendants. There is no consideration of the verb khala meaning "to boast," for that is a different root, other than that from which the verb khawwala is derived.

Al-nisyan (النسيان): the absence of the memory's retention of a matter previously known.

The referent of "ma" in His saying ﴿he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before﴾ is the harm, that is: he forgets the harm for which he had been calling upon Allah, i.e., for its removal from him. The object of "yad'u" is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿he called upon his Lord﴾, and the pronoun in "ilayhi" refers back to "ma", meaning: he forgot the harm for which he had been calling upon Allah, i.e., for its removal.

It is also permissible for "ma" to refer to the supplication, as the relative clause indicates, with the pronoun governed by "ila" referring back to "rabbihi", meaning: he forgot the supplication. The supplication was here construed with the meaning of entreaty and humble submission, so it took the preposition "ila".

The returning pronoun of the relative clause is omitted, indicated by the relative clause's verb, to avoid repetition of pronouns. The meaning: he forgot the worship of Allah and the entreaty to Him.

Al-andad: the plural of nidd, with a kasra on the nun, which is an equal or peer, meaning: he added to forgetting his Lord by making for Him partners.

The lam in His saying ﴿so that he may mislead (others) from His way﴾ is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), that is, the metaphorical lam of causation, because misguidance, being the result of the making of rivals, made it permissible to attribute the making to it, as if it were the cause for the one who makes. The meaning: he made for Allah rivals, which strayed (others) from the way of Allah.

The majority read "liyudilla" with a damma on the ya', meaning: that he may mislead people after he himself had gone astray, since none misleads people except one who is astray. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ya', meaning: that he himself may mislead, i.e., the one who makes the rivals, and he, when he goes astray, misleads people.

* * *

﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."﴾ This is an explanatory resumptive sentence, because the mention of the condition of the disbelieving man who turns away from thanking his Lord prompts the listener to ask about the end of this disbeliever. That is: say, O Muhammad, to the man who made rivals for Allah, i.e., say to each one of that category; or the singular was observed in respect of the word "insan." The implied meaning: say, "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."

On the same two considerations comes the singular of the second-person pronoun after the report about "man" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Man will say on that Day, "Where is the escape?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10] ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11] ﴿To your Lord, that Day, is the place of rest﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 12] in Surat al-Qiyamah.

Al-tamatto' (التمتع): benefiting for a limited time. It has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And for you on earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24] in Surat al-A'raf.

The "ba'" in "bi-kufrika" is either for location (zarfiyyah) or for accompaniment (lil-mulabasah), and it is not for making the verb of enjoyment transitive. The object of the enjoyment is omitted, indicated by the context of threat. The implied meaning: enjoy safety from punishment during the time of your disbelief, or, gaining through your disbelief a little enjoyment; then you are heading toward punishment, because you are of the companions of the Fire.

The description of the enjoyment as "little" is because the duration of the life of this world is little in comparison with the punishment in the Hereafter, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then the enjoyment of this worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but little﴾ [at-Tawbah: 38].

The imperative form in His saying "tamatta'" is used for granting respite, the intended purpose of which is warning and threat.

The sentence ﴿indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾ explains the intended meaning of the sentence ﴿enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾, which is the warning of the destination to the Fire after the duration of the life of this world.

"Min" (من) is partitive, because the polytheists are a part of the nations and groups who are sentenced to remain eternally in the Fire.

Ashab al-nar (أصحاب النار, "the companions of the Fire") are those who never depart from it, for companionship implies constancy; so "the companions of the Fire" means those who abide forever therein.

﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord...﴾

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hamzah alone read ﴿أمَن﴾ (*amman*) with a light *mim*, on the basis that the interrogative hamzah (*hamzat al-istifham*, the interrogative particle "a") entered upon the relative pronoun ﴿مَن﴾ (*man*, "one who"). On this reading, the hamzah may be the interrogative hamzah, and ﴿مَن﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is omitted, its meaning being indicated by the preceding context, namely the mention of the disbeliever in His saying ﴿وجَعَلَ لِلَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾ ("and he sets up rivals to God," 39:8) up to His saying ﴿مِن أصْحابِ النّارِ﴾ ("among the companions of the Fire," 39:8). The interrogation is then one of denunciation (*istifham inkari*), and the indication that denunciation is intended is that it is followed by His saying ﴿قُلْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ والَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal?" 39:9), since it is evident that ﴿هَلْ﴾ (*hal*) here is the particle of denunciatory interrogation, and also by the relative clause (*silat al-mawsul*). Its estimated form is: "Is the one who is devoutly obedient better, or the one who is a disbeliever?" The interrogation is then one of confirmation (*istifham taqriri*), and for it an omitted counterpart (*mu'adil*) is estimated, indicated by his statement following it: ﴿قُلْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ والَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾.

Al-Farra' made the hamzah a particle of address (*lil-nida'*), and ﴿مَن هو قانِتٌ﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ): God addressed him with the four great attributes, because they are his attributes, and it is an address to those who share these attributes, meaning the believers, that they should say: "Are those who know and those who do not know equal?" On this view, the singular ﴿قُلْ﴾ (*qul*, "say") is in keeping with the wording of ﴿مَن﴾ as the one addressed.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿أمَّنْ هو قانِتٌ﴾ with the *mim* of ﴿مَن﴾ doubled, on the basis that it is a compound word from two words, ﴿أمْ﴾ (*am*) and ﴿مَن﴾, and the *mim* of ﴿أمْ﴾ was assimilated into the *mim* of ﴿مَن﴾. As to its meaning there are two possibilities:

The first: that ﴿أمْ﴾ is a conjunction (*mu'adilah*) corresponding to an omitted interrogative hamzah together with its clause, which ﴿أمْ﴾ indicates, since it requires a counterpart. This is indicated by his statement following it, ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ والَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, because equality is only between two things. The estimated meaning is: "Is this one who sets up rivals to God, the disbeliever, better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" The interrogation is then real, and what is intended is its consequence, which is to draw attention to the error upon reflection.

[Page 346]

The second: that ﴿أمْ﴾ is disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), serving merely as a transitional turning away (*al-idrab al-intiqali*). ﴿أمْ﴾ requires an estimated interrogation after it. The meaning of the discourse is: "Leave off threatening them with the punishment of the Fire, and move on with them to this question: Who is one who is devoutly obedient, standing, wary of God, and hoping for His mercy?" The meaning is: "Is that human being, who set up rivals to God, one who is devoutly obedient, etc.?" The interrogation is used in mockery (*al-tahakkum*), since it is evident that those four attributes do not agree with the attribute of "setting up rivals to God."

Al-qanit (the devoutly obedient) is the worshipper. It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿وقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قانِتِينَ﴾ ("and stand before God in devout obedience," 2:238) in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ana' (the hours) is the plural of *anan* (or *ana*), like *am'a'* and *ma'an*, and *aqfa'* and *qafan*. *Al-anan* means "the time"; it is also said *inan*, with a kasra on the hamzah, as already discussed at His saying ﴿غَيْرَ ناظِرِينَ إناهُ﴾ ("waiting not for its time," 33:53) in Surat al-Ahzab.

﴿آناءَ﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*) governed by ﴿قانِتٌ﴾. The specification of the night for their devout obedience is because worship at night is more helpful in purifying the heart for the remembrance of God, further from the intrusion of showing off (*riya'*), and more indicative of preferring the worship of God over the soul's share of rest and sleep; for the night is more inclined to seek rest. When a person prefers worship during it, his heart is illumined with love of drawing near to God, the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ ناشِئَةَ اللَّيْلِ هي أشَدُّ وطْئًا وأقْوَمُ قِيلًا﴾ ("Indeed, the rising at night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech," 73:6). Therefore the mention of the night specifically indicates, by the implication of the address (*dalalat fahwa al-khitab*), that this devoutly obedient one does not lack prostration and standing during the hours of the day as well. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿إنَّ لَكَ في النَّهارِ سَبْحًا﴾ ("Indeed, for you by day is a long stretch of occupation," 73:7). By this the application of this relative clause to the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) is completed.

His saying ﴿ساجِدًا وقائِمًا﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (*hal*) explaining ﴿قانِتٌ﴾ and emphasizing its meaning. The clause ﴿يَحْذَرُ الآخِرَةَ ويَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ﴾ is also a circumstantial clause. The first and second circumstances describe his outward deeds, while the two clauses which are the third and fourth describe the deeds of his heart: that he is between fear of his evil deeds and his slips, and hope for the mercy of his Lord that He reward him for his good deeds.

In this is the complete contrast between the state of the believers, conforming to the state of their Prophet (ﷺ), and the state of the people of polytheism (*shirk*), who call upon God only at rare moments, which are the moments of necessity, and then associate partners with Him after that. They have no concern except for the immediate life of this world; they do not beware of the Hereafter nor hope for its reward.

Al-raja' (hope) is, according to the way-farers (*maqamat al-salikin*, the stations of those travelling the spiritual path), fear. That is, their attributes which do not change.

Al-raja' is awaiting what contains bliss and agreeableness to the soul. Al-khawf (fear) is awaiting what is disagreeable to the soul. What is meant here is agreeableness in the Hereafter, corresponding to His saying ﴿يَحْذَرُ الآخِرَةَ﴾, that is, he fears the punishment of the Hereafter. Thus it is determined that hope too is what is desired in the Hereafter.

Fear has its distinction in restraining the soul from what does not please God, and hope has its distinction in urging it toward what pleases God. Both are a companion (*anis*) of the way-farers.

Hope arises only upon the presence of its causes, because a person does not hope for anything except what he supposes to be attained, and a person does not suppose a matter except when its indications and necessary consequences appear to him, since supposition is not deception, and a person does not deceive himself. Hope therefore follows striving to attain what is hoped for. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿ومَن أرادَ الآخِرَةَ وسَعى لَها سَعْيَها وهو مُؤْمِنٌ فَأُولَئِكَ كانَ سَعْيُهم مَشْكُورًا﴾ ("And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving while he is a believer, those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated," 17:19). For a person's anticipation of benefit without its causes is called delusion (*ghurur*).

Hope or fear is only supposition, accompanied by doubt regarding what is supposed. As for what is definitively established, it is certainty (*yaqin*) and despair (*yas*), and both are blameworthy. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَلا يَأْمَنُ مَكْرَ اللَّهِ إلّا القَوْمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾ ("None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people," 7:99), and He said: ﴿إنَّهُ لا يَيْأسُ مِن رَوْحِ اللَّهِ إلّا القَوْمُ الكافِرُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, no one despairs of relief from God except the disbelieving people," 12:87).

Hujjat al-Islam Abu Hamid (al-Ghazali) expounded this in the Book of Hope and Fear from the *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din*. How excellent was Abu al-Hasan al-Tihami when he said:

"And if you hope for the impossible, you are only building hope on the edge of a crumbling precipice."

Al-Hasan al-Basri was asked about a man who persists in sins yet hopes, and he said: "This is wishful thinking (*tamanni*); true hope is His saying: ﴿يَحْذَرُ الآخِرَةَ ويَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ﴾."

Some exegetes said that ﴿مَن هو قانِتٌ﴾ refers to Abu Bakr; it was also said to refer to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and it was said to refer to Abu Dharr, and it was said to refer to Ibn Mas'ud. These are weak reports (*riwayat da'ifah*). Undoubtedly, these individuals are among those most deserving of this relative clause, so it includes them; but the sense of the relative pronoun in the verse is to generalize to everyone to whom the meaning of the relative clause applies.

* * *

﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal? Only those of understanding remember.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), whose position is like the position of ﴿قُلْ تَمَتَّعْ بِكُفْرِكَ قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Say: Enjoy your disbelief for a little while," 39:8). It was prompted by the description of the believer who obeys. The meaning: "Inform them, O Muhammad, that this believer who knows the right of his Lord is not equal to the disbeliever who is ignorant of his Lord."

The repetition of the verb ﴿قُلْ﴾ here is for the sake of emphasis on this spoken matter and to draw ears to it.

The interrogation here is used in denunciation. The intended meaning is the affirmation of the inequality between the two groups, and inequality is used as a metonymy for superiority. What is meant is the superiority of those who know over those who do not know, like His saying: ﴿لا يَسْتَوِي القاعِدُونَ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ غَيْرِ أُولِي الضَّرَرِ والمُجاهِدُونَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ بِأمْوالِهِمْ وأنْفُسِهِمْ فَضَّلَ اللَّهُ المُجاهِدِينَ﴾ ("Not equal are those believers who sit [at home] other than those with a disability and those who strive in the cause of God with their wealth and their lives. God has preferred the strivers," 4:95). Or it is by the context, as in His saying here, ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ etc., since it is evident that knowledge is a perfection, and because it is followed by His saying: ﴿إنَّما يَتَذَكَّرُ أُولُو الألْبابِ﴾. For this reason the negation of equality in this verse is more eloquent than the negation of similarity in the words of al-Nabigha:

"One of their nobles informs you about me, and their learned one; and the one ignorant of a thing is not like the one who knows."

The verb ﴿يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ in both places is treated as intransitive (*munazzal manzilat al-lazim*), so no object is mentioned for it. The meaning is: those who are characterized by the attribute of knowledge. What is not meant is those who know some specific thing, such that it would be an ellipsis of the two objects for brevity, since that is not the meaning intended. This is shown by His statement following it, ﴿إنَّما يَتَذَكَّرُ أُولُو الألْبابِ﴾, that is, the people of intellect. Intellect and knowledge are synonymous. That is, those who possess knowledge, who perceive the realities of things as they are and whose actions proceed in accordance with their knowledge, are not equal to those who do not know, who do not perceive things as they are, but for whom realities are confused and whose actions proceed without order. This is like the state of those who imagined stones to be gods and placed disbelief in the place of gratitude.

Thus it is determined that the meaning is: "Not equal are the one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, wary of his Lord and hoping in Him, and the one who sets up rivals to God in order to lead astray from His path." Since it has been established that those who set up rivals to God are the disbelievers, by the ruling of His saying ﴿قُلْ تَمَتَّعْ بِكُفْرِكَ قَلِيلًا﴾, it is established that those who are not equal to them are the believers, that is, they are superior to them. And since it has been established that the disbelievers are among the companions of the Fire, it follows that those who are preferred over them are among the companions of Paradise.

He turned away from saying "Are this one and that one equal?" to the expression by the relative pronoun, as an integrating praise of one group and censure of another, that the people of faith are the people of knowledge and the people of polytheism are the people of ignorance. The sentence, with what it contains of integration, sufficed in place of two sentences. Thus, those who know are the people of faith; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿إنَّما يَخْشى اللَّهَ مِن عِبادِهِ العُلَماءُ﴾ ("Only those fear God among His servants who have knowledge," 35:28). And those who do not know are the people of polytheism, the ignorant; He, the Exalted, said: ﴿قُلْ أفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ تَأْمُرُونِّي أعْبُدُ أيُّها الجاهِلُونَ﴾ ("Say: Is it other than God you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?" 39:64).

In this is an indication that faith is a sibling of knowledge, because both are light and true recognition, and that disbelief is a sibling of misguidance, because it and misguidance are darkness and vain delusions.

Furthermore, the occurrence of the verb ﴿يَسْتَوِي﴾ within the scope of negation gives it generality of negation for all aspects of equality. Since the negation of equality was a metonymy for superiority, it led to the affirmation of superiority for those who know in a general manner. For you will not reflect upon any situation in which a learned person and an ignorant person are involved without finding that the learned one has in it of happiness what you will not find for the ignorant one. Let us illustrate this with six situations which constitute most of the functions of social life.

The first situation: reaching the object desired to be obtained by acting upon it, which is the situation of action. The one who knows a thing is guided to its ways, and so attains the goal with ease and in proximity, and knows which of the actions is more worthy of undertaking. Whereas one who does not know it loses its paths and wastes his time in seeking it; either he fails in his effort, or he attains it only after being tossed about by misfortunes and afflicted by calamities, and realities become confused for him, so that he may imagine that he has reached the goal until, when he wakes up, he finds himself in other than his intended aim. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أعْمالُهم كَسَرابٍ بِقِيعَةٍ يَحْسَبُهُ الظَّمْآنُ ماءً حَتّى إذا جاءَهُ لَمْ يَجِدْهُ شَيْئًا﴾ ("And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert which the thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing," 24:39).

[Page 350]

For this reason it has become common to liken knowledge to light and ignorance to darkness.

The second situation: which arises from the first, namely the situation of safety from the calamities of error and the slips of humiliations. The one who knows is protected from that by his knowledge, while the ignorant one seeks safety and falls into ruin, for error may lead to destruction from the very direction of seeking success. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾ ("So their commerce did not profit," 2:16), where He likened them to a merchant who went out seeking profits from his trade and returned with loss. For this reason the effort of the ignorant one is likened to blundering in darkness (*khabt al-'ashwa'*). Therefore the people of counsel have never ceased to facilitate for students of knowledge the means which protect them from falling into what has no benefit in their actions.

The Fourth Station: the independence from people in proportion to knowledge and what is known. Whenever the knowledge of the scholar increases, his independence from people grows stronger, in his religion and in his worldly affairs.

The Fifth Station: the enjoyment of knowledge. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) restricted pleasure to the pursuit of knowledge; it is a pleasure that abundance does not cut off. God has given an example through shade when He said: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir: 19] ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir: 20] ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ [Fatir: 21]. For people of hot lands take pleasure in sitting in the shade.

The Sixth Station: the emergence of beneficial works throughout one's lifetime, which earns the praise of people in this world and the reward of God in the next. The scholar is a source of guidance and knowledge, a guide to goodness and a leader towards it. God the Exalted said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. Knowledge, in its practice, carries a great reward. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No people gather in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book of God and studying it among themselves, except that the angels descend upon them, mercy covers them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him."

The same applies to its dissemination. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge which he spread among people, and a righteous child who prays for him."

This difference between the scholar and the ignorant in the forms that we have mentioned is included in the negation of equality found in His saying: ﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know alike?﴾ Numerous branches spring from these stations, and although they are many, they all fall under the meaning of this verse.

His saying ﴿Only those of understanding will remember﴾ comes in the position of a causal explanation for the negation of equality between the scholar and others. Its intended purpose is the preference of the scholar and of knowledge. The word ﴿innama﴾ ("only") is composed of two particles, ﴿in﴾ and the ﴿ma﴾ which is either the restrictive (kafffa) or the negating particle. So the ﴿in﴾ in it conveys causal explanation of what precedes it, serving the function of the causal fa' (fa' al-ta'lil), since there is no difference between the single ﴿in﴾ and ﴿inna﴾ combined with ﴿ma﴾. Rather, the combination adds further emphasis, namely the negation of the ruling that ﴿inna﴾ affirms from anyone other than the one to whom it is affirmed.

In explaining this, the side of affirming remembrance for those of knowledge is taken, and its negation for others is expressed by way of restriction, because the side of remembrance is the side of religious practice, which is the most important aim in Islam, since through it comes the purification of the soul and eternal happiness. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whomever God intends good for, He gives him understanding in religion."

Al-albab (الألباب) means the intellects, and ulu al-albab (أولو الألباب) are the people of sound intellects, and they are the people of knowledge. Since the people of knowledge are the only people of remembrance, the verse conveys the non-equality of those who know and those who do not know. Thus, His saying ﴿Only those of understanding will remember﴾ is not an independent statement.

[Page 352]

When praise was bestowed upon the believers for their devotion to the worship of God in the most demanding hours, their intense vigilance (muraqabah) of Him through fear and hope, and their distinction through the qualities of knowledge, reason, and remembrance, in contrast to the state of the polytheists in all of this, it was followed by the command to the Messenger of God ﷺ to address them, in order to increase their steadfastness and firmness of heart. The implied sense is: "Say to the believers." This is indicated by the context of His words ﴿O My servants who believe﴾ and so on.

The beginning of the speech with the command to "say" follows the same approach as in a similar instance mentioned just before. The beginning of what is said with the vocative and with the description of servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah), attributed to the pronoun of God the Exalted, all of this indicates attention to what is about to be said, and that it will be said to them on behalf of their Lord. This places them in the station of being directly addressed by God, which is a great rank.

The first-person pronoun suffix (yāʾ al-mutakallim) attached to "ʿibād" has been omitted. This is a common usage in the vocative construction with a first-person pronoun suffix. The Ten Readers (al-ʿashara) read "yā ʿibād" without the yāʾ, both in continuous recitation (waṣl) and in pause (waqf), as in Ibrāz al-Maʿānī by Abū Shāmah, and as in al-Durrah al-Muḍiyyah fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Thalāth al-Mutammimah lil-ʿAshr by ʿAlī al-Ḍabbāʿ al-Miṣrī. This contrasts with His words ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], which come later in this surah. The difference between them is merely a matter of stylistic variation (tafannun). This difference may be explained by the fact that those addressed in this verse are the God-fearing servants of God, so their belonging to God is established, and therefore the pronoun of majesty in their attribution to Him was dispensed with. By contrast, in the later verse, the word "yā ʿibād" in this verse has only one reading, agreed upon by the Ten Readers, and for this reason the scribes of the Muṣḥaf wrote it without a yāʾ after the dāl.

What occurs in the tafsir of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, where he says: "The majority of the reciters read ‘Say: O My servants’ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ. Abū ʿAmr also, and ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, and Ibn Kathīr read ‘yā ʿibād’ without a yāʾ in continuous recitation," is an error (sahw). The reciters differed only over the later verse ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] in this surah, for in it the yāʾ of the first person is retained, and they differed over it as we will mention.

Enjoining taqwā is intended to mean persistence in what is commanded, because they were already God-fearing before. It also indicates that some harm in religion had befallen them, such that there was concern they might fall short in their taqwā.

This command is a preparation for what will be directed to them regarding the order to emigrate (hijrah) for safety from harm to their religion, which is what is alluded to in His words ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾.

Bringing them to mind through the relative pronoun and its clause indicates that the firm establishment of their faith requires taqwā and compliance with emigration. The clause ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ and what is conjoined to it is an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī), because the mention of the command to taqwā addressed to those who already possess it raises the question of a questioner about the purpose of that command. Its explanation is then given by His words ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾. However, His words ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ were placed as a preparation for it, with the aim of hastening the guarantee to them of a good outcome in their emigration.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ is presented as a justification (taʿlīl) for the command to taqwā that comes after it.

By "those who do good" is meant those who feared God, namely the believers described by what preceded in His words ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night...﴾ [al-Zumar: 9] and so on, because those qualities indicate the goodness (iḥsān) explained by the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "That you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." So He turned away from the expression in the form of direct address, such as "For you in this world is good," to the use of the explicit relative pronoun "those who do good," so that it would include those addressed and others who possess this attribute. This carries the meaning: "Fear your Lord so that you may become doers of good, for those who do good have a great good, so be among them."

The placing of the predicate first in ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ is for the sake of attention to those who are benefited and to the fact that they are deserving of goodness.

By "good" (ḥasanah) is meant a good condition, and the adjective is used in place of the noun modified, following the pattern of His words ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], and His words in the opposite sense ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shūrā: 40]. The placement of His words ﴿in this world﴾ between ﴿for those who do good﴾ and "good" is an arrangement (naẓm) of the kind particular to the Qur'an in the placement of words, to increase the meanings that the arrangement permits, and this is one of the ways of the Qur'an's inimitability (iʿjāz).

It is therefore possible that His words ﴿in this world﴾ are a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) related to "good," placed before its referent to draw attention from the beginning of the speech that this is their reward in this world, since such a thought rarely comes to their minds. God guaranteed them the hastening of a good reward in this world before the reward of the Hereafter, in the manner of what He praised concerning those who say ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201]. A similar clause appears in Sūrat al-Naḥl, in His words ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ [al-Naḥl: 30], meaning better than the affairs of this world. The restriction to the good of this world in this verse is because it is presented to strengthen the Muslims in what they face of harm, and to command them to emigrate from the abode of polytheism and of trial in religion. As for the reward of the Hereafter, it is a matter already established among them before, and it is alluded to by His words after it ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning﴾, meaning they will be given their reward in the Hereafter. Al-Suddī said: "The good in this world is health and well-being." It is also possible that His words "in this world" are connected to the verb "did good" (aḥsanū) as an adverbial complement (ẓarf lughawī), meaning: "They performed good deeds in this world." In that case the intended meaning is an alert to hastening good deeds in the life of this world before they pass, and an alert against falling short in that.

The nunation of "ḥasanah" is for magnification. With respect to the good of the Hereafter, it is magnification in its essence (taʿẓīm dhātī); with respect to the good of this world, it is magnification by description (taʿẓīm waṣfī), meaning a good greater than what is customary. In either case, the demonstrative in His words ﴿in this world﴾ is to distinguish the thing referred to and to bring it to mind. Accordingly, "ḥasanah" may refer to the good of the Hereafter or to the good of this world, as in His words ﴿And among them is one who says: Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. A parallel to this verse has already been mentioned in Sūrat al-Naḥl, in His words ﴿And it was said to those who feared God: What has your Lord sent down? They said: Good. For those who do good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ [al-Naḥl: 30], so what is established here has been joined to it.

What is conjoined to it is ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾, conjoined as an aim conjoined to a preparatory statement (tawṭiʾah). It is a declarative statement used indirectly (taʿrīḍ) to urge emigration across the land, fleeing with their religion from trials, as indicated by the fact that the spaciousness of the earth is a known matter, whose informing is not the purpose; rather it is used as a metonymy (kināyah) for its necessary implication, as Iyās ibn Qabīṣah al-Ṭāʾī said:

"Did you not see that the earth is wide and vast? Would any patch of its expanses defeat me?"

The better view is that the clause ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), and the waw is parenthetical, because that clause has come to function as a proverb (mathal).

The meaning is: God promised them that they would find good if they emigrated from the lands of polytheism. Good living, or its opposite, is not restricted to a specific place, and what is alluded to here has been stated explicitly in His words ﴿They said: Was not God's earth spacious, so that you could emigrate in it?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 97].

The intended meaning is an allusion to emigration to Abyssinia. Ibn ʿAbbās said regarding His words ﴿O My servants who believe, fear your Lord﴾: he means Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib and those who went out with him to Abyssinia.

The point of the metonymy here is to convey the indication to them with gentleness and reassurance, rather than an explicit command, because leaving one's homeland involves grief for the soul. As for the verse in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, it is a report of the rebuke of the angels to those who did not emigrate.

The placement of the clause ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning﴾ is that of a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to the clause ﴿For those who do good﴾ and what is conjoined to it, because leaving one's homeland, being a stranger, and travel are hardships that only the patient can bear. Therefore the command to it is concluded with the magnification of the reward of the patient, so that it serves as information to those addressed that their reward for it is great, because at that time they are among the patient, whose reward is without reckoning.

Patience (ṣabr) is the calm of the soul upon the arrival of pains and calamities, such that it neither becomes distressed nor agitated by them. It was discussed previously under His words ﴿And give good news to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155] in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The general form in His words "the patient" includes everyone who is patient through hardship in carrying out the obligations of religion, in complying with its commands, and in avoiding its prohibitions. The levels of this patience vary, and the reward varies in accordance with them.

Tawfiyah means giving a thing in full, that is, complete.

Ajr (reward) means the recompense in the Hereafter, as is the established usage of the Qur'an.

His words ﴿without reckoning﴾ are a metonymy for abundance and magnification, because a great quantity is not undertaken to be counted, and a great thing cannot be encompassed by its measure, since encompassing a measure is a form of reckoning. This is the nature of the reward of the Hereafter, which does not occur to the heart of any human being.

In the mention of "fully given" and the attribution of the reward to their pronoun, there is reassurance to them that they deserve it, with no favor (minnah) upon them in it, although favor belongs to God in every case, as in His words ﴿For them is a reward never cut off﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 8].

The restriction derived from "innamā" is directed at the qualifier, which is ﴿without reckoning﴾. The meaning is: "The patient will not be given their reward except without reckoning." This is a corrective restriction (qaṣr qalb), based on overturning the supposition of the patient that the reward of their patience is in proportion to their patience, that is, that their reward does not exceed the measure of the hardship of their patience.

The emigration to Abyssinia took place in the fifth year before the emigration to Medina. Its cause was that the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he saw what his companions suffered of affliction, and that his uncle Abū Ṭālib protected his nephew from the harm of the polytheists but could not protect his companions, said: "If you went out to the land of Abyssinia, for there is a king there under whom no one is wronged, until God brings you relief from what you are in." So most of the Muslims went out, fearing trial, and there went out eighty-three men and nineteen women, apart from their children whom they took with them as young ones. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq had asked the Messenger of God ﷺ for permission to emigrate, and he granted it, so he went out intending the lands of Abyssinia, but Ibn al-Dughunnah met him, turned him back, and placed him under his protection.

Since God's will was tied to spreading Islam in Mecca among the Arabs, for a wisdom that required it, and since some believers were excused for what they suffered of harm in their religion, He permitted them to emigrate. Because His wisdom required that His Messenger ﷺ remain among the polytheists to spread the call of Islam, He did not permit him to emigrate to another homeland until God's purpose was fulfilled in the sprouting of the seed of the religion in that land where His Messenger ﷺ grew up, and the Messenger's move to another city became more conducive to the spread of Islam on earth. Then God permitted His Messenger ﷺ to emigrate to Medina, after He had prepared for him, by His kindness, the entry of its people into Islam. All of this took place by decree, wisdom, and kindness toward His Messenger ﷺ.

[p. 357]

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾ ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ After Allah had commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to address the Muslims by His saying ﴿Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 10], He then commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say a statement which is clearly intended for other than the Muslims.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported from Muqatil: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'What drives you to this religion you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion.﴾"

In truth, if the announcement to the Prophet of this is taken in its plain sense, it is only fitting that it be directed at the polytheists who seek to turn him away from this.

It is also possible that it is directed at the Muslims whom Allah permitted to emigrate to Abyssinia, with the meaning that it is an instruction for him to remain in Mecca and not emigrate with them. The permission given to them to emigrate was for the safety of their religion from trials. Perhaps they were hoping that the Messenger (ﷺ) would emigrate with them to Abyssinia, so the Messenger (ﷺ) informed them that Allah had commanded him to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, i.e., to affirm His oneness in Mecca. Thus the verse would be looking to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists. Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 94]. That is, Allah commanded him to persist in conveying the message in Mecca, for if he had emigrated to Abyssinia, the call would have been cut off. Their emigration to Abyssinia was only a concession (rukhsah) for them, since they were weak in defending their religion against the polytheists, and this concession was not granted to the Prophet (ﷺ).

A statement close to this verse has come after the mention that the life and death of the Messenger (ﷺ) belong to Allah, i.e., he should not fear death in the cause of the religion. This is His saying, Exalted is He, in Surah al-An'am: ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. No partner has He. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 162].

[p. 358]

So His saying ﴿to be the first of the Muslims﴾ is the reason (ʿillah) for ﴿to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾. The implied sense is: "And I have been commanded with that so that I may be the first of the Muslims." The object of ''umirtu'' (I have been commanded) is therefore omitted, the implication being shown by His saying ﴿to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾.

Here, ''awwal'' (أوَّلَ, "first") is used only in its figurative sense (majaz), since the intended meaning of "firstness" is not merely precedence in time, for that has already occurred and there is no benefit in announcing it. Rather, what is intended is that he is commanded to be the most complete of the Muslims in Islam, such that what the Messenger (ﷺ) does of the affairs of Islam is greater than what any other Muslim does, as he said: "Indeed, I am the most fearful of Allah among you and the most knowledgeable of Him."

The conjunction of the second "wa-umirtu" (and I have been commanded) to the first "umirtu" serves to emphasize this second command, and because it differs from the first command by the addition of the restriction of causation. Thus the mention of the first command explains what he was commanded to do, and the mention of the second explains the purpose for which he was commanded, to indicate that he was commanded with two great matters: one of them is shared with others, namely that he worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion; and the second is specific to him, namely that he worship Him in this manner so that by his worship he may be the first of the Muslims. That is, Allah commanded him to reach the utmost degree in the worship of Allah, being sincere to Him in religion. Thus He made his very existence wholly devoted to sincerity in every state, as He said in the other verse: ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 162], ﴿No partner has He. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [al-An'am: 163].

Know that since Islam is the religion of the prophets in their particular circumstances, as has been explained earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132] in Surah al-Baqarah, and its counterparts are many, this verse indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the messengers, since the word "Muslims" includes the earlier messengers.

[p. 357]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 13:

﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great Day.﴾ This statement is necessarily one that the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to address to the polytheists, who were attempting to make the Prophet (ﷺ) abandon the call and follow their religion. And these two are one of the two alternatives to which the preceding address was directed. The specification of each of them to what it was directed at is indicated by the context and by the indication of what follows it, namely His saying ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 15].

The repetition of the command to speak (qul) here is for emphasis, showing concern for this statement. As for the second of the two aspects mentioned earlier concerning the intended meaning of the directive in His saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, making my religion sincerely for Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 11] and what follows, then the repetition of the verb "qul" is due to the difference in the two groups intended by directing the statement to them. The statement of Muqatil has already been mentioned: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet: "What has moved you to this religion which you have brought us? Will you not look at the religion of your father and your grandfather and the chiefs of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 14:

﴿Say, "It is Allah I worship, sincerely devoting my religion to Him."﴾ ﴿So worship what you will besides Him.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15] This is a command to restate the declaration that he worships Allah alone, as an emphasis on His saying ﴿Say, "I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincerely devoting the religion to Him."﴾ [Az-Zumar: 11], because of its importance. Although the two sentences convey the same meaning, together they indicate that he worships none but Allah the Exalted, through two considerations: the first restriction of "أعْبُدَ اللَّهَ" (a'budu Allah, "I worship Allah") by the qualifier ﴿sincerely devoting the religion to Him﴾ [Az-Zumar: 11], and the fronting of the object before the second "أعْبُدُ" (a'budu, "I worship"). Thus the meaning of monotheism is affirmed twice, so that it is established three times, and as a preparation for His saying ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15], which is the intended point.

The "ف" (fa) in His saying "فاعْبُدُوا" (fa'budu, "so worship") and what follows it is for linking the sentence after it to the sentence before it, so it is a mentioned linkage (tafriʿ dhikri), i.e., a connection made by the discourse itself.

The command in His saying ﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15] is used in the sense of takhliyah (leaving someone to their own choice), which is also expressed as taswiyah (indifference or equalization). The intended meaning is indifference on the part of the speaker regarding that matter. The taswiyah is therefore a kinayah (indirect expression) for little concern with the addressees' action, meaning: that does not harm me. This is like His saying in Surah al-Kahf ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [Al-Kahf: 29]. The meaning is: worship whatever you wish to worship besides Allah. The relative clause here is the verb of willing (المَشِيئَة), indicating that their guide in determining what they worship is mere desire and whim without any evidence.

[Page 360]

﴿Say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss."﴾ After the command of leaving them to their own affairs, he follows it with some admonition, out of concern for their reform, in keeping with the Qur'an's manner. In delivering this admonition, the situation of the earlier abandonment of them to their own affairs is taken into account, combining guidance with reproach. So the admonition is delivered by way of allusion (ta'ridh) and by speaking of an absent party, while the intended audience is those being addressed.

The statement opens with the particle of emphasis (harf al-tawkid) to alert the listener that it is真 established fact. The definite article in "al-khasirin" (the losers) is the definition of genus (ta'rif al-jins), meaning: the category of people known for loss are those who have lost themselves and their families.

The definition of the predicate and the subject through restriction (qasr) means that this construction restricts the genus of the losers to those who have lost themselves and their families. This is a restriction of hyperbole (qasr mubalaghah), indicating that the complete essence of loss belongs to those who have lost themselves and their families, so the loss of others is as if it were no loss at all. For this reason, it is said that the definite article in such a construction indicates the meaning of completeness. They do not mean that completeness is one of the meanings of the definite article itself.

Since the speech is directed by way of allusion at those with whom the debate had taken place, from His saying ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾ [Az-Zumar: 7] up to His saying ﴿so worship what you will besides Him﴾, it is known that the intended ones by "those who have lost themselves and their families" are the very people with whom the debate took place. Thus it conveys the meaning: "Indeed, the losers are you." However, the reason for shifting from the pronoun to the relative construction in His saying ﴿those who have lost themselves﴾ is to embed (idmaj) their threat within it, namely that they will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning of their losing themselves is that they caused their own punishment, while they reckoned that they were striving for their own good in bliss and success. This is an analogy (tamthil) for their condition of casting themselves into punishment while thinking they are casting themselves into bliss, likened to the condition of a merchant who exposes his wealth to growth and profit, but then suffers destruction. So the phrase ﴿lost themselves﴾ has been applied to this state, and it has already occurred in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves because they had been wronging through Our verses﴾ [Al-A'raf: 9], at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 361]

As for their losing their families, it is like their losing themselves, because they enticed their families, from among their wives and children, into disbelief, just as they had cast themselves into it. Thus they gained nothing from their families in the Hereafter, and their families did not benefit them: ﴿For every one of them that Day, there will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ [Abasa: 37]. This is close to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a fire﴾ [At-Tahrim: 6]. So their loss was a great loss.

As for His saying ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, it is a resumed statement (isti'naf) which serves as a summation (fadhlakah) and conclusion of the preceding speech. This is because describing those who lost as having lost what they held most dear, and that they are the ones in whom the genus of losers is confined, implies that their loss is the greatest loss and the most evident to the eye. For this reason their loss was expressed by the term "al-khusran" (the loss), which is a verbal noun of loss, indicating the strength of the verbal noun and emphasis upon it.

Attention to and concern with describing their loss is indicated by opening the statement with the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih), attached to the demonstrative noun, which conveys the fullest distinction of the one pointed to. It also includes the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which conveys restriction, and this is a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i). The discussion of it is like the discussion of the confinement in His saying ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families﴾.

[Page 362 marker omitted]

﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers below them﴾ is a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition) from the clause ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [al-Zumar 39:15]. It was singled out for apposition because it is the most severe of their losses, since it has power over destroying their bodies. Loss includes other things besides this, such as disgrace, the wrath of Allah, and despair of salvation. The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ ("for them") refers to the whole group of their own selves and their families.

Al-zulal (ظُلَل) is the plural of ظُلَّة (zullah), which is a raised structure of building or wood, like a porch (suffah), under which a person sits for shade. It is derived from ظِلّ (zill, shadow), because such a structure casts a shadow in the sun. This was discussed earlier at Allah's words ﴿except that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His words ﴿and when a wave covers them like canopies﴾ [Luqman 31:32] in Surat Luqman. Here it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the layer that rises above the people of the Fire within the fire of Jahannam, indicated by the context of His words "of the Fire". It is likened to a canopy in height and covering, with an element of mockery (tahakkum), because they wish for something that would shield them from the heat of the Fire. Thus the layers of the Fire are referred to as zulal, to show that they have no protection from the heat of the Fire, in the manner of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite. The words ﴿lahum﴾ ("for them") are a tarshih (supporting element) for the metaphor.

As for the use of zulal for the layers beneath them, it is by way of mushakalah (contextual association). Also, the layers beneath them of the Fire are canopies for other disbelievers, since Jahannam has many levels (darakat).

* * *

﴿That is how Allah frightens His servants with it﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding statement) to the threat of punishment in His words ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾ [al-Zumar 39:15], and so on. It may also be an istinaf bayani (explanatory resumption), assuming a question that arises in the hearer's mind upon the description of their punishment as a canopy of fire above them and a canopy beneath them: a questioner might ask, "Is the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter after the opportunity to amend their disbelief has passed?" The answer is that Allah made that punishment in the Hereafter so that He may frighten His servants when He commands them to be upright and legislates laws for them, so that they know that if they do not respond to Allah and His messengers, this will be their end. Since Allah's threat is a report from Him and can only be true, He fulfills in the Hereafter what He threatened them with in this life. Allah's frightening with it means that He frightens them by informing them of it and describing it. As for making them taste it, that is the realization of the threat.

From this, by way of contrast (muqabalah), it is understood that Paradise was made to encourage His servants towards taqwa (God-consciousness). However, He omitted mention of it because the context is an admonition to the people of polytheism. Allah created Paradise and Jahannam to complete His wisdom and His purpose in the system of the present life, so that people may be in it at the highest level to which a pure soul can rise. It is apparent that Allah made Paradise a dwelling for the people of sanctified souls among the angels and humans, such as the messengers; therefore it was created before the onset of obligation (taklif). As for Jahannam, it is possible that it was created in advance, and this is the apparent meaning of the hadith: "The Fire complained to its Lord, saying: 'My parts have consumed one another.' So He permitted it to breathe twice: one breath in winter and one breath in summer." It is also possible that it will be created on the Day of Recompense, and the hadith would then be interpreted otherwise.

His words ﴿that﴾ are a reference to what was described of the loss and the punishment, interpreted as "the aforementioned".
