Al-takhwif (تَخْوِيف, frightening) is the verbal noun of خَوَّفَهُ, meaning he made him afraid, when he showed him something and described to him something that stirs fear in his soul. Fear is the feeling of what pains the soul through one of the five senses.

The word ﴿ʿibad﴾ ("servants"), which is attached to the pronoun of majesty (Allah) in both places here, encompasses every servant of humankind, believer and disbeliever alike, since all of them fear punishment for disobedience. Punishment varies in degree, and its furthest extent is eternal abiding for the people of polytheism. The word ʿibad here does not refer to those brought near (to Allah), because that would not suit the context of frightening, and because the context of His words "His servants" indicates that the ones addressed are all the servants. Thus it is distinguished from expressions like ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:68].

* * *

﴿O servants, so fear Me﴾ is a tafri' (consequential linkage) and ta'qib (immediate sequel) to the clause ﴿That is how Allah frightens His servants with it﴾, because frightening indicates that the punishment has been prepared for the people of disobedience. It is therefore fitting that it be followed by a command to people to have taqwa, so that they may avoid the punishment.

The vocative (al-nida') is placed before the consequential clause, although the apparent order would be to place it after, as in His words ﴿and fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:197] in Surat al-Baqarah. This is because the context here is one of warning and intimidation, so it is appropriate to draw the minds of the addressees to what will follow of the consequences of the frightening. By contrast, the verse in al-Baqarah is in a context of encouragement to complete the acts of Hajj and provision oneself for the Hereafter; therefore the command to taqwa there came joined with the conjunction "waw".

The ya' of the first person (ياء المتكلم) was deleted from the words يَا عِبَادِ in accordance with one of five possible forms for a vocative noun that is attached to the ya' of the first person.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 17–18:

﴿And those who avoid the Taghut (false deities), not worshipping them, and turn back in repentance to Allah — for them is good news. So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding.﴾

When the warning to the polytheists and the admonition to all creatures had come to an end, the direction of address was turned toward the believers, regarding what is specific to them of good tidings, as a counterpart to the warning given to the polytheists.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 15], and so on.

The expression of the believers as ﴿those who avoid the Taghut﴾ is because of what the relative clause implies about the reason for the predicate, namely ﴿for them is good news﴾. This corresponds to His saying ﴿With this Allah frightens His servants﴾ [az-Zumar: 16].

Al-Taghut: it is either a verbal noun or a noun of action from "ṭagha", on the pattern "fa'alūt" with the ʿayn vowelled, like raḥamūt and malakūt. In its root there are two dialectal forms, with waw and with yā', as in their saying "ṭagha ṭughūwan" like "ʿulūw", and their saying "ṭughwān" and "ṭughyān". The apparent reading of the Qamus is that it is waw-based. Since its final radical is a weak letter and a waw follows it, on the pattern "fa'alawt", the damma was felt to be heavy upon it, so they moved it before the ʿayn so that it could be turned into an alif, since it became vowelled and what preceded it was open. Thus it became "ṭāghūt", on the pattern "falʿūt", with the lām vowelled, and its tā' is an added letter for intensification in the verbal noun.

Among the scholars there is one who made al-Taghut a non-Arabic (aʿjamī) name on the pattern fāʿūl, like Jālūt, Ṭālūt and Hārūn. He mentioned it in al-Itqan among what occurs in the Qur'an of arabicised words, and said: it is the soothsayer in Abyssinian. Ibn Ḥajar corrected this in what he added to the verses of Ibn al-Subkī on the arabicised words occurring in the Qur'an. It was mentioned earlier, more briefly than here, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in jibt and ṭāghūt?﴾ [an-Nisa: 51], in Surat an-Nisa.

Al-Taghut is applied in the Qur'an and the Sunnah to whoever is powerful in disbelief or wrongdoing. Thus it is applied to an idol, to a group of idols, and to the leader of the people of disbelief, such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. As for its plural "ṭawāghīt", that is by way of giving precedence to the nominal character, as a proper noun through dominance, since al-Taghut has been made the singular of the idols, which is rare. Here it is intended to mean a group of idols, and the feminine pronoun is applied to it in His saying "that they worship them", on account of its being a plural of non-rational beings; and the masculine plural pronoun is applied to it in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut; they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], in Surat al-Baqarah, on account of its having occurred as a predicate about the protectors, which is a masculine plural, and on account of treating it as rational beings in the opinion of its worshippers.

And "an yaʿbudūhā" is a substitute for al-Taghut, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

Al-Inabah: repentance, and it was mentioned at His saying ﴿Indeed Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving, and turning back﴾ [Hud: 75], in Surat Hud. What is intended here is repentance from every sin and act of disobedience, and the highest of them is repentance from the shirk in which they were in the Jahiliyyah.

Al-Bushra: good news, and it is the announcement of the attainment of a benefit. It was mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64], in Surat Yunus. What is intended here is good news of Paradise.

In the fronting of the predicate in "lahumu al-bushra" there is the conveying of restriction (qasr), and it is like the restriction in ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾.

Following upon "lahumu al-bushra" is His saying ﴿So give good tidings to My servants who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾, and they are those who avoided the Taghut. He turned away from expressing them by their pronoun, saying "so give them good tidings", to the explicit mention of the servants, annexed to the pronoun of Allah, exalted is He, and by the relative clause, to increase their praise with two further attributes: the attribute of servanthood to Allah, meaning servanthood of drawing near, and the attribute of listening to speech and following its best.

The ten readers, other than al-Susi, the transmitter of Abu 'Amr, read the word "ʿibād" with a kasra on the dal without a yā', which is lightening and suffices with the presence of the kasra on the dal. Al-Susi read it with a yā' after the dal, vowelled with a fatha in continuation and quiescent in pause; and it is transmitted from him that the yā' is omitted in pause. Both are sound options in Arabic, as in al-Tashil. However, the codices agree on writing "ʿibād" here without a yā' after the dal, and this weakens al-Susi's reading, unless it is interpreted as being of the kind of recitation as it was delivered (al-adaʾ).

The definiteness in "al-qawl" is definiteness of the genus, meaning: they listen to the sayings that call to guidance, such as the Qur'an and the guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ), and they listen to the sayings by which their speakers wish to turn them away from faith, the trifles of the leaders of disbelief. When they hear that, they follow its best, which is what calls to the truth.

The meaning is: they follow the good speech among those sayings. So the superlative here is not used to express the excellence of the thing described over others; rather it indicates the strength of the attribute, like His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. God praised them by saying that they are people of critical discernment who distinguish between guidance and error, and between wisdom and delusions; they are examiners of the genuine proofs and critics of sophistical arguments.

In the relative pronoun there is an indication that following the best speech is a cause for Allah's guidance reaching them.

The sentence ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ is resumptive, to draw the mind to receive this information. This drawing of attention is emphasised by making the subject a demonstrative, so that those indicated are distinguished in the fullest distinction, together with an alert that they were worthy of this divine care because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative, namely the attributes of avoiding the worship of idols along with turning to Allah, and their listening to the speech of Allah and following it, rejecting what the polytheists cast of misleading talk.

Placing the demonstrative after a series of attributes or predicates is an Arabic method of emphasising both the judgement and the one judged. Sometimes the one judged is indicated, as here, and sometimes the predicate is indicated, as in His saying ﴿This; and indeed for the tyrants is the worst return﴾ [Sad: 55], in Surat Sad.

The definiteness of both parts in ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ has conveyed restriction of guidance to them, which is restriction of an attribute to a subject, and it is a relative restriction of the kind that specifies (qasr taʿyin), that is, rather than the losers who have lost themselves and their families.

The meaning of "Allah has guided them" is that they attained this excellence in that Allah created their souls receptive to the guidance with which the Messenger (ﷺ) addresses them, so their souls were prepared for it, and they turned to hearing guidance with their whole being, strove toward what conveys them to His pleasure, and sought deliverance from His anger.

The meaning of Allah's guidance of them is not that He directed to them commands of instruction, because that is available to those who were addressed by the Qur'an and turned away from it and did not seek to inquire into what pleases Allah, the Exalted, and so persisted in disbelief.

The sentence ﴿and those are the people of understanding﴾ points to the meaning of their being prepared to be guided by what Allah has instilled in them of complete intellects, and the original constitution inclines toward grasping realities, unconcerned with the familiar or with respecting falsehood, with variation among those intellects in the extent of speed in reaching guidance. Among them is one who believed at the first call of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Khadijah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib; and among them is one who believed after that or later. So the firm establishment of these conditions in their intellects is indicated by the use of the separating pronoun together with the word "ulu", which indicates that the one described by it holds fast to what the word "ulu" is annexed to, and by what the definiteness of "al-albab" indicates of the meaning of perfection. Therefore the definiteness in it is not definiteness of the genus, because the genus of intellects is established for all rational beings. The repetition of the demonstrative indicates their distinction by this quality from among their peers and the people of their age.

In it there is an alert that the attainment of guidance must have an agent and a receiver. The agent is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, "Allah has guided them", and the receiver by His saying "they are people of understanding". In this sentence there is the restriction found in ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾.

The praise of Allah for His perfect believing servants, that they have attained the attribute of following the best speech they hear, indicates the nobility of reflection and reasoning, for distinguishing between truth and falsehood, for distinguishing between correctness and error, for closing the field against doubt, and for negating the adoption of sophistry.

Of this, part is obligatory upon every individual, and it is what sound belief is acquired by, according to the capacity of the one who reflects; and part is obligatory as a communal duty (kifayah), and it is a virtue and perfection for individuals: namely reflection and reasoning in the laws of Islam, grasping their proofs, understanding and comprehension of them, and earnestness in observing their objectives in the rules of worship and transactions and the manners of social life, to establish the order of the Islamic community in its truest and most complete form, and to restrain those who plunge into these matters with blindness and delusion, and to check the over-scrupulous and the heretics.

Among what follows from this is the absence of the best proofs and the most eloquent statements that lead to this aim without defect or fault, through refining the sciences and their compositions. It has been said: "Take from every science its best", from His saying here, ﴿those who listen to the word and follow its best﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, and Salman al-Farisi, who avoided the Taghut from worshipping it in their Jahiliyyah, and followed the best speech that reached them.

From Ibn 'Abbas: His saying "So give good tidings to My servants who listen to the word", the verse, was revealed concerning 'Uthman, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who came to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq when he had embraced Islam, asked him, and he informed them of his faith, so they believed.

Since the restriction (*ḥaṣr*) expressed in His words, "For them is good news" (*lahumu al-bushrā*), and the two restrictions in His words, "Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding" (Q. 39:18), indicate that whoever is other than them, namely the polytheists, has no good news, has not been guided by Allah, and has no understanding, because they do not benefit from their minds, the outcome of this is that the polytheists are deprived of a good end, with everlasting bliss, because they are deprived of obedience, which is its cause. Upon this is built a denying interrogative (*istifhām inkārī*), which conveys an alert to the absence of any hope for the guidance of the group against whom the word of punishment has been justified. They are the ones whose exclusion from good news, from guidance, and from benefiting from their minds is intended, by the restriction shaped by the three forms of restriction mentioned earlier, as we have pointed out.

The structure of the speech has come in an original manner in the report that is being emphasized: its established content is confirmed for the subject of the report by affirming the opposite or contrary of that content for the opposite of the subject, so that the content of the report is established twice, once by its original form and once by its opposite or contrary for the opposite of the subject. An example is His saying, may He be exalted: "This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return" (Q. 38:55), after His saying, "This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return" (Q. 38:49). This often occurs after the use of a demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*) referring to the preceding report, as in the verse just mentioned, or referring to the subject of the report, as in this sura in His saying just before: "Those are the ones whom Allah has guided" (Q. 39:18). Once those described have been indicated twice, the reversal of their judgment is built upon them for those who are characterized by the opposite of their condition.

By this, the good placement of the *fa'* (the particle "then") becomes evident, marking this sentence as a consequence of the sentence "Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding" (Q. 39:18). This is because consequence (*tafrī'*) requires connection and linkage between what is derived and what it is derived from. This is like the consequence in the words of Labid:

*"Is that [a cow] or a wild cow, pursued by wolves, abandoned, and the one leading the herd, its strength...?"*

Here he derived one comparison from another comparison, because the two things compared differ.

The word "punishment" (*al-'adhāb*) is the speech of Allah's threat to them of punishment in the Hereafter.

The meaning of "has been justified" (*ḥaqqa*) is "has been realized in fact," i.e., the word of punishment with which they were threatened was true and not a lie. So the meaning of *ḥaqqa* here is "realization." The justification of the word of punishment upon them is the opposite of Allah's guidance of the others, and their being in the Fire is the opposite of the others having good news. The ordering of the two opposites follows the manner of what is called *shibh al-laff wa-al-nashr al-makūs* (a resemblance to the reversed "folding and unfolding" figure), like His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has set a seal upon their hearts..." (Q. 2:6–7), up to "and for them is a great punishment," after His saying: "And those who believe in what has been revealed to you..." (Q. 2:4), up to "Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful" (Q. 2:5). His saying "Allah has set a seal upon their hearts" (Q. 2:7) is the opposite of His saying "Those are upon guidance from their Lord" (Q. 2:5), and His saying "and for them is a great punishment" is the opposite of His saying "and those are the successful."

As for the word *man* (whoever) in His saying "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been justified," it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by it is Abu Lahab, his son, and whoever turned away from faith from the family of the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case, *man* is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate has been omitted. The estimate is: "you save him from the Fire," as indicated by what follows it. The sentence "Then can you save those in the Fire?" would then be an appendix (*tadhyīl*), meaning: you do not save those who are in the Fire.

The *hamzah* is an interrogative of denial, and the second *hamzah* is likewise. One of them is an emphasis for the other that precedes it, for the sake of giving attention to this denying interrogative, in the manner of the repetition of *anna* (that) in the verse of Qass ibn Sa'idah:

*"The tribe of Yemen surely knew that I, when I said, 'As for what follows,' I am its orator."*

What Sahib al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari, author of *al-Kashshaf*) followed, and his commentators followed him in, is that *man* in His saying "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been justified" is a conditional particle. This is based on the view that the *fa'* in His saying "Then can you save those in the Fire" may be for a meaning other than the consequence derived from the preceding sentence. Otherwise it would be an emphasis of the first, and that would diminish a meaning from the verse.

It is also permissible that the first *man* be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*), a subject whose predicate is "Then can you save those in the Fire?" In that case, the *fa'* in His saying "Then can you save those in the Fire?" is an emphasis of the first *fa'* in His saying "Then is one [for whom] ... has been justified," so the *hamzah* and the *fa'* together are emphases of the first *hamzah*, and the *fa'* that goes with it, because of their connection. Also, the sentence "Then can you save" applies to what the sentence "Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified" applies to. The denying interrogative then proceeds according to its most common usage, turning toward a speech that has no condition in it.

The original form of the speech, on the view that *man* is conditional, is: "Whoever will have the word of punishment justified against him in the future, you do not save him from it." So the *hamzah* of "Then can you save those in the Fire?" is a denying interrogative, and the *hamzah* of "Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified" is a *hamzah* with which the speech begins, containing denial, in order to alert from the outset that the speech contains denial, just as a speech containing negation may be opened with a negative particle before they utter the negation, as in the words of Muslim ibn Ma'bad al-Walibi of the Banu Asad:

*"No, by Allah, what is in me will not be found [to be cured], nor what is in them, ever, a remedy."*

Mentioning the particle serves to emphasize the meaning of the denying *hamzah* as a subordinate meaning.

The original form of the speech, on the view that the first *man* is a relative pronoun, is: "Those against whom the word of punishment will be justified, you do not save them from the Fire." So the *hamzah* in "Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified" is a denying interrogative, and the *hamzah* of "Then can you save those in the Fire?" is an emphasis of the first *hamzah*.

The *man* in His saying "those in the Fire" (*man fī al-nār*) is a relative pronoun.

"Those in the Fire" are those against whom the word of punishment has been justified, because the word of punishment is that they should be among the people of the Fire. So a noun is placed in the position of a pronoun, and the original would be: "Then can you save him from the Fire?"

[Page 371]

The benefit of this explicit noun is to magnify their condition, because of the preposition of location in the relative clause, which depicts the state of the Fire encompassing them. That is, "Do you intend to save them from falling into the Fire, while they are now in the Fire, since their destination to the Fire is certain?" So the realization of falling into it in the future is likened to its realization in the present. A similar omitted predicate has been stated explicitly in His saying, may He be exalted: "Is one who will be thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?" in the sura of Fussilat (Q. 41:40), and in His saying: "Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?" (Q. 67:22) in the sura of al-Mulk.

The interrogative is a rhetorical question of affirmation (*taqrīrī*), as an allusion (*kināyah*) to the lack of equality between this person and the believer.

The word "punishment" (*al-'adhāb*) is the speech of Allah that necessitates that the disbeliever is in punishment, i.e., Allah's decree of that for the disbeliever in His repeated threat in the Qur'an. The omission of the feminine *ta'* from the verb *ḥaqqa* (has been justified), although its subject is feminine in wording, namely *kalimah* (word), is because the subject has acquired the masculine quality from what it is attached to (*al-'adhāb*), given that it is possible to dispense with the first noun by the noun it is attached to. It is as if it were said: "Then is one upon whom the punishment has been justified."

The benefit of inserting *kalimah* (word) is to indicate that this is the command of Allah and His threat.

The fronting of the subject (*musnad ilayhi*) before the verbal predicate in "Then can you save" serves to strengthen the judgment, which is the denial that the Prophet (ﷺ), by repeatedly calling them, could rescue them from the realization of the threat, or that guidance could come to them if Allah has not decreed it for them.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), to ease for him some of his eagerness to repeatedly call them to Islam and his grief over their turning away and their misguidance. Otherwise, the Prophet (ﷺ) was not one who thinks that he could save them from the threat of Allah. For this reason, the verb "to save" (*al-inqādh*) is brought here, as a comparison of the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his eagerness for their guidance and his exertion to the utmost in persuading them to believe his call, and the state of them in their immersion in the causes of their threatened punishment, to the state of one who tries to save a person who has fallen into the Fire, around whose sides the Fire has surrounded, by a necessity decreed by one whose purpose he does not get to determine. Their condition resembles the condition of their falling into the Fire now, because its falling is certain. The compound expression that indicates the state being compared has been omitted, and its meaning is indicated by mentioning something from the fitting elements of that omitted compound, namely the verb "you save those in the Fire," which is among the fitting elements of their falling into the Fire, in the manner of metaphorical representation (*tamthīl*) by the implicit metaphor (*al-makniyyah*). That is, applying the implicit metaphor (*isti'ārah makniyyah*) to the compound. The phrase "you save those in the Fire" is the indicator (*qarīnah*) of this implicit metaphor, and it is in itself an explicit metaphor (*isti'ārah taḥqīqiyyah*), as in His saying: "They break the covenant of Allah" (Q. 2:27).

This is among what al-Kashshaf pointed to and al-Taftazani (the commentator on al-Kashshaf) clarified, so it is counted among the original refinements of their insights. With it the division of the metaphor of image (*al-isti'ārah al-tamthīliyyah*) into two kinds is completed: the explicit and the implicit. This was overlooked in the science of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayān*).

By this you know that "saving" (*al-inqādh*) was applied to insistent warning, by the use of the name of the effect for its cause. And that "those in the Fire" means those who are destined for the Fire. So the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) have no basis for using this verse as evidence to deny Muhammadan intercession (*al-shafā'ah al-muḥammadiyyah*) for the people of major sins. Moreover, even if we grant that the verse is directed toward the theme of intercession, it denies intercession only for the people of polytheism, because "those in the Fire" may refer to the specific group, namely those spoken of in this verse. There is no disagreement that intercession is not for the polytheists. Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them" (Q. 74:48). Furthermore, what is negated is that the Prophet (ﷺ) would be one who saves whom Allah has willed not to be saved. As for intercession, it is the asking of Allah that He save him.

This verse includes wondrous points of inimitability (*i'jāz*), for it conveys that this group of polytheists, in whose hearts disbelief lies hidden, have had the word of Allah justified against them for their punishment, so they do not believe. Their present condition is like that of one who has fallen into the Fire, so he is certainly destroyed. And the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his eagerness for their guidance is like that of one who sees a person fallen into the Fire and is moved by compassion to try to save him, but he is unable to do so. For this reason, the intensity of his eagerness to rescue them is denied. So placing this meaning in two sentences is the utmost in brevity, together with what is conveyed by the emphasis of the *hamzah* and the *fa'* in the second sentence, which is prolixity in a place requiring explicitness.

Then, with what has been deposited in these two sentences of the wondrous metaphor of image in the manner of the implicit metaphor, and of the explicit metaphor in the indicator of the implicit metaphor.

The sum of the structure of this composition is: "Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified, so he is in the Fire? Then can you save him, and save those in the Fire?"

The hadith of Abu Hurairah has indicated this depicted state in this verse: that he heard the Prophet

[Page 373]

(ﷺ) say:

"The likeness of me and of people is like the likeness of a man who kindled a fire, and when it lit up what was around him, the moths and these creatures that fall into the fire began to fall into it. He began to pull them away, but they overpowered him and plunged into it. So I am taking hold of your waistbands to keep you from the Fire, while you are plunging into it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 20:

﴿But those who fear their Lord—for them are chambers, above which are built chambers, beneath which rivers flow. The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾ The glad tidings given to those who avoided the tyrant (al-taghut) are repeated as a detailed explanation of the general statement that came before.

The reporting about them is introduced with the particle of exception (harf al-istidrak), to add emphasis to the distinction between the condition of the believers and the condition of the polytheists and the opposition between the two. So the particle of exception here serves merely to signal the contrast between the two states, so that the listener knows he is about to hear a ruling opposite to what preceded, as occurred in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But look at the mountain﴾ [al-A'raf: 143] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying ﴿But Allah disliked their being sent forth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 46] in Surat Bara'ah. Thus there occurred, in the matter of those who avoided the worship of the tyrant, an affirmation upon an affirmation, which began in the two indications in His saying ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding﴾ [al-Zumar: 18], then by what followed of the arrangement of the condition of their opposites after mention of their conditions, then by the particle of exception distinguishing their condition from the condition of their opposites.

By ﴿those who feared their Lord﴾ is meant: those who avoided the worship of the tyrant, turned penitently to Allah, followed the best of speech, were guided by the guidance of Allah, and were people of understanding. The turn away from saying "they" (hum) here to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) serves the purpose of praising them through the meaning conveyed by the relative clause, and to indicate that the relative clause is the cause of the ruling predicated of the relative, namely their being granted the chambers.

The name of Allah is turned away from in favor of the description "the Lord," annexed to the pronoun of the God-fearing, because of the honor in that annexation, namely the honor of their Lord's being pleased with them.

The lam in "lahum" denotes exclusivity (al-ikhtisas). The meaning: they are theirs in Paradise, i.e., they have been prepared for them in Paradise.

Al-ghuraf is the plural of ghurfah, with the ghayn vowelled with a damma and the ra' sukun (it is a room resting upon another room; it is also called al-'uliyyah, with the ayn vowelled with a damma or kasra, and with a kasra on the lam and a shadda, and the tahtiyyah likewise). The word ghurfah was discussed at the end of Surat al-Furqan.

The meaning of ﴿above them are chambers﴾ is that they are described as having other chambers raised above them. All of this falls within the scope of the lam of exclusivity: the chambers that are above the chambers are theirs too, since what is above a building follows it, and this is what the jurists call al-hawa' in their terminology. So the meaning is: for them are tiers of chambers. This is the counterpart of what was assigned to the people of the Fire in His saying ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them and canopies beneath them﴾ [al-Zumar: 16].

The two states are contrasted: the God-fearing are given chambers described as having other chambers above them, while the polytheists are given canopies of fire, and it is conjoined to this that beneath them are canopies, to indicate that the God-fearing enjoy moving about among those chambers, and that the polytheists are confined in their place, and that the canopies of fire are above them and beneath them, so that the canopies reinforce one another by directing the blast of the fire at them from every direction.

Mabniyyah (built) means: its walls are raised with stone and plaster, or stone and earth, or with sun-dried brick, and then a roof is placed upon them. This is an adjective of ghuraf. From it is known that the chambers resting upon others are built, by way of implication (dalalat al-fahwa). The commentators have been perplexed about the reason for describing the chambers, given that a ghurfah is only ever made of building, and they did not take it to be a clarifying description (wasf kashif), and they have an excuse for that, because of its little benefit. It was said: the mention of "built" serves to indicate that they are real chambers and not things resembling chambers, to distinguish them from the canopies assigned to those who lost on the Day of Resurrection, for their canopies were of fire. Thus the listener does not think that the chambers of the God-fearing are a metaphor for clouds of shade or the like, since there is no call for metaphor here, unlike there, where the context of mockery required it.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "mabniyyah" is like the dwellings adhering to the ground; that is, he mentioned the description as a preparation for His saying "beneath which rivers flow," because it is known that rivers flow only beneath lower dwellings; that is, nothing of the excellences of the lower dwellings was missed by the chambers.

It was also said: what is meant is that they are prepared for them from now. So they exist, because the passive participle, like the active participle, in requiring the attribute at the time of the present, indicates that Paradise is already created.

In my view it is also permissible that the description is a precaution against a kind of chamber that is hewn out of rock in the mountains, such as the chambers of Thamud, and like what the people of southern Tunisia call ghuraf, which are dwellings carved out in the mountains of Medenine, Matmata and Tataouine. Consider whether those dwellings are called ghuraf in Arabic, for the books of lexicography did not describe the meaning of ghurfah with an adequate description.

It is also permissible that "mabniyyah" is an adjective of the chambers with regard to what its word indicates of the meaning of "built and elevated," so that the adjective denotes the firmness of the described meaning, i.e., built with a construction reaching the utmost in its kind, like their saying: "a night that is extremely dark" (layl alyal) and "a deep shade" (zill zalil).

The flowing of rivers beneath them is from the perfection of the beauty of their view for one who looks down upon them. The meaning of "beneath them": the rivers pass by what is adjacent beneath them, as was discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Al 'Imran: 15] in Surat Al 'Imran, so the name "beneath" is applied to what is adjacent to it.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: rivers flow beneath their foundations, i.e., they cut through their foundations and pass through them and through their courtyards, and this is among the finest things seen in houses, like the houses of Damascus, the palace of the Alhambra in al-Andalus, and the houses of the affluent in the city of Fez; in that case the use of "beneath" is literal.

The meaning: each chamber of them has a river flowing beneath it. This is from the counterpart of the plural, to be distributed among the individuals, and that is by the water rising to each chamber and flowing beneath it.

"Wa'da Allah" is a verbal noun in the accusative, functioning as an absolute object emphasizing itself, since His saying "for them are chambers" means: Allah promised them chambers, a promise from Him. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state from "ghuraf," on the pattern of His saying "a promise upon us." The annexation of "wa'da" to the name of Allah indicates that it is a promise that has been fulfilled, and so the clause ﴿Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ came as an explanation of the meaning of "wa'da Allah."

Al-mi'ad is a noun of place-and-time-like form (masdar mimi) meaning "the promise."

[Page 376]

﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky, then makes it flow as springs in the earth, then brings forth with it crops of varying colours, then they wither and you see them turning yellow, then He makes them into debris? Indeed in that is a reminder for people of understanding.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a fresh sentence beginning a new topic), which moves to the purpose of highlighting the Qur'an and the guidance of Islam contained in it. This was the purpose with which the surah began, and the discourse turned away from it by way of digression (*istitrad*, a shift to a related point) with God's words ﴿So worship God, making your religion sincerely His﴾ [al-Zumar: 2] up to here. So this serves as a preface to His words ﴿Is one whose breast God has opened to Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar: 22] up to His words ﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides with it whom He wills﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. Thus the situation of the Qur'an's descent, the believers' being guided by it, and the promise of the growth of that guidance, are likened to the situation of rain descending, plants growing from it, and reaching full maturity.

This simile may be divided into parts corresponding to the parts of the situation being likened to it. The descent of water from the sky is a likeness of the descent of the Qur'an to revive hearts; the making of water flow as springs in the earth is a likeness of the conveying of the Qur'an to people; the bringing forth of crops of varying colours is a likeness of the state of people's differing, some good and some otherwise, some beneficial and some harmful; and the flourishing of the crop is a likeness of the multiplication of believers among polytheists. As for His words ﴿then He makes it into debris﴾, it is an *idmaj* (an embedded addition, inserting one theme within another) to remind of the state of death and of people being equal in it, the beneficial and the harmful alike. And in following this with His words ﴿Is one whose breast God has opened to Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar: 22] up to His words ﴿And whom God leads astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], there is an indication of the lesson to be drawn from this simile.

Close to the imagery of this verse is what is in the two *Sahihs* (Bukhari and Muslim) from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which God has sent me is like rain that fell upon a land; part of it was fertile, which absorbed the water and produced abundant grass and herbage; part of it was hard ground which held the water, so God benefited people with it; they drank from it, gave drink, and pastured their animals; and it fell upon another part which was barren, which neither holds water nor produces grass. That is the likeness of one who acquires understanding of the religion of God and benefits from what God has sent me with, so he knows and teaches; and the likeness of one who does not lift his head to this and does not accept the guidance of God with which I have been sent."

It is possible that the meaning is primarily the stated one but embedded in reverse, as we have explained. In that case, it returns to the argument for God's sole divinity by means of evidence from His creatures which people witness repeatedly. Then His words ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky﴾ up to His words ﴿Only people of understanding are reminded﴾ [al-Zumar: 9] are connected to His words ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], which is connected to His words ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth; He wraps the night over the day﴾ [al-Zumar: 5]. The simile we have explained, of the situation of the Qur'an's descent and the benefit of believers, would then be an embedded addition within this argument.

On both interpretations, there is embedded in the discourse an allusion to the possibility of people being revived to a second life.

The statement is an interrogative of affirmation (*istifham taqriri*, a question seeking the listener's affirmation of a known fact). The address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed, so it does not target a specific addressee. The seeing is visual sight.

His words ﴿sends down water from the sky﴾ have a parallel which preceded in His words ﴿And it is He who sends down water from the sky﴾ [al-An'am: 99] in Surah al-An'am.

"*Salakahu*" means "caused it to enter", i.e., made it a passer-through, i.e., inside. So the verb *salaka* here is transitive. It has been discussed before at His words ﴿and made for you therein roads﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53] in Surah Ta-Ha, where we noted that *salaka* can be both intransitive and transitive. This causing to enter is a second piece of evidence.

"*Yanabi'*" is the plural of *yanbu'*, which is a spring of water. It was discussed at His words ﴿until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra': 90] in Surah al-Isra'. "*Yanabi'*" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the pronoun in "*ma'an*". Making the water that enters the earth into springs is a third piece of evidence of God's great power.

The particle "*thumma*" ("then") connects His words ﴿then brings forth with it crops﴾ to indicate a delay in rank (*tarakhi rutbi*, a sequence of importance rather than time), as is its function in connecting sentences; for bringing forth crops from the earth after it has become barren is more striking to people's minds, since it is closer to their sight and more beneficial to their livelihood, and this is the intended purpose of rain. This bringing forth is a fourth piece of evidence.

"*Al-alwan*" is the plural of "*lawn*" (colour). *Lawn* is a quality which becomes apparent on the outer surface of a body in light; it was discussed in Surah Fatir.

[Page 377]

As for the variety of the crops' colours in the first sense, each kind of crop has a colour, and its blossoms have colours, and each variety of crop has different colours in the stages of its growth and its reaching maturity. This variation, with the land in which they grow being one and the water by which they grow being one, is a fifth sign of great power and of sole authority in disposing affairs.

The meaning of "*yahiju*" is: it becomes thick and rises.

The true sense of *hiyaj* is the agitation (turmoil) of a human or an animal. *Hiyaj* is used metaphorically for the intensity of something other than an animal; one says: "a wind has stirred" (*hajat rih*). From this is the *hiyaj* of the crop in the verse, because the crop's stalks and ears lengthen, its drying is completed, and when it is moved by the passing of the wind over it, it produces a rustling and a crackling sound. This applies to both grain and herbage. This stage is a sixth sign of God's oneness.

"*Al-hutam*" means the broken, i.e., the shattered and crushed. The pattern *fu'al* (with a *dammah* on the *fa'*) indicates the passive object, like *futat* (crumbs) and *duqaq* (fine powder). Similar to it is the pattern *fu'alah*, like *subabah* (dregs), *qulamah* (parings) and *qumamah* (sweepings). The meaning is that it reaches such dryness that it breaks and shatters by its parts rubbing against each other, falling apart, and the wind breaking it.

This stage is a seventh sign of God's power.

All of them are signs of the precision of His craftsmanship, and of how He deposited many stages in a single thing, each succeeding the other from the stage of its existence to the stage of its decay.

The clause ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for people of understanding﴾ explains the interrogative of affirmation and serves as a summation (*fadhlaka*, a concluding summary) of the stages about which the question was asked. So the reference of "*dhalika*" (that) is to what has been mentioned, from the descent up to the final stages.

What is meant is a reminder by way of indicating what the heedless person overlooks. It is also possible that the reminder is of what the thoughtless person forgets, of what these states contain from their beginning to their end. Among that: they are suitable as an example for bringing the Resurrection close, for the sending down of water upon the earth and its growing plants by it is a matter that recurs after the plants upon it have become debris, and their seeds spread through the earth, and then it grows again when water descends. Likewise, a person returns after his death, as indicated by His words ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as plants﴾ [Nuh: 17] ﴿then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a (new) bringing forth﴾ [Nuh: 18]. So the verse includes an embedded addition bringing the Resurrection near and showing its possibility, together with evidence of God's sole authority in disposing affairs.

[Page 378]

Among that: they are suitable as a parable for the life of this world, as in the verse in Surah Yunus and in Surah al-Kahf, and the intended meaning is to liken one state to another. So one does not consider the figurative sense (*tajawwuz*) in the individual terms of this composite image, by seeking for each stage of worldly life a stage among the stages of plant growth that resembles it.

Among them: they are a parable for the stages of the human being from the stage of drops of semen, to youth, to old age, and then to death. The intended meaning is to liken one state to another, with the possibility of distributing the likeness of each stage of the state being likened to a stage of the state it is likened to. This is the most complete kind of parabolic likeness (*tamthiliyyah*).

"*Ulu al-albab*" are those who benefit by their minds, so they are guided by the proofs set out for them, as was mentioned just before at His words ﴿Only people of understanding are reminded﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. They are those who reasoned and believed. In this there is an implicit rebuke that those who did not benefit from the proofs are in the position of those who lack reason.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 22:

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...?﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of what preceded in His saying ﴿But those who have feared their Lord, for them are chambers﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], and of what was attached to it of the depiction of their condition in benefiting from the Qur'an. Upon it this interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri) is made a consequence.

"Man" (من) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿But those who have feared their Lord, for them are chambers﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], by what the particle of exception (harf al-istidrak) requires of the contrast between his condition and the condition of the one upon whom the word of punishment is due.

The estimate (taqdir) is: "Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord, like the one upon whom the word of punishment is due, so that he is in the darkness of disbelief?" Or its estimate is: "like one whose heart has hardened," indicated by His saying ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾, and this is an indication by what follows (dalalat al-lahiq).

The expansion of the breast for Islam (sharh al-sadr li'l-Islam) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the intellect's acceptance of Islam's guidance and its love for it. The literal meaning of sharh is: cutting open the flesh. From it was named the science of observing the inner parts of bodies and their structure: 'ilm al-tashrih (anatomy), because it depends on cutting through skin and flesh and examining what lies beneath.

Since a person, when he is perplexed and hesitant about a matter, finds in himself something by which his nervous system is affected, and its effect appears in the constriction of his self, until his breathing becomes difficult and his sighing increases, and since the organ of breathing is in the chest, that constriction was likened to tightness and closing, so they said: "his chest became tight" (daqa sadruhu). Allah the Exalted said concerning Moses: ﴿and my chest tightens﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 13]. They also said: "his chest closed" (inṭabaqa sadruhu) and "his ribs closed." And for the opposite of that they said: "Allah expanded his chest" (sharaha Allahu sadrahu). Both were combined in His saying: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam, and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-An'am: 125], in Surat al-An'am. From it also is their saying: "So-and-so is in expansion (infirah)," meaning he feels as if his chest has been expanded and widened.

Among the elegance of the Qur'an's wording is its preference for the word "sharaha" to indicate the acceptance of Islam, because Islam's teachings, morals and manners give the Muslim joy in his state, gladness in the good pleasure of his Lord, and ease toward calamities and disasters, because he is certain that he is upon the truth in his affair, that he is rewarded for his hardship, and that he hopes for the mercy of his Lord in this world and the Hereafter; and because doubt and bewilderment do not mix with his inner self.

Indeed, the believer, when he first believes that Allah is One and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is His Messenger, his breast expands, since he has risen in degrees from the state he was in during polytheism, in that he has avoided worshipping stones that are more noble than he is, and most of his possessions are nobler than they, such as his horse, his camel, his male and female slaves, his livestock and his palm trees. So he feels the dignity of his self, elevated above the former humiliation that was revealed to him, which Islam washed away from him. Then he begins to recite the Qur'an, speak with wisdom, adorn himself with noble morals, original judgment and love of doing good for the sake of Allah, not for show and reputation; his inner self harbours no rancour, envy or hatred for the sake of Allah; and he begins to count the Muslims as brothers to himself. He has abandoned earning by raiding and gambling, and has become self-sufficient through contentment, needing to plead to no one except Allah the Exalted. When harm touches him, he hopes for its removal and does not despair of a change in his condition, and he is certain that he is rewarded for his endurance and patience. When blessing touches him, he praises his Lord and anticipates more. Thus his breast is expanded by Islam, receiving events with insight, not fearful, brave of heart and proud of soul.

The lam in "for Islam" (li'l-Islam) is the lam of cause (lam al-'illah): i.e., He expanded it for the sake of Islam, i.e., for the sake of its acceptance.

Consequent upon the statement that "Allah expanded his breast for Islam" is His saying ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾, the pronoun referring back to "man" (man).

"Light" (nur) is a metaphor for guidance and the clarity of truth, because by light things become manifest, and the one who sees comes out of the darkness of error and the confusion of ambiguity between realities and shadows.

It is used, by a subsequent (tab'iyyah) or figurative (tamthiliyyah) metaphor, for being firmly established in the light, just as it is used in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Luqman: 5], on the two aspects established there. "From his Lord" (min Rabbihi) is a qualifier of "light," and "min" is the min of origin (ibtida'iyyah), i.e., a light described as having come to him from the presence of Allah; so it is a perfect light, not mixed with darkness. This is the light which was attributed to the Name of Allah in His saying ﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 35], in Surat al-Nur.

* * *

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. Those are in manifest error.﴾

This is a consequence of describing the condition of one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord, which indicates the condition of its opposite: those whose breasts Allah has not expanded for Islam, so there is hardness in their hearts with which they were created, so the call to good does not penetrate their hearts.

The badness of their condition is stated in summary by what the word "woe" (wayl) indicates of their reaching the furthest ends of wretchedness and misery. The detailed meanings of this were already given at His saying ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Qasi" (hardened): one characterised by hardness in condition. The literal meaning of qaswah is harshness and firmness in bodies, and it was discussed at His saying ﴿Then they are like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. The hardness of the heart is a metaphor for the intellect's small effect from admonitions and the like delivered to its owner. This metaphor is counterpart to the metaphor of softness (lin) for quickness of response to advice and the like, as will come in His saying ﴿Then their skins soften﴾ [al-Zumar: 23].

"Min" in His saying "from the remembrance of Allah" may be in the sense of "'an" (away from), by including in "hardened" the meaning of "turning away" and "repelled." The synonym of the meaning of "'an" has been counted among the meanings of "min," and this was cited in Mughni al-Labib by this verse and by His saying ﴿You were in heedlessness of this﴾ [Qaf: 22]. But this is open to question, since it is possible to take them in two common meanings of "min": the meaning of causation in the first verse, like the saying: "He gave them to drink from the cloud," i.e., because of thirst, as al-Zamakhshari said. The meaning becomes: their hardness of heart came about in them because of the remembrance of Allah. And the meaning of beginning in the second verse: i.e., their hearts became hard from the outset upon hearing the remembrance of Allah.

The "remembrance of Allah" here means the Qur'an; its attribution to "Allah" is an addition of honour to it. The meaning is that when a verse is recited, they recoil, so repulsion takes hold of them and their hearts harden.

The summary of the meaning: their disbelief leads them to dislike what they hear of the call to Islam through the Qur'an. So whenever they hear it, they turn away and oppose, and the dislike of Islam is renewed in their hearts until that dislike becomes firmly rooted in their hearts, and their hearts become hard.

Thus the Qur'an, by its being, caused the hearts of the believers to be at rest, as He said: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28], and it was a cause of the hardening of the hearts of the disbelievers.

The cause of this is the difference in receptivity (qabiliyyah), for one single cause has effects and actions that differ according to differences in receptivity. The properties of things are known only by considering the majority of their effects upon the majority of those affected. So the remembrance of Allah is a cause of the softening and illumination of hearts when the hearts are sound, free from the disease of obstinacy, stubbornness and arrogance. But when this disease settles in them, then when Allah is remembered in their presence they become sicker than they were.

The sentence ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), because what precedes, the judgment that the hardness of their hearts is because the remembrance of Allah is mentioned in their presence, arouses in the listener's mind the question: how was the remembrance of Allah a cause of the hardness of their hearts? So it is explained that the cause of that is that they are firmly established in error, immersed in its mire, so their error is too strong to clear when they hear the remembrance of Allah.

The opening of this sentence with the demonstrative noun ("those") right after their description with hardness of heart is to indicate that what will be mentioned of their condition after the pointing to them is what they have become worthy of because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative, as was discussed in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Luqman: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah. So the content of His saying ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾, which is the severe error, is the cause of the hardness of their hearts, as the resumptive nature of the sentence requires. And its content is an effect of the hardness of their hearts, as the opening of the sentence with the demonstrative and following the description of those indicated with attributes requires.

Likewise is the nature of psychological accidents: they are both agent and patient according to the difference in what provokes them and the effects they leave, because they are causes and effects in relation, where the existence of neither of the two depends on the existence of the other in the sense called circular dependence (dawr ma'i).

"Mubin" (manifest): that which is intense and not hidden because of its intensity. So "mubin" is a metaphor for strength and firmness; it becomes clear to the reflective observer that it is error.

[Page 384]

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 39, verse 23 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent in its parts, repeating [its themes], whereby the skins shiver of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence of explanation (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a sentence that arises to clarify and answer an implied question). It arises from the opposition between the meaning of the sentence ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [39:22] and the meaning of this sentence, which is that the Qur'an softens the hearts of those who fear their Lord. The meaning of the previous sentence provokes the question of a questioner about the reason for the hardness of the hearts of the misguided against the remembrance of Allah. So the sentence ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾ up to His saying "from any guide" [39:23] explains that the hardness of the hearts of the misguided toward hearing the Qur'an is only due to a rust (*rayn*) upon their hearts and minds, not to any deficiency in its guidance. This is like His saying in Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [2:2], then He said: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾ [2:6].

This sentence completes the praise of the Qur'an with which the surah opens, the purpose of the surah. It will be followed by another praise at His saying ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may be reminded﴾ [39:27], and then with His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [39:41], and then with His saying ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [39:55].

Beginning the sentence with the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalālah*, "Allah") indicates the magnification of the best statement that was sent down, that its Sender is the greatest of the great. Then, the predicate about the Name of Majesty being a verbal predicate (*khabar fiʿlī*) indicates the strengthening and confirmation of the judgment, in the manner of their saying: "He gives abundantly."

[Page 385]

It also conveys, together with the emphasis, a restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), i.e., the restriction of the sending down of the Book to Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is: "Allah sent down the Book, not other than Him; He composed it." So in it is an affirmation that it was sent down from the world of holiness (*ʿālam al-quds*). This is also a metonymy (*kināyah*) for its being a revelation from Allah, not from the composition of human beings.

Thus the sentence indicates an emphasis and a restriction explicitly, and a restriction implicitly. When the implication of the restriction (*mafhūm al-qaṣr*) and the implication of the metonymy (*mafhūm al-kināyah*), which is what differs from their explicit wording, are taken in this way, the contrary of the sending down is likewise taken as an action befitting human composition. So the implied meaning is: "Not other than Allah composed it," in refutation of the saying of the polytheists: "It is the fables of the ancients."

The verification that the author of *al-Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) adopted regarding His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [2:15] is that emphasis and restriction are combined in the attribution of a verbal predicate to the subject. The scholars who commented on *al-Kashshāf* agreed with him on this.

The effect of this fronting before the verbal predicate is the realization of what the genitive construction (*iḍāfah*) contains of glorifying the status of the term it is attached to, in His saying ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾, as you have just known. So the intended meaning of *aḥsan al-ḥadīth* ("the best statement") is the very same as the intended meaning of *dhikr Allāh* ("the remembrance of Allah"), which is the Qur'an. The pronoun referring to it was avoided in order to apply the three descriptions to it. They are His saying: "a Book consistent in its parts, repeating [its themes], whereby the skins shiver of those who fear their Lord," etc.

So *kitāban* is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) from *aḥsan al-ḥadīth*, or as an appositive (*badal*) of *aḥsan al-ḥadīth*. And *mutashābihan* is in the accusative as an adjective (*naʿt*) of *kitāban*.

**The first description:** that it is the best statement, i.e., the best report. The definite article is for the genus. *Ḥadīth* means "report," and it was called a *ḥadīth* because the nature of reporting is that it concerns a matter that has occurred and become new. The Qur'an was called *ḥadīth* by the name of part of what it contains of reports about nations and of promise and threat.

As for what it contains of injunctive speech (*inshāʾ*), such as commands, prohibitions and the like, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was its conveyor to people, it ultimately amounts to a report about the command and prohibition of Allah.

The Qur'an has been called *ḥadīth* in many places, such as His saying ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [7:185] in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf,

[Page 386]

and His saying ﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this message﴾ [18:6] in Sūrat al-Kahf.

The meaning of the Qur'an being the best statement is that it is the most excellent of reports, because it includes the most excellent of what reports include: beneficial meanings that comprehend the foundations of faith, legislation, argumentation, alerting to the greatness of the worlds and created beings, the wonders of the creation of man, the intellect, the dissemination of good manners, the summoning of minds to true reflection and reasoning. It also includes the eloquence of its words and the perfection of its meanings, which reach the limit of inimitability. And it includes its being confirmatory of what preceded it of the books of Allah and its being a guardian over them. In attributing its sending down to Allah there is a testimony to its excellence, since the All-Knowing has sent it down with the utmost of the excellences of reports and of remembrance.

**The second description:** that it is a Book, i.e., a collection of speech intended to be read, recited and benefited from, commanded to be written down so that it remains a proof across the passage of time. If speech is made a book, this requires the importance of that speech, the care for its arrangement, and the concern for preserving it in its state.

Since Allah named the Qur'an a Book, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to order the scribes of the revelation from among his companions to write every verse that descended from the revelation in its specific place among its counterparts, relying on a command from Allah. For Allah indicated the command to write it down in many places, the first of which is His saying ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ [85:21] ﴿in a preserved tablet﴾ [85:22], and His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [56:77] ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ [56:78].

**The third description:** that it is *mutashābih*, i.e., its parts are alike (*mutashābihah*), equal in the eloquence of their words and the nobility of their meanings. So they are equivalent in nobility and excellence (and this is like what they say: "a woman who is equal in beauty" (*imra'ah mutanāṣifat al-ḥusn*), meaning her attributes are equitable to one another, such that none of them exceeds another. Ibn Harmah said:

"Indeed I longed for the symmetry of her face,
the longing of a lover for the absent beloved."

From this is their saying: "a face that is divided" (*wajh muqassam*), i.e., equal in beauty, as if its parts divided beauty among themselves and balanced it. Arqam ibn ʿUlbāʾ al-Yashkurī said:

"And one day we met with a face that was divided,
as if a gazelle were stretching toward the leaves of the sallam tree.")

[Page 387]

That is, with a face whose beauty has been apportioned into its parts as portions.

Its meanings are therefore alike in their soundness, their rulings, their being founded on truth and sincerity, their hitting the mark of proof, the rebuking of opponents, and their being a reform and guidance for people. Its words are alike in nobility, eloquence and their hitting the aims of meanings, to the extent that its words and meanings reach the furthest limit that the noblest language of human beings can bear, which is the Arabic language in its vocabulary and composition. For this reason it was inimitable to every eloquent person who might attempt to produce its like. In this there is an indication that all the verses of the Qur'an reach the highest extreme of eloquence and are equal in that according to what the state of each verse requires. As for their variation in the abundance and scarcity of particular features, that follows from the difference of contexts and the requirements of situations. For the eloquence of speech is its conformity to what the situation requires, and the highest extreme of eloquence is the conformity of speech to all that the situation requires. So the verses of the Qur'an are alike and similar in beauty for people of taste among the eloquent, whether by natural disposition or by knowledge. In this it differs from other eloquent speech, for that does not escape variation, which at times reaches the point that some of it does not resemble the rest. This meaning falls under His saying ﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [4:82]. For the eloquent writer and the skilled poet, neither's speech is free of weakness in some part of it. Likewise, neither's sayings resemble each other; rather you find for each of them pieces that vary in beauty, eloquence and soundness of meanings.

From what we have established you know that *mutashābih* here means something other than what is meant in His saying ﴿and others that are *mutashābihāt*﴾ [3:7], because of the difference in the type of similarity involved.

**The fourth description:** that it is *mathānī*. *Mathānī* is the plural of *mathnā* (with a damma on the *mīm* and a shadda on the *nūn*), pluralized irregularly, or it is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*). It may also be the plural of *mathnā* with a fatḥa on the *mīm* and a light *nūn*, which is a noun for making the counted items into pairs, two by two. Both possibilities are used to mean repetition. Repetition is expressed by the root of duality because duality is the first degree of repetition, just as the form of duality is used for repetition in His saying ﴿Then return the vision twice﴾ [67:4], and the Arabs' saying *labbayka wa-saʿdayka* ("at Your service, and again at Your service"), i.e., many responses and many assistances.

The meaning of *mathānī* has already been explained in His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [15:87] in Sūrat al-Ḥijr. So the Qur'an is *mathānī* because its aims are repeated.

[Page 388]

This includes a favour upon the community, that the aims of its Book are repeated in it so that its purposes are more firmly established in their souls, and so that whoever missed hearing their like before may hear them.

It also includes an alert to one aspect of its inimitability: that it is not tiresome to listen to, and that whenever one of its aims is repeated, its repetition increases its acceptance and sweetness in the souls of the listeners. It is like the beautiful face of which Abū Nuwās said:

"Its face increases in beauty for you
whenever you look at it again."

ʿIyāḍ, in *al-Shifāʾ*, counted among the aspects of the inimitability of the Qur'an that its reader does not tire of it, and its listener does not find it distasteful; rather, devotion to its recitation increases its sweetness, and its repetition brings love for it. It never ceases to be fresh and new, whereas other speech, even if it reaches a great degree of beauty and eloquence, becomes tiresome with repetition and is disliked when repeated. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) described the Qur'an as "that which does not wear out through much repetition." Narrated by al-Tirmidhī from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, as a *marfūʿ* (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

ʿIyāḍ also mentioned that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) the verse ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct﴾ [16:90], and he said: "By Allah, it has a sweetness, and upon it is a radiance."

From this you know that the description of the Qur'an here as *mathānī* is other than the description in His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [15:87], because what is meant by duality in each is different, even though the derivation of the description is the same.

*Kitāban*, although singular, is described by *mathānī*, which requires plurality. This indicates that this description was applied to it with regard to its parts, i.e., its surahs or verses, in the sense that each aim within it is repeated, i.e., with regard to its subdivisions.

**The fifth description:** that the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and their hearts soften. This description is consequent upon the description before it, which is the Qur'an being *mathānī*, i.e., its aims repeated. It contains three aspects.

The first: the description of the Qur'an with awe and majesty in the hearts of its hearers. This is because in its many verses there is the admonition at which hearts tremble. This is a description of perfection, for it is one of the effects of the strength of its speech's influence on souls. The concern of the people of oratory and wisdom has always been to achieve the aim of their speech, because speech is addressed to listeners in order to obtain hoped-for benefits from acting upon it. The orators and eloquent people have competed in the arenas of speech only to race toward the goals of persuasion. As Qays ibn Kharijah said, when he was asked: "What do you have?" "I have the hospitality of every guest, the contentment of every angry person, and a sermon from the rising of the sun until its setting, in which I command kinship and forbid severing it." Aristotle also mentioned, regarding the aim of rhetoric, that it is the stirring of passions, and he said: "They are emotions in the soul that stir in it sorrow or joy."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 23 (part 2 of 2):

The phrase ﴿the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it﴾ implies that the Qur'an contains meanings that make the skins shiver, namely the meanings characterized by jazala (majesty and forcefulness of expression), which stir in souls a awe, grandeur and dread that move the listeners to obey it and to act upon what they receive of the Qur'an's admonitions and warnings. This is expressed by a state that accompanies the emotion of khashya (fear) and awe in the soul, because when a person is startled and fears, his skin shivers as an effect of the emotion of awe. So the meaning of ﴿shiver from it﴾ is: they shiver from hearing it and understanding it, since hearing and understanding are concurrent on that occasion, because the listeners are people of the tongue. It is said: iqshaʿarra al-jild (the skin shivered) when it contracts intensely, like what occurs at the intensity of the cold of the body and its trembling. It is said: iqshaʿarra jiluduhu (his skin shivered) when he hears or sees something that disturbs him and startles him. Thus, the shivering of the skins is a metaphor for the trembling of hearts, which is generally accompanied by a goose-bump sensation in the skin.

ʿIyad, in al-Shifa', counted among the aspects of the Qur'an's inimitability: the awe that reaches the hearts of its listeners when they hear it, and the reverence that seizes them when it is recited, due to the elevation of its rank above every speech, which is such that its listener must revere it. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, split asunder from the fear of God. And these are the parables We present to people that perhaps they may reflect﴾ [al-Hashr: 21].

On the authority of Asma' bint Abi Bakr: the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, when the Qur'an was recited to them, as God described them, their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver.

The shivering is specified to "those who fear their Lord" in view of what follows it in His saying ﴿then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God﴾, as will come.

ʿIyad said: and it — that is, the awe that reaches the hearts of its listeners when they hear it — is greater for the deniers of it, to the extent that they found its hearing burdensome, as God the Exalted says: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion﴾ [al-Isra': 46].

This awe has seized a group before Islam, and among them were those who embraced Islam immediately because of it. It is related in the authentic hadith from Jubayr ibn Mut'im who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ reciting in the Maghrib prayer Surat al-Tur, and when he reached His saying ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35] up to His saying ﴿the controllers﴾, my heart almost flew away, and that was the first time Islam settled in my heart."

And among them were those who did not embrace Islam. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi who said: "I was informed that ʿUtba ibn Rabi'a spoke to the Prophet ﷺ about refraining from reviling their idols and misguiding them, and he offered him matters while the Prophet ﷺ was listening. When he finished, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'Listen to what I say,' and he recited to him Ha-Mim [Surat Fussilat] until he reached His saying ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13]. Then ʿUtba placed his hand over the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ and adjured him by the ties of kinship to stop; that is, to stop reciting."

"As for the believer, the awe and reverence that it inspires in him, along with its recitation, keeps him drawn to it and gives him gentleness, because his heart inclines towards it. God the Exalted says: ﴿their skins shiver from it, then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of God﴾."

The second aspect of this description: the softening of the hearts of believers upon hearing it, after their momentary awe arising from hearing it before.

Softness (al-liyn) is used metaphorically for acceptance and joy, and it is the opposite of the hardness mentioned in His saying ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God﴾. When the believer hears verses of threat and warning, he fears his Lord and avoids what he was warned against, so his skin shivers. When this is followed by verses of glad tidings and promise, he rejoices and is delighted, and he compares his deeds with those verses, seeing himself adorned with the deed for which God promised reward, so his soul becomes tranquil and the dread and fear turn into hope and expectation. That is the meaning of the softening of hearts.

What arouses this softness in hearts is the meanings of mercy in the Qur'an, namely in the verses whose meanings are described as easy, such as His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God; indeed God forgives all sins; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and those whose meanings are described as tender, such as: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve, those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims﴾. It is known in the art of rhetoric (khitaba) that majesty (jazala) has its situations, and ease and tenderness have their situations.

The third aspect of this description: the marvel of its combining two opposite effects: at one time through the effect of dread, and at another time through the effect of desire, so that the Muslims conduct themselves toward their Lord in accordance with what His majesty requires and what His forbearance and mercy require. This aspect is required by the combination of the two aspects explicitly stated, namely the aspect of shivering and the aspect of softness, while the one described by both is a single group, namely those who fear their Lord. The intent is to describe them by the two effects upon the succession of verses of mercy after verses of dread. Al-Fakhr said: "The realized people of perfection have said: the wayfarers at the beginning of the majesty of God, if they look at the world of majesty they are overwhelmed, and if a trace of the world of beauty appears to them, they live." End of quotation. So the verse here mentions for them both states because it comes after the word "mathani," as we pointed out just above. Otherwise, God described the believers with trembling only in His saying ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ in Surat al-Anfal. The context here is to explain the believers' being affected by the Qur'an, while the context there is praise of the believers for fear of God outside of the state of reciting the Qur'an.

The reason both skins and hearts are combined in His saying ﴿then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God﴾, and one of the two was not left to stand for the other as in His saying ﴿the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it﴾, is that the shivering of the skins is a state that befalls them and can only come from the trembling and dread of the hearts, so it is used as a metaphor for that dread.
