As for the softening of the skins after that shivering, it is the return of the skins to their earlier state before they shivered, and that may occur through forgetfulness or preoccupation after that dread. So the softening of hearts is attached to it, to make known that it is a special softness arising from the tranquility of hearts through remembrance, as God the Exalted says: ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God hearts find rest﴾. It is not merely the return of the skins to the state they were in before the shivering. The hearts were not left out in favor of the softening of the skins because the intent is that the softness of the hearts had filled them until its effect appeared upon the outer surface of the skins.

"The remembrance of God," which is "the best of speech," and the pronoun referring to Him was set aside because of the distance of the return, and the repetition of His name previously mentioned was set aside in favor of praising it as a remembrance from God after it was praised as the best speech. The intended meaning of "the remembrance of God" is what is in His verses of the mention of mercy and glad tidings, because the Qur'an never mentions admonition and intimidation without following it with encouragement and glad tidings.

The verb "talin" (softens) is followed by the preposition "ila" (to) because "talin" is implicitly used with the sense of: "tutma'inn" (is at rest) and "taskun" (is calm).

* * *

﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides thereby whom He wills, and whoever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾

This is a bayani resumption (istinaf bayani), for the attribution to the Qur'an of those brilliant qualities, indicating that it has achieved the utmost that a eloquent speech can be described with, and how its effects reached the souls of those who fear their Lord, raises a question that occurs to the listener's mind: "How were the souls of the group persisting in disbelief not affected by it, while it strikes their ears day after day?" So the sentence "That is the guidance of God; He guides thereby whom He wills" comes as an answer to this occurring question.

So the reference is to the content of the described qualities of the Qur'an and the believers' being affected by its guidance; that is: that which was mentioned is the guidance of God, meaning God made it a complete cause comprising all means of guidance. Whoever God has created with a mind and soul disposed to accept guidance, quickly or slowly, is guided by it. Likewise, whoever God has created with a heart disposed to obstinacy or corruption of understanding goes astray and is not guided until he dies in his error. Thus the name of guidance and the name of misguidance are applied to this natural disposition, and both are attributed to God, because He is the one who molds hearts upon their natural disposition, the creator of the means for that, and the manager of its laws and systems.

So the meaning of attributing guidance to God in His saying "That is the guidance of God" returns to what God prepared for guidance from the qualities of the Qur'an, so its attribution to Him is because He sent it down for that purpose.

The meaning of attributing guidance and misguidance to God returns to the degrees of the addressees' being affected by the Qur'an and their not being affected, such that the Qur'an was complete in the causes of people's being guided by it, so some of them were guided by it and some of them strayed from it.

It is also possible that the reference is to "the best speech," which is the Book; that is: that Qur'an is the guidance of God, meaning a sign of God's guidance. Its purpose: whoever God wills to guide is guided by it, and whoever God wills to misguide disbelieves in it.

So the clause "and whoever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide" is a concluding tailpiece (tadhyil) to the bayani resumption.

The meaning of "He guides thereby whom He wills" is according to the estimate: whom He wills to guide, that is, whose guidance is subject to His will, which is His determination that he be guided. So He created him affected by that will, and decreed guidance for him. It is understood from "whom He wills" that He does not guide by it whom He does not will to guide, which is what the contrast with "and whoever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide" indicates: that is, whom He does not will to guide, so he does not desist from his error, and so there is no path to his guidance.

The meaning: that this is due to a deficiency in the one who strays, not in the Book, whose nature is guidance.

﴿Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...﴾

This sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ, an interjected phrase that interrupts the main line of speech) between the praise of the Qur'an in what came before and His saying that follows: ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾.

The exegetes (mufassirun) made it a consequence (tafri', a clause that follows from and builds on what precedes it) of the preceding sentence, ﴿This is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills, and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾. By the combination of the two sentences, they indicate two groups: a group that is guided and a group that is astray. On this basis, this interrogative, used in a figurative sense, follows.

The exegetes posited an ellipsis (hadhf) in the speech, the supplied element being: "like one who is safe from the punishment," or "like one who is in bliss." They took the interrogative to be either affirmative-confirmatory (taqrir) or reproachful (inkar). The intended meaning is that there is no equality between the one who is in punishment, namely the astray, and the one who is in bliss, namely the one whom Allah has guided. The state of the other group is omitted because it is evident from the contrast that the interrogative implies. This is based on the view that this construction is similar to His saying ﴿Is one upon whom the word of punishment has come due...﴾ and His saying ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar: 22]. The discussion of it is the same as the discussion of the preceding one regarding the interrogative and the omission of the predicate. Its supplied form is: "Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment (like one who is safe), because Allah has led him astray, like one who is safe from the punishment because Allah has guided him?" This is like His exalted saying ﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord like one to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive?﴾ [Muhammad: 14]. The meaning is that those who were guided will not be touched by the punishment.

In my view, it is also permissible that the speech be a consequence of the sentence ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾, a consequence that specifies what the word "whoever" (man) refers to in His saying ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. Then "one who shields himself" (man yattaqi) is the predicate of an omitted subject, its supplied form being: "Is it he who shields his face from the evil of the punishment?" and the interrogative is for confirmation (taqrir).

Al-ittiqa' (self-protection, from the root w-q-y, meaning to guard or shield): it is the exertion of wiqaya (protection), which is guarding and warding off. Its verb is transitive to two objects; it is said: "he protected himself the striking of the sword," and it is transitive with the preposition bi- to the means of protection; it is said: "he protected himself with his shield." Al-Nabigha said:

"The veil fell, though she did not intend to drop it, so she caught it and shielded us with her hand."

When a person's face is not, by nature, something that is shielded by something of the body, since the face is the most honored part of the body and it is shielded but is not itself used as a shield, then, because it is in human nature that when a person anticipates that something will strike his body he covers his face out of fear for it, it becomes necessary that "shielding by the face" is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for not being protected, in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum) or wit (tamlih). It is as if it were said: "whoever seeks the protection of his face will find nothing to protect it with except his face." This is the affirmation of a thing by something resembling its negation. Close to this is His saying ﴿If they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

﴿the evil of the punishment﴾ (su' al-'adhab) is in the accusative as the object of the verb "yattaqi." Its original form is the second object, since the original is: "he protected himself the evil of the punishment." When the reflexive form (iftial) was derived from it, the verb became transitive to one object, which was the one that had been the second object.

* * *

﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn.﴾

It is permissible that "and it will be said" (wa qila) be coordinated with the relative clause (silla), the supplied sense being: "Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment...and it will be said to them?" Here "man" is intended to mean a plural. The expression "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) is an explicit noun in the place of the pronoun, to indicate that what they encounter of punishment is caused by their wrongdoing, that is, their shirk (associating others with Allah).

The meaning: "Is one who shields his face from the evil of the punishment, and so finds no protection that saves him from tasting the punishment, when it is said to them: Taste the punishment?"

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" be all those among the nations who associated others with Allah, not restricted to the polytheists spoken of here. Then "the wrongdoers" is an explicit noun in its original place for the purpose of generality. The sentence then serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil, a closing statement that generalizes the lesson), meaning: "And this is said to these and to those like them." By this, the reason for its being followed by His saying ﴿The people before them denied﴾ becomes clear.

The verb "wa qila" came in the past form while it refers to the future, because its occurrence is certain, so it was treated as a verb in the past.

It is also permissible that the clause "And it was said to the wrongdoers" be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with "qad" (indicating completion) understood, and for this reason there is no need to interpret the past form as a certain future event.

Al-dhawq (tasting) is used metaphorically for the sensation of the outer body, because the sensation of tasting by the tongue is more intense than the sensation of the outer skin. So the point of resemblance is the intensity of the kind of perception.

The thing tasted is the punishment, and it is the recompense for what they earned in the world of shirk and its laws. So the thing tasted was made to be the very thing they used to earn, as an exaggeration (mubalagha) indicating that the recompense corresponds to their deeds and that Allah is just in punishing them.

"You used to earn" (taksibun) was preferred over "you used to do" (ta'malun) because their address occurred while they were shielding themselves from the evil of the punishment, and the state of one being punished is never free of impatience, which is like denial toward the one who punishes him. So there was brought the relative clause that indicates that what they tasted is the recompense of what they earned, in order to cut off their impatience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 25–26:

[Page 395]
﴿Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because what was mentioned before it concerns the destiny of the polytheists, who will face the evil punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and on the Day when it is said to the wrongdoers, them and their like: "Taste what you used to earn." This raises in the souls of the believers a question about the polytheists' enjoyment of blessings in this world, and their wish that punishment be hastened upon them. So the answer to that is His saying ﴿Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ That is: they are liable to have the punishment come upon them as it came upon those before them, since the punishment came upon them in this world without a warning, while they were not awaiting its arrival. This is similar to His exalted saying ﴿Then do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed before them?﴾ [Yunus: 102]. So the punishment of this world was a disgrace, with which Allah recompenses whomever He wills of the wrongdoers, while the punishment of the Hereafter is a requital with which Allah recompenses the wrongdoers for their wrongdoing.

The fa' in His saying "fa-atahumu al-'adhab" (then the punishment came upon them) indicates that denial caused the punishment to come upon them. Since the polytheists of the Arabs shared with them in denying the Messenger (ﷺ), the cause of the punishment's descent upon those people was present in them too, so it is a warning that there will befall them the like of what befell those.

The pronoun in "min qablihim" (before them) refers to those who protect themselves, by their face, from the evil punishment, considering that the meaning of "man" is plural. In this there is an allusion warning the polytheists of a punishment that will befall them in this world, namely the punishment of the sword, with which Allah disgraced them on the day of Badr. Thus what is meant by the punishment that came upon those before them is the punishment of this world, because it is that which is described as coming "from where they did not perceive."

"Haythu" (from where) is a adverb of place; that is, the punishment came upon those before them from a place they did not perceive. Thus, for some people it came from the sky in the form of thunderbolts; for some it came from the air, like the wind of 'Ad, as He, exalted, said: "So when they saw it as a cloud coming toward their valleys, they said, 'This is a cloud bringing us rain.' Rather, it is what you were hastening: a wind in which is a painful punishment" [al-Ahqaf: 24]; for some it came from beneath them with earthquakes

[Page 396]
and sinking, like the people of Lut; for some it came from the gushing of water from the earth, like the people of Nuh; and for some the sea overwhelmed them, like the people of Pharaoh.

The punishment that struck the disbelievers of Quraysh had never crossed their minds: the cutting of their necks by swords while they were in honour and esteem among their people and among the Arab tribes. They never imagined that hands would cut their necks, as was the case with Abu Jahl when he was in the throes of death on the day of Badr, when Ibn Mas'ud said to him, "Are you Abu Jahl?" He replied, "And is there any man greater than one whom his own people have killed?"

The metaphor of "tasting" (idhaqah) for the experience of disgrace is an imaginative metaphor (takhyiliyyah), being of the type of likening an intelligible matter to a sensible one.

"Wa la'adhabu al-akhirati akbar" is joined to it as a safeguard (li-l-ihtiras), meaning: the punishment of the Hereafter is the requital, whereas the punishment of this world may befall some of the wrongdoers by Allah's will, as an increase of disgrace for them.

His saying "﴿if only they knew﴾" is an intervening clause (jumlah mu'taridah) at the end of the statement.

The object of "ya'lamun" (they know) is indicated by the preceding discourse; that is: if these people knew that Allah made the others taste disgrace in this world because of their denial of the messengers, and that Allah has prepared for them a punishment in the Hereafter that is more severe, [they would have believed].

The pronoun in "ya'lamun" refers to what the pronoun in "qablihim" refers to.

The answer of (law) is omitted, indicated by the allusion to threat in His saying "those before them denied," etc.; its estimate is: if they knew that what befell them was caused by their denial of their messengers, just as these people denied Muhammad (ﷺ), [they would have been warned].

The description of the punishment of the Hereafter as "akbar" (greater) means "ashaddu" (more severe): it is more severe in quality than the punishment of this world, and more severe in quantity because it is everlasting.

﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may remember.﴾ ﴿An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they may be mindful of God.﴾

This is a conjunction with the statement ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾ up to His saying ﴿for him there is no guide﴾. It completes the praise of the Qur'an and its guidance, and it contains an implicit rebuke of the foolish understanding of those who denied it

[Page 397]

and turned away from being guided by its direction.

The emphasis of the statement with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of certainty (harf al-tahqiq) is directed at the state of the group who did not reflect upon the Qur'an, who slandered it and who denied that it is from God.

The definite article in "al-nas" (the people) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), meaning all people, since God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to all of mankind.

Daraba al-mathal (to strike an example) means to mention it and describe it. It has already been discussed in His saying, ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present an example﴾, in Surat al-Baqarah.

The nunation (tanwin) of "mathal" is for magnification and nobility, meaning: from every most noble of examples. The meaning is: We have mentioned to the people in the Qur'an examples that are part of every most beneficial and most noble of examples. What is intended is the nobility of its benefit.

The examples of the Qur'an were singled out for mention among the Qur'an's virtues in order to draw their insight to reflect upon a great aspect of its inimitability, namely the eloquence of its examples, since their eloquent ones used to compete in the excellence of examples and in hitting the mark in likening one situation to another.

This was already mentioned at His saying ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Isra: 89], in Surat al-Isra, and it was mentioned at His saying ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [al-Rum: 58], in Surat al-Rum.

The meaning of hope in ﴿that they may remember﴾ is directed toward the fact that their state, when the Qur'anic examples are presented, is like the state of one from whom people hope he will remember. This is like the similar instances of this expression of hope occurring in the Qur'an, and it was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of remembrance (tadhakkur) is reflection and deep contemplation, so that there becomes clear to them what they are heedless of. This applies both to what had already been known to them and then forgotten, with them being occupied away from it by trivial matters, and to what had not previously been known to them but which a sound mind would be expected to perceive; once it becomes clear to him, it is as if it were something whose knowledge he already had but had forgotten. Thus the meaning of remembrance is a wonderful and comprehensive meaning that includes these characteristics.

This is the description of the Qur'an in itself: if it encounters a clear intellect and a soul free

[Page 398]

from obstinacy, then the believers who were already believers are reminded by it, and whoever was reminded by it becomes a cause for his faith after his disbelief, either quickly or slowly. As for those who were not reminded by it, their failure to be reminded is due to a deficiency in their natural disposition and to stubbornness covering their minds.

The same applies to the meaning of His saying ﴿that they may be mindful of God﴾.

"Qur'anan" (an Qur'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the demonstrative pronoun explained by "al-Qur'an". So the state here is a preparatory state (hal muwatti'ah), because it serves as a preparation for the qualifier (na't) in His saying ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat: 3]. Although by the apparent wording "Qur'anan" is an emphatic state (hal mu'akkadah), the consideration is with what follows it. For this reason al-Zajjaj said: "Arabiyyan" is in the accusative as a state, meaning: because it is a qualifier of the state.

The purpose of this state is an implicit censure of the polytheists, in that they received the Qur'an as one who hears speech he does not understand, as if it were in a language other than his own, so he gives it no attention. This is like His saying ﴿We have only made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember﴾ [al-Dukhan: 58], together with the challenge to them that they were unable to produce its equal, though it is in their own language. It is also a praise of the Qur'an in that it is speech with soundness of its wording, since the Arabic language is the most eloquent of human languages.

Al-'iwaj (crookedness), with a kasra on the 'ayn, is intended to mean the disruption of meanings rather than of physical forms. As for al-'awaj, with a fatha on the 'ayn, it includes both. This is the preferred view of the leading lexicographers such as Ibn Duraid, al-Zamakhshari, al-Zajjaj and al-Firuzabadi. Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on al-Fasih, held that the two are the same. This was already discussed at His saying ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness﴾ in Surat al-Kahf, and at His saying ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness﴾ [Ta-Ha: 107], in Surat Ta-Ha.

This is a praise of the Qur'an for the completeness of its meanings, after it has been praised for the soundness of its wording.

The reason for shifting from describing it as sound (istiqamah) to describing it as free of crookedness is to achieve the indefinite noun "'iwaj" in the context of what has the sense of negation, which is the word "ghayr" (without). This conveys the negation of the whole category of crookedness in a general sense, meaning: there is no crookedness in it at all. Also, the word "'iwaj" is specific to the disruption of meanings, so the statement is an explicit text on the soundness of the meanings of the Qur'an, since the indication of the soundness of its wording and arrangement has already been drawn from describing it as Arabic, as you have just understood.

[Page 399]

His saying "that they may be mindful of God" is like His saying ﴿that they may remember﴾. It mentions "yattaqun" (be mindful) here because when they are reminded, piety becomes easy for them. Also, remembrance is more appropriate to the striking of examples, since in examples there is a lesson from the circumstances of the thing used as the example, so they lead to remembrance; whereas mindfulness is more appropriate to the absence of crookedness, since when its meanings are sound and clear, acting upon what it calls to becomes easier, and that is piety.

The examples of the Qur'an were singled out for mention among the Qur'an's virtues in order to draw their insight to reflect upon a great aspect of its inimitability, namely the eloquence of its examples, since their eloquent ones used to compete in the excellence of examples and in hitting the mark in likening one situation to another.

This was already mentioned at His saying ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Isra: 89], in Surat al-Isra, and it was mentioned at His saying ﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [al-Rum: 58], in Surat al-Rum.

The meaning of hope in ﴿that they may remember﴾ is directed toward the fact that their state, when the Qur'anic examples are presented, is like the state of one from whom people hope he will remember. This is like the similar instances of this expression of hope occurring in the Qur'an, and it was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of remembrance (tadhakkur) is reflection and deep contemplation, so that there becomes clear to them what they are heedless of. This applies both to what had already been known to them and then forgotten, with them being occupied away from it by trivial matters, and to what had not previously been known to them but which a sound mind would be expected to perceive; once it becomes clear to him, it is as if it were something whose knowledge he already had but had forgotten. Thus the meaning of remembrance is a wonderful and comprehensive meaning that includes these characteristics.

This is the description of the Qur'an in itself: if it encounters a clear intellect and a soul free

[Page 398]

from obstinacy, then the believers who were already believers are reminded by it, and whoever was reminded by it becomes a cause for his faith after his disbelief, either quickly or slowly. As for those who were not reminded by it, their failure to be reminded is due to a deficiency in their natural disposition and to stubbornness covering their minds.

The same applies to the meaning of His saying ﴿that they may be mindful of God﴾.

"Qur'anan" (an Qur'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the demonstrative pronoun explained by "al-Qur'an". So the state here is a preparatory state (hal muwatti'ah), because it serves as a preparation for the qualifier (na't) in His saying ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Fussilat: 3]. Although by the apparent wording "Qur'anan" is an emphatic state (hal mu'akkadah), the consideration is with what follows it. For this reason al-Zajjaj said: "Arabiyyan" is in the accusative as a state, meaning: because it is a qualifier of the state.

The purpose of this state is an implicit censure of the polytheists, in that they received the Qur'an as one who hears speech he does not understand, as if it were in a language other than his own, so he gives it no attention. This is like His saying ﴿We have only made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember﴾ [al-Dukhan: 58], together with the challenge to them that they were unable to produce its equal, though it is in their own language. It is also a praise of the Qur'an in that it is speech with soundness of its wording, since the Arabic language is the most eloquent of human languages.

Al-'iwaj (crookedness), with a kasra on the 'ayn, is intended to mean the disruption of meanings rather than of physical forms. As for al-'awaj, with a fatha on the 'ayn, it includes both. This is the preferred view of the leading lexicographers such as Ibn Duraid, al-Zamakhshari, al-Zajjaj and al-Firuzabadi. Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on al-Fasih, held that the two are the same. This was already discussed at His saying ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness﴾ in Surat al-Kahf, and at His saying ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness﴾ [Ta-Ha: 107], in Surat Ta-Ha.

This is a praise of the Qur'an for the completeness of its meanings, after it has been praised for the soundness of its wording.

The reason for shifting from describing it as sound (istiqamah) to describing it as free of crookedness is to achieve the indefinite noun "'iwaj" in the context of what has the sense of negation, which is the word "ghayr" (without). This conveys the negation of the whole category of crookedness in a general sense, meaning: there is no crookedness in it at all. Also, the word "'iwaj" is specific to the disruption of meanings, so the statement is an explicit text on the soundness of the meanings of the Qur'an, since the indication of the soundness of its wording and arrangement has already been drawn from describing it as Arabic, as you have just understood.

[Page 399]

His saying "that they may be mindful of God" is like His saying ﴿that they may remember﴾. It mentions "yattaqun" (be mindful) here because when they are reminded, piety becomes easy for them. Also, remembrance is more appropriate to the striking of examples, since in examples there is a lesson from the circumstances of the thing used as the example, so they lead to remembrance; whereas mindfulness is more appropriate to the absence of crookedness, since when its meanings are sound and clear, acting upon what it calls to becomes easier, and that is piety.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 29:

﴿Allah sets forth an example: a man in whom are partners quarrelling with one another, and a man belonging wholly to one man. Are the two equal in comparison? All praise is for Allah. But most of them do not know.﴾

This is a resumption (isti'naf), and it is one of the ways of approaching the intended point after a preface. His saying ﴿And We have certainly set forth for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [Az-Zumar: 27] is a preparation (tawti'a) for this example that is struck for the state of the people of polytheism and the state of the people of monotheism. In this transition there is a shift (takhallus) that follows their reminder of what was set forth for them in the Qur'an, every kind of example, in a general and comprehensive manner, as an extended reminder and a renewed guidance, and also as a shift away from the description of the Qur'an as containing every kind of example, to the depiction of the state of those who disbelieved through a particular state.

This example is connected to His saying ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22] up to His saying ﴿those are in manifest error﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22]. It is therefore an example for the state of the one whom Allah has expanded in breast for Islam, and for the state of those whose hearts have hardened.

The verb ﴿ḍaraba Allāh﴾ (Allah set forth) comes in the past form, although the setting forth of this example did not take place except at the time of the revelation of this verse. This is to bring the time of the present state close to the time of the past, for the purpose of creating eagerness to know this example. It is therefore treated as a report about something that has already happened, because souls are more inclined to act upon it, like the words of the muaththin (caller to prayer): "The prayer has been established." In it there is also an alert that this is a matter whose occurrence is certain, as was previously mentioned at His saying ﴿And Allah set forth an example: a town﴾ [An-Nahl: 112] in Surat An-Nahl.

As for the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), he made the verb ﴿ḍaraba﴾ used in the sense of a command, since he explained it with his words: "Set forth for them an example, and say to them what you say about a man from among the slaves in whom partners share, and so on to the end of his words." The apparent meaning of his words is that the report here is used in the sense of a demand. His commentators al-Tibi, al-Qazwini and al-Taftazani established this with a summary whose essence is: he meant that when the Prophet ﷺ heard His saying ﴿And We have certainly set forth for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [Az-Zumar: 27], he knew that an example from the examples of the Qur'an would be revealed to him, so Allah informed him of the truth of what he knew and made it, because of its certainty, as if it were past.

And so that it would suit the directing of the question to them in His saying ﴿Are the two equal in comparison?﴾ (for it is a question of rebuke, tabkit), the parts of the structure of the speech would fit together. Thus the form of the example from its expected form of a command was turned to the form of the past, in order to convey the truthfulness of the knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ. All of this is a more subtle meaning and more suitable to the eloquence of the Qur'an than the view of those who keep the past in the verb ﴿ḍaraba﴾ on its literal sense and say: its meaning is "the setting forth of the example is in His knowledge, so inform your people of it."

What led al-Zamakhshari to adopt this meaning specifically in this verse is his observance of the contextual connections that the context of the speech in which it occurs has specifically. There is no need for it in other verses of similar form, where no such circumstance requires this interpretation. Do you not see that it does not apply to His saying ﴿Have you not seen how Allah set forth an example: a good word﴾ [Ibrahim: 24], as in Surat Ibrahim? We have already pointed to this at His saying ﴿And Allah set forth an example: a town﴾ [An-Nahl: 112] in Surat An-Nahl.

It may be said regarding this and its counterparts that the turning away from being phrased in the form of a command, as in His saying ﴿And set forth for them the example of the people of the town﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13], ﴿And set forth for them the example of two men﴾ [Al-Kahf: 32], ﴿And set forth for them the example of the life of this world﴾ [Al-Kahf: 45], to being phrased in the form of a report, is a means of attributing it to Allah, as an honouring of the status of the example, as we pointed out in Surat An-Nahl.

The attribution of the setting forth of the example to Allah is because He formed its structure without an intermediary, then revealed it to His Messenger ﷺ. The whole Qur'an is by the making of Allah, and in this its examples and other parts are alike. The whole of it is something His Messenger ﷺ is commanded to convey. It is as if He said to him: "Allah has set forth an example, so set it forth for the people and make it clear to them," since the purpose of setting forth this example is to argue against the polytheists and rebuke them with it, by exposing the evil of their condition in associating partners with Allah. The apparent requirement is that the speech proceed in the manner of its counterparts, such as His saying ﴿And set forth for them the example of the people of the town﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13]. Likewise is what came before of commands in such verses as His saying ﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9], ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10], ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 11], ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship﴾ [Az-Zumar: 14], ﴿Say: Indeed the losers﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15], ﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾ [Az-Zumar: 17].

Its purpose may require distinguishing between what was phrased in the form of a report and what was phrased in the form of a command. We distinguish between the two categories in that what was phrased in the form of a report was in a more important context, because it is either an illustration for the invalidating of polytheism, or for the warning of the polytheists, or for something similar. This is unlike what was phrased in the form of a command, which occurs in a context of admonition and exhortation for the Muslims or the People of the Book. This is what we pointed out in general terms in Surat An-Nahl.

His saying ﴿a man in whom are partners﴾ and what follows it is in the position of explanation for ﴿mathalan﴾ (as an example).

Making the example's subject a man is not for the purpose of excluding a woman or a child, but because the man is the one who first comes to people's minds in speech and in stories, and because what is required of men in deeds is more than what is required of a woman or a child, and because a man is more acutely aware of what he is in of ease or toil, whereas a woman and a child may be heedless and distracted.

The clause ﴿in whom are partners﴾ is a qualifier (na't) for ﴿a man﴾. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before ﴿partners﴾ is because the predicate of an indefinite noun may be fronted before it when the noun is qualified, and when it is not qualified the predicate must be fronted, because of the dislike of beginning with an indefinite noun.

The meaning of ﴿fihi shuraka'﴾ (in whom are partners) is: in his ownership are partners.

Al-tashakus (quarrelling) is intense disagreement; and intense disagreement concerning a man is disagreement about his service and his direction.

The majority read ﴿salaman﴾ with a fatha on the sin and a fatha on the lam after it, with a mim; it is the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) of "salima lahu," when it became purely his. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿saliman﴾ in the form of the active participle, from "salima," when it became pure. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, but there is no basis for it. The truth is that the two are equal, as al-Nahhas and Abu Hatim supported. The meaning is: there is no sharing in him for the man.

This is an illustration for the state of the polytheist in the division of his mind among many gods, so he is in bewilderment and doubt about whether some of them are pleased with him and some angry, and in the wavering of his worship if he pleases one of his gods, lest by it he angers its opposite. Their desires are divergent, and some tribes are more entitled to some idols than others. Allah says ﴿and some of them would overpower others﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 91]. He remains lost, not knowing which of them to rely on. His thought is scattered and his heart divided, like a slave in whom partners share, who are owners who cannot be free of disagreement and dispute among themselves. They pass him around in various tasks and push him between their needs. He is bewildered in pleasing them, weary in discharging their rights, never able to be independent for a moment or to gain any rest.

Opposite to this is the illustration of the state of the Muslim monotheist, who performs what his Lord has charged him with, knowing His good pleasure, hoping for His approval and His reward, at ease in mind, like a slave belonging purely to one master who knows his master's will and knows what he has made obligatory upon him. His understanding is one, and his heart is gathered.

The situation is likewise for every follower of truth and every follower of falsehood. Truth is what agrees with what exists in being and reality, while falsehood opposes what is in reality. The follower of truth is not confronted by anything that confuses him concerning Allah, nor anything that burdens his deeds. The follower of falsehood stumbles over slippery paths and flounders in his deeds between contradiction and error.

Then He said ﴿Are the two equal in comparison?﴾, that is: would these two men who are compared be equal in state after you have known the difference between the two states of those to whom they are compared?

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Are the two equal?﴾ may be affirmative (taqriri, seeking confirmation), and it may be negative (inkari, denying). ﴿Hal﴾ (is it that) is used to establish the affirmation or the denial.

﴿Mathalan﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) for the predicate ﴿yastawiyan﴾ (are equal).

Al-mathal means the state. The estimate is: are their two states equal? Equality requires two things or more, and the specification here is in the singular because it denotes the genus, and the plurality is already known from the subject of ﴿yastawiyan﴾. Had the verb been attributed to what the specification refers to, it would have been said: "Are their two examples equal?"

The sentence ﴿All praise is for Allah﴾ may be an answer to the confirmatory interrogative, on the basis that one of the two alternatives on which confirmation is sought is established, and the one to whom confirmation is directed can say nothing but acknowledgement of it. So it is assumed that they acknowledged the non-equality of the two in state, that is, that one of them is better than the other. Such a question does not expect the questioner to receive an answer from him, so it is permissible for the questioner himself to give the answer before the one questioned answers, as in His saying ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [An-Naba': 1], ﴿About the great news﴾ [An-Naba': 2]. It may also be built on the basis that the one questioned has confessed, so the answer is given in accordance with his confession, as here,

[p. 403]

so it is as if they had said: "They are not equal," and that is what the speaker aims at by his question. When their answer matched the aim of the questioner, he praised Allah for the success of his argument. The sentence is then a resumption, and its position is like that of the conclusion after the proof. The sentence ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ is an indication that they were treated as if they had known and acknowledged, while in reality they are not like that.

It may also be an intervening sentence (mu'tariḍa) if the interrogative is taken as negative, so that it is an intervening sentence between the denial and the transitional ﴿bal﴾ (but) in His saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning: they do not know that the two states are unequal. Had they known, they would have chosen for themselves the better of the two, and would not have persisted in polytheism.

This indicates that what they adopted of polytheism and its falsehoods has no connection with knowledge at all; it is ignorance and fabrication. ﴿Bal﴾ here is for the transitional turn (idrab intiqali). The lack of knowledge is attributed to most of them because most of them are the common followers of their leaders, who established for them polytheism and its laws, seeking advantage through status and false praise, to such an extent that this covered their deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 30–31:

﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die.﴾ ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute.﴾

When the discourse from the beginning of the surah proceeded along the course of refuting polytheism and establishing the Oneness of God, and clarifying the difference between the state of the polytheists and the state of the monotheistic believers, in a manner that indicates the preference of the believers' state, and along the course of establishing proof against the falsehood of polytheism and the truth of faith, and guiding the polytheists to reflect upon this Qur'an, and what was interspersed in that implies that they do not desist from their falsehood, and it was concluded with recording their ignorance and their lack of knowledge, this purpose was concluded by referring them to God's judgment between them and the believers on the Day of Resurrection, when they will be unable to deny, and when they turn around and see nothing but the Fire.

It was preceded by a reminder to them that all people are heading toward death, for death is the last thing by which one is admonished who is heedless in his excess, when he has been deceived by the grandeur of life and has not reflected on choosing the path of safety and salvation. This is among the Qur'an's seizing of opportunities for guidance and admonition.

The intended point is His saying, ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute.﴾ So this purpose was seized upon in order that, along with it, an admonition be brought forth through what precedes it of events, perhaps there will be a lesson for them in it. Thereby several benefits were achieved: among them, the preparation for the mention of the Day of Resurrection; and among them, the reminder of the passing of this life. These two are general for both the polytheists and the believers. Among them: urging the believers to hasten to righteous deeds. Among them: informing them that the Messenger ﷺ will die just as the prophets before him died, so that they may seize the benefit of him during his life and be eager to remain in attendance upon his gathering. Among them: that they should not dispute about his death as the nations disputed about others. Among them: teaching the Muslims that God equalized among creation in death without regard to their differences in life, so that consolation may abound and regret may diminish.

So the two clauses, "Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die," are a resumptive statement (isti'naf). And "Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute" is conjoined to them by the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates a sequence of rank, because the announcement of the separation between them on the Day of Resurrection is more important in this context than the announcement that they are heading toward death.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is a statement used in an allusive manner regarding the polytheists, since they used to say, "We await for him the vicissitudes of fate" (natarabbasu bihi rayba al-manun). The meaning is: death comes to you and comes to them, so those who say "We await for him the vicissitudes of fate" do not know that they may die before you. And so it was. The Messenger of God ﷺ saw the places of fall of the fiercest of his enemies at the well of Badr. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said:

"The Messenger of God ﷺ invoked against Abu Jahl, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, Umayya ibn Khalaf, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and 'Umara ibn al-Walid. By Him in whose hand my soul is, I indeed saw those whom the Messenger of God had named lying slain in the well, the well of Badr."

The pronoun of the third person in "and indeed, they will die" refers to the polytheists being spoken of. As for the believers, there is no purpose here in informing that they will die, as is clear from the explanation of the verse.

The emphasis of the two statements with "inna" is to realize the allusive meaning intended by them.

What is meant by "mayyit" is one who is heading toward death, so it is the use of the attribute for one who will possess it in the future, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, like the use of the active participle for the future, as in His saying, "Indeed, I am placing upon the earth a khalifa" (vicegerent).

"Mayyit" means one who has become characterized by death, that is, life has departed from him. Similar to it is "maytu" with the sukun on the ya' lightened. The verified view is that there is no difference between them, contrary to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

The emphasis of the clause "Indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute" is to refute the polytheists' denial of resurrection. The placement of "before your Lord" before "you will dispute" is for emphasis and for preserving the rhyme (fasila).

"Al-ikhtisam" (disputing) is a metaphor for judgment between them, that is: He will judge between you concerning what you disputed about in the world, from the polytheists' affirming gods and your negating that. It is like His saying, "Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ" [al-Nahl: 124].

It is also possible that "al-ikhtisam" is applied to the narration of what occurred between them in the world when their deeds are presented, as one says, "This is the dispute of so-and-so and so-and-so," at the opening of a record of a litigation and altercation between the two that is read before the judge.

It is also possible that a dispute between the two groups be imagined on that day, so that the wrongdoers are exposed and the people of truth are delighted, in the manner of His saying, "Indeed, that is the truth: the dispute of the people of the Fire" [Sad: 64].

According to the first interpretation, the pronoun in "you will dispute" refers to the totality of what the pronouns "you" and "they" referred to.

According to the last two interpretations, it may be as in the first interpretation. It may also refer to the entire community, and it is the dispute of the wrongs. The interpretation of the pronoun in this sense has been transmitted in what al-Nasa'i and others narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: "When this verse was revealed, we said: How will we dispute while we are brothers? But when 'Uthman was killed and some of us struck the faces of others with swords, we said: This is the dispute our Lord promised us." Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri a similar statement to that of Ibn 'Umar, but Abu Sa'id said: "When the day of Siffin came and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: Yes, this is it."

Whether the verse includes these interpretations, which is the more fitting, or it does not include them, the intended meaning of it is the dispute of the people of faith and the people of polytheism.

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri a similar statement to that of Ibn 'Umar, but Abu Sa'id said: "When the day of Siffin came and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: Yes, this is it."

Whether the verse includes these interpretations, which is the more fitting, or it does not include them, the intended meaning of it is the dispute of the people of faith and the people of polytheism.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. (Surat az-Zumar)

﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾.

The *fa'* (فاء, the particle of consequence) indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it, in the manner of a judgment following a dispute, referring to the dispute in His words ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute﴾ [39:31]. For you know that *al-ikhtisam* (الاختصام, "disputing") is used metaphorically for the ruling between them concerning what they differed over and denied. The meaning is: He will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and the judgment will be against the one who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him, for he is the one than whom there is no greater wrongdoer. That is, the judgment will be against the polytheists, since they lied against Allah by attributing partners to Him and daughters, and they denied the truth, which is the Qur'an. The referent of "the one who lies against Allah" is the group mentioned in His words ﴿Indeed, they are dying﴾ [39:30], and they are the ones intended in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn"﴾ [39:24].

Their being indebted (to judgment) has been expressed metaphorically by affirming that they are the most unjust, because it is part of justice that the wrongdoer not be left in his wrongdoing. So when the adversary is described as a wrongdoer, it is known that he is the one to be judged against, as He, exalted is He, said, relating about Dawud, ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes﴾ [38:24].

The judgment against them has been turned away from the form of a declarative statement to the form of an interrogative, to indicate that the listener cannot do otherwise than answer that they are the most unjust.

So the interrogative is used figuratively, as *majaz mursal* (مجاز مرسل, a figure of speech where a word is used in a broader or related sense without the metaphorical link of resemblance), or as *kinaya* (كناية, allusive or indirect expression), and what is intended by it is that they are the most unjust of wrongdoers, and that there is no wrongdoer more unjust than them. Its meaning amounts to negating that any group could be more unjust than them, for they committed several kinds of great injustice: the injustice of transgressing against the sanctity of the Lord by lying about His attributes, when they claimed He has partners in lordship; and lying against Him by claiming He commanded them to do what they were upon of falsehood; and the injustice toward the Messenger ﷺ by denying him; and the injustice toward the Qur'an by attributing it to falsehood; and the injustice toward the believers by harming them; and the injustice toward the realities of the world by reversing and corrupting them; and the injustice toward themselves by casting themselves into the everlasting punishment.

The speech departed from using the pronoun "*hum*" (هم, "they") to using the relative pronoun, because of what the relative clause contains of indication of the reason they are the most unjust of people.

The explanation was restricted to their having lied against Allah and denied the truth, because these two lies are the sum of the aforementioned injustice they committed.

*As-sidq* (الصدق, truth) is the opposite of *al-kadhib* (الكذب, falsehood).

By "the truth" is meant the Qur'an, which the Prophet ﷺ brought. The coming of the truth to them means its reaching them, that is, their hearing it and understanding it, for it is in their language and came with the most eloquent clarity, such that no one turns away from it except an obstinate person who prefers the portions of desire and falsehood over the portions of fairness and salvation.

In the combination of the word "*as-sidq*" (the truth) and the verb "*kadhdhaba*" (denied) there is a *muhassin al-tibaq* (محسن الطباق, the embellishment of antithesis).

The phrase ﴿when it came to him﴾ is connected to "*kadhdhaba*" (denied). "*Idh*" (إذ) is an adverb of past time, and it implies a simultaneity between the time indicated by the clause it is annexed to and the occurrence of its complement. So His words ﴿when it came to him﴾ indicate that they denied the truth immediately upon its reaching them, without delay, that is, they hastened to deny the truth at the moment it reached them, without pausing to exercise sight or to take care in distinguishing truth from falsehood.

The clause ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ explains the content of the clause ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah﴾; that is, their injustice necessitated that their dwelling be in Hell.

The interrogative is *taqriri* (تقريري, affirmative, seeking acknowledgment), and the interrogative was directed toward a negation, while the intended meaning is affirmation, following the common usage of the affirmative interrogative, which is the method of giving the one being affirmed room to deny, since the speaker knows that the addressee cannot deny it, so he will soon acknowledge the affirmation.

It is also possible that the interrogative is *inkari* (إنكاري, rejecting), a refutation of their belief that they would be saved from the Fire, which is indicated by their insistence on turning away from reflecting on the call of the Qur'an.

"*Al-kafirun*" (الكافرون, the disbelievers) are those who disbelieved in Allah, so they ascribed partners to Him, or who denied the messengers after the evidence of their truthfulness had become manifest. The definite article in "*al-kafirun*" is for the genus, which conveys comprehensiveness, so it includes the disbelievers being spoken of, in a primary inclusion.

The clause may also be *mufida li-l-tadhyil* (مفيدة للتذييل, serving as a concluding generalization), and the requirement that the destiny of the disbelievers being spoken of is the Fire is established by a kind of evidence that encompasses the destiny of the whole class of which they are a type.

There is no *izhar fi maqam al-idmar* (إظهار في مقام الإضمار, using a noun in place of a pronoun where a pronoun would be expected) in the speech.

*Al-mathwa* (المثوى, dwelling) is the noun of place from *al-thuwa* (الثواء, staying), which is residence. So *al-mathwa* means the abode.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 33–35:

﴿And he who brings the truth and he who confirms it—those are the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿That God may expiate from them the worst of what they did and reward them with their best deeds.﴾

Alladhi jā'a bi-l-ṣidq (he who brings the truth) is Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-ṣidq (the truth) is the Qur'an, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿and denied the truth when it came to him﴾.

The clause wa-ṣaddaqa bihi (and confirms it) is a relative clause of an elided relative pronoun; its implied form is: wa-alladhi ṣaddaqa bihi (and he who confirmed it), because the one who confirms is other than the one who brought the truth. The indication is clear, since the one who confirms is other than the one who brought the truth, so the conjunction is a conjunction of a complete sentence and not a conjunction of a relative clause.

Page 8

The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to "al-ṣidq" and may refer to alladhi jā'a bi-l-ṣidq; confirming both is mutually entailed. Since those who confirmed the Qur'an or the Prophet (ﷺ) and were characterized by this description are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are a group, their description cannot be a relative clause for "alladhi," because its basic form is for the singular. Therefore it must be interpreted as referring to a group, and its indicator is ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾. The reference of the relative pronoun in "wa-ṣaddaqa" was made singular out of regard for the wording of "alladhi," and all of this is part of concision.

Al-Tabari narrated with his chain to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "He who brought the truth is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he who confirmed it is Abu Bakr." This was also said by al-Kalbi and Abu al-'Aliya, and its meaning is that Abu Bakr was the first to confirm the Prophet (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾ is a predicate of the relative noun.

The demonstrative noun was used for the sake of distinguishing them with the utmost distinction.

The pronoun of separation in His saying ﴿they are the God-fearing﴾ conveys the restriction of the class of the God-fearing to he who brought the truth and he who confirmed it, because there is no God-fearing person at that time other than the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions; and all of them are God-fearing, because when the lights of the Messenger (ﷺ) shone upon the souls of those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), their consciences were purified from every evil, so they were preserved by God through piety. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 110].

The meaning: those are the ones in whom was realized what was intended by the sending down of the Qur'an, which was alluded to in His saying ﴿that they may be God-fearing﴾ [al-Zumar: 28].

The clause ﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption, because when the class of the God-fearing was restricted to them, this indicated a great excellence, and so the listener should ask about the reward of this excellence; thus it explained to him that for them is whatever they wish with God.

And ﴿whatever they wish﴾ is what they desire and long for, i.e., God gives them what they seek in Paradise.

The meaning of ﴿with their Lord﴾ is that God has stored up for them what they seek, and this is of the forms of obligation and promise of benefit: one says, "You have such-and-such with me," meaning, "I undertake for you such-and-such." Then it is possible that God inspires them to wish for only what does not exceed the measure of the ranks in Paradise which God has determined, for the people of Paradise differ in ranks. In a hadith: "God says to one of them: Wish! So he keeps wishing until his wishes run out; then God says: For you is that and ten times its like with it."

Page 9

It is also possible that ﴿whatever they wish﴾ refers to what falls within their sight in their palaces, while God withholds from them what is beyond that, such that they do not ask for what is of the gifts of their peers, though it is great; and God uproots from their souls what is not among their portions.

It is also possible that ﴿whatever they wish﴾ is a metonymy for the abundance of what they are given, as in the hadith: "What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human." This is like one who says to someone to whom he has done a great deed: "For you is my judgment," or "For you with me is whatever you ask," while he means what is the utmost of kindness for the likes of him.

He turned from the divine name to the description "their Lord" in His saying "with their Lord," as an allusion that He gives them the gift of lordship and preference with good.

Then He highlighted this promise by His saying: ﴿That is the reward of the good-doers﴾, and the thing referred to is ﴿whatever they wish﴾, because of what it includes of being a reward for them for their confirmation. It was pointed to with a demonstrative noun because it includes exaltation of the status of the one referred to.

By "the good-doers" is meant those described as God-fearing. The apparent requirement was that their pronoun be used, saying, "That is their reward," but the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to convey praise of them as good-doers.

Ihsan (excellence) is the perfection of piety, because the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as: "that you worship God as if you see Him." What greater excellence and piety is there than their rejecting what they were raised upon of worshipping idols, and their bearing the opposition of their families and kin, their enmity and harm, and their patience over the confiscation of their wealth and separation from their wives, confirming him who brought the truth and preferring God's pleasure over the desire of the self and the pleasure of the tribe.

Page 10

His saying: ﴿That God may expiate from them the worst of what they did﴾: the lam is for causation, and it is connected to an elided verb indicated by His saying: ﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾; the implied sense: God promised them that and undertook for them that, so that He may expiate from them the worst of what they did.

The meaning: God promised them an absolute promise so that He may expiate from them the worst of what they did; that is, He promised them that reward only because He wanted to expiate from them the evils of what they did.

The purpose of this report is to inform them of it, so that they may be reassured that they will not be held accountable for what proceeded from them of polytheism and its states.

As for "the worst" (aswa'), it may remain on the apparent sense of the superlative requiring a comparison, so what is meant by "the worst of their deeds" is the greatest of them in evil, and that is polytheism. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." Its annexation to "what they did" is a true annexation. The meaning of polytheism being among what they did is either by way of it being an inward act or by way of what it entails of prostrating to an idol. If He expiates from them the worst of what they did, He expiates from them what is lower than it of their evil deeds by implication, so it conveys that He expiates from them all the evils they did. If by this is meant what preceded before Islam, then the verse covers everyone who confirmed the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Qur'an after having been a disbeliever, for Islam wipes out what came before it. If by this is meant what any of them might do of major sins within Islam, then this expiation is a particular privilege of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for the virtue of companionship is great. It is related from the Messenger of God that he said:

"Do not revile my Companions. By Him in whose hand my soul is, if one of you spent gold equal to Mount Uhud, he would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it."

It is possible that "aswa'" is stripped of the sense of comparison, and it is merely a metaphor for great evil, as in His saying: ﴿He said: My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they call me﴾ [Yusuf: 33], i.e., the act of greatest evil, which is the major sins, and its annexation is then explanatory.

In this verse there is evidence that the rank of companionship with the Prophet (ﷺ) is great.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) also said: "God, God, regarding my Companions! Do not take them as a target after me. Whoever loves them, it is through my love that he loves them; and whoever hates them, it is through my hatred that he hates them; whoever harms them has harmed me; whoever harms me has harmed God; and whoever harms God, He is about to seize him."

The leaders of our righteous predecessors enjoined that none be mentioned of the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ) except in the best mention, and to refrain from what arose among them, and that they are most deserving that the best interpretations be sought for them regarding what passed between some of them, and that the best courses be attributed to them. For this reason the predecessors agreed on declaring as corrupt (tafsiq) Ibn al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i and those who went along with him of the rebels who came from Egypt to Medina to depose 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. They agreed that the Companions of the Camel and the Companions of Siffin were in dispute out of ijtihad, and that what impelled them to it was only the striving for the good of Islam and the defense of its community from division and disorder seeping into it. They are all our exemplars and the intermediaries for conveying the Shari'a to us, and disparaging some of them leads to fears for the religion. For this reason our scholars established the uprightness (adala) of all the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The divine name is made explicit in the place of the pronoun, "their Lord," in His saying ﴿That God may expiate from them﴾, to increase the firmness of the report of the expiation of their evils, establishing the reassurance of their souls with the promise of their Lord.

Coordinated with the verb made a cause first is a second verb which is a second cause: ﴿and reward them with their best deeds﴾, and this is the real aim of the causation for the promise contained in His saying ﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾.

The preposition in His saying "bi-aḥsan alladhi kānū ya'malūn" (with the best of what they were doing) is for causality (sababiyya), and it is a fixed adverbial phrase describing (ajrahum); it is not connected with the verb (yajziyahum). The meaning: He rewards them with a reward for their best deeds. Since the reward for their best deeds is by this promise, "For them is whatever they wish with their Lord," this indicates that they are rewarded for what is less than the best of their good deeds; by the indication of the description "the best" that the cause of the reward is being the best, and this entails that the good has an effect on the reward. So if the reward for their best deeds is that for them is whatever they wish with their Lord, the reward for what is less than the best of their deeds is a reward less than that, by their being recompensed with an increase and a bonus beyond what they deserved for their best deeds, in the form of greater luxury, honor, or the like.

**Page 13 (commentary on Surah al-Zumar, 39:36)**

﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they threaten you with those other than Him.﴾

When Allah struck a parable for the polytheists and the believers, using the example of a man who has partners who are at odds with one another, and a man who belongs wholly to one master, that parable was apt to prompt a polytheist speaker to say: "Our partners will gang up against the one who came to belittle and revile them." It was also apt to stir the polytheists' zeal (*hamiyyah*) to defend their gods, as the polytheists of Abraham's people said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ [al-Anbiya: 68]. Their zeal may even have moved them to threaten the Messenger (ﷺ). In al-Kashshaf and in Tafsir al-Qurtubi it is reported that the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We fear that our gods will unhinge you (*takhbilaka*), and we fear for you their harm (*ma'arrah*) through an evil eye (*ʿayn*)," where *ma'arrah* (with *ʿayn* after the *mīm*) means being struck by something harmful, and they meant that they feared the harm that would come to you for reviling them. Ibn ʿAtiyyah's Tafsir contains something with the same meaning. So when Allah related their denial of the Prophet, He turned the discourse to what they had threatened him with and the fear they had instilled in him from the evil of their idols, saying: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they threaten you with those other than Him.﴾

This statement is joined (*maʿtuf*) to His words ﴿Allah has struck a parable: a man in whom there are partners at odds, and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾ [al-Zumar: 29]. The meaning is: Allah, whom you have singled out for worship, is sufficient to protect you from the evil of the polytheists and the falsehood of the gods they worship besides Him. His words ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ are a preface (*tamhid*) to His words ﴿yet they threaten you with those other than Him﴾. The preface is placed first in order to hasten the distress of the polytheists at this, and this entails hastening the joy of the Messenger (ﷺ), since Allah guarantees him protection, as in His words ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137].

The original arrangement of the wording was: "They threaten you with those other than Allah, while Allah is sufficient for you." He altered the order of the wording for this purpose. You may also keep the wording in its ordinary sequence, so that the clause ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ is a new sentence (*isti'naf*) and the clause ﴿they threaten you﴾ becomes a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

The Prophet (ﷺ) is referred to by the explicit noun "His servant" rather than by a pronoun of address, because the aim is to direct the speech toward the polytheists. The second object of *kafin* (sufficient) is omitted, since it is evident that the intended meaning is "sufficient for you against their harm." As for the idols, they cannot inflict harm until the Messenger (ﷺ) is protected from it. The interrogative form is a denial of their assumption that the Messenger (ﷺ) has no protector against the harm of the idols.

By "His servant" (*ʿabdahu*) is necessarily meant the Messenger (ﷺ), as indicated by the context of ﴿they threaten you﴾.

Mentioning the Messenger (ﷺ) by the attribute of servanthood and attaching it to the divine name (Allah) carries a great meaning: it honours him with this attachment and establishes that He will not hand him over to his enemies.

The address in ﴿they threaten you﴾ is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third-person pronoun referring to "His servant." The purpose of this shift is to make clear that the intention of the Prophet (ﷺ) is exclusively directed at the content of this clause, unlike the clause ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾, as you have understood just now.

"Those other than Him" are the idols. He referred to them, though they are stones, with the relative pronoun used for rational beings, because their designation in speech very often takes the forms used for rational beings. The phrase "other than Him" is the complement of the relative pronoun, with an implied verb to which the prepositional phrase is attached, indicated by the context; its estimated form is: "they took them besides Him" or "they worshipped them besides Him."

In the Tafsir of al-Baydawi it occurs that the cause of revelation of this verse was the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to demolish al-ʿUzzaa, and that the guardian (*sadin*) of al-ʿUzzaa said to Khalid: "I warn you about her, O Khalid, for she has a power that nothing can withstand." Khalid then went to al-ʿUzzaa and smashed her nose until he broke her with the axe, and Allah revealed this verse. He interpreted the address in His words ﴿they threaten you﴾ as meaning that their threatening of Khalid was intended as a threat to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that this verse would be Medinan, and the context of the verse stands in for this. Perhaps whoever said this intended only to cite a well-known example of the polytheists threatening the Prophet (ﷺ) with their idols.

﴿Whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide. And whoever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾ [al-Zumar: 37].

This is a parenthetical clause (*iʿtiraḍ*) placed between the clause ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ (the verse) and the clause ﴿Is not Allah the Mighty, the Possessor of retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar: 37]. Its purpose in this parenthesis is that their misguidance is an incurable disease, because it is an error established in their souls and their natures, which the passage of days has firmed up and the succession of generations has entrenched, so that a veil has covered their minds. When their misguidance became like something innate and ingrained, its origination was attributed to Allah, as a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the difficulty or impossibility of uprooting it from their souls.

By the negation of a guide in ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ is meant the negation of the attainment of guidance. So the absence of attaining guidance is expressed by the non-existence of a guide, because the failure to attain guidance makes their guide as though he did not exist.

His words in Surah al-Aʿraf have already been mentioned: ﴿Whoever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 186].

The two verses are equivalent in conveying the negation of the category of guide. However, in this verse that meaning is conveyed by the addition of *man* (whoever/anyone) as an explicit statement of the negation of the category. In the verse of al-Aʿraf, *hadin* is built on the fatha after *la* (the negation of the category), because the building of its noun on the fatha indicates that the intended meaning is the explicit negation of the category. The difference between the two styles is a variation in speech (*tafannun*), and it is one of the aims of eloquent speakers.

The fronting of *lahu* (for him) before *hadin* (guide) is for emphasis on their state (*idtimam bi-damirihim*) in the context of negating a guide for them, because their misguidance described here is extremely shameful, since it has reached the point where they hope to threaten the Prophet (ﷺ) with their idols, while it is plain to anyone who considers his call that he pays no heed to their idols, and since they believe in the power of their idols while being heedless of the power of the true Lord. This differs from the verse of al-Aʿraf, which mentions their turning away from reflecting on the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that is a lesser misguidance than the misguidance of fearing the might of their idols.

"﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah should intend me some harm, could they remove His harm? Or if He should intend me mercy, could they withhold His mercy? Say: Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely the reliant.﴾"
The clause ﴿Say: Have you considered﴾ comes in the style of recounting a dialogue and exchange with respect to their stated words, the clause ﴿they would surely say, "Allah"﴾. For this reason the second is not conjoined with waw nor with fa'. The meaning is: "They would surely say, 'Allah,' so say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah, etc." The fa' in (Afara'aytum) is for the consequence of the rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) upon their answer, a consequence that serves to argue against them based on the necessary implication of their acknowledgment that Allah is the creator of the heavens and the earth, as in His saying, ﴿Say: Will you then order me to worship other than Allah, O ignorant ones?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64]. "What you invoke besides Allah" is the first object (maf'ul) of (ra'aytum), and the second object is elided, its place taken by the conditional clause's answer that intervenes after the first object, according to the rule of the Arabic language: when a subject (mubtada') and a conditional occur together, what follows them takes the form appropriate to the conditional clause, because the first object of the verbs of the heart is in the sense of the subject.
