Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read with tanwin of the two descriptive words and nasb of "durrihi" and "rahmatihi." This is a difference in the wording of the attachment of the descriptive word to its complement, and the meaning is one.

When Allah had silenced them with this argument, stopping their mouths so that they could not utter a word, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to say, ﴿Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely the reliant﴾. The command to speak was repeated, and "Sufficient for me is Allah" was not included in the first command, because the one commanded to say this is not intended to be addressed to the polytheists, for what preceded it already contains a sufficient persuasion through their scant regard for their idols. Rather, what is intended is that this statement become the emblem (shi'ar) of the Prophet ﷺ in all his affairs, and in it there is a share for the believers with him, which is obtained from His saying, ﴿upon Him rely the reliant﴾. Allah says, ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for those of the believers who follow you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64]. Thus the repetition of the verb "Say" serves to alert to the independence of this purpose from the purpose preceding it.

Hasb means "sufficient." It has preceded in His saying, ﴿And they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], in Al 'Imran.

The omission of the complement in this clause is for the generality of complements, that is: Allah is sufficient for me from everything and in every state.

What is meant by His saying is its belief, then its remembrance, then its public declaration, to teach the Muslims and to enrage the polytheists.

Page 19
Tawakkul is the entrusting of one's affairs to one who suffices for them. It has preceded in His saying, ﴿And when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah; indeed, Allah loves those who rely﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿upon Him rely the reliant﴾ may be part of what he was commanded to say, as a reminder from the Prophet ﷺ and as teaching for the Muslims, in which case the clause is a concluding generalization (tadhyil) of the one before it, because it is more general in terms of those who say it, since "Sufficient for me is Allah" amounts to the meaning: "I have relied upon Allah," that is, sufficient for me and sufficient for every reliant, that is, every believer who knows Allah as He truly should be known and depends on His sufficiency rather than on other than Him. So the definiteness of "the reliant" is for customary generality, that is, the true reliant ones, since no account is taken of others.

It may also be that the clause is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, addressed to His Messenger ﷺ without commanding him to say it, in which case the clause is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to say "Sufficient for me is Allah," that is: make Allah your sufficiency, because the people of tawakkul rely upon Allah alone, and they are the Messengers and the righteous; since you are among their companions, be like them in that, in the manner of His saying, ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. The fronting of the prepositional phrase "upon Him" before "rely" serves to convey exclusivity, because the true people of tawakkul rely upon none but Allah the Exalted, and this is an allusion (ta'rid) against the polytheists who depend in their affairs upon their idols.

[Page 20]

When God had conveyed to them the admonition to its utmost extent, set before them the most compelling of proofs, and firmly established His Messenger ﷺ in the most unshakeable manner, He therefore commanded His Messenger ﷺ to take leave of them as one who expects victory soon, and to promise them the loss that has been prepared for them.

The non-conjunction of the sentence ﴿قُلْ﴾ ("Say") with the sentence ﴿قُلْ حَسْبِيَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Say: God is sufficient for me") [Az-Zumar: 38] is to prevent the misconception that the command "Say: God is sufficient for me" was for the purpose of conveying it to the polytheists. This is similar to the omission of the conjunction in the well-known verse cited in the science of ma'ani (rhetoric, the science of meanings):

[Page 20 continued]

*And Salma thinks that I desire another in her place,*
*while I see her wandering in error.*

He did not conjoin the clause "I see her wandering in error" (*arāhā fī al-ḍalāl*) to the clause "I desire another in her place" (*abghī bihā badalan*), lest it be supposed that it is coordinated with it. It is also because it is a shift from the purpose of invitation and argument to the purpose of warning.

He began the speech with the address by describing them as "my people" (*qawm*), because of what this conveys of tenderness toward their condition and grief over their error, since their being his people requires that he not withhold sincere advice from them.

Al-makāna (position/station) means "place," and its feminine form has been regarded in terms of the meaning of a locality. It is used metaphorically for the condition that surrounds its possessor just as a place surrounds what is in it.

The meaning is: "Act according to your way and your state of enmity toward me." A parallel to this has already been mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

The majority of readers recited *makānatikum* in the singular form. Abū Bakr, from 'Āṣim, recited *makānātikum* in the plural form with an alif and a tā'.

Here He said ﴿مَن يَأْتِيهِ عَذابٌ يُخْزِيهِ﴾ ("upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him"), so that the warning would be of a punishment of disgrace in this world and a lasting punishment in the Hereafter.

As for His saying in Surat al-An'am, ﴿قُلْ يا قَوْمِ اعْمَلُوا عَلى مَكانَتِكم إنِّي عامِلٌ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ مَن تَكُونُ لَهُ عاقِبَةُ الدّارِ﴾ ("Say: O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting, so you will come to know to whom will belong the ultimate outcome of the abode") [Al-An'am: 135], the punishment is not mentioned there because it came after their having been warned by His saying ﴿إنَّ ما تُوعَدُونَ لَآتٍ وما أنْتُمْ بِمُعْجِزِينَ﴾ ("What you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape") [Al-An'am: 134].

The object of "indeed I am acting" (*innī ʿāmilun*) has been omitted, so that it encompasses every object that could be attached to the verb "acting," together with brevity. Its contrast with His saying ﴿اعْمَلُوا عَلى مَكانَتِكُمْ﴾ indicates that by "indeed I am acting" He meant that he remains steadfast in his work of advising them and calling them to what will save them. The omission of that object also indicates that his effort is not limited to the measure of his position and state; rather, his state grows in strength and intensity at every moment, not subject to slackness, and their turning away does not weaken it. This is one of the implications of the omission. We did not point this out in Surat al-An'am or in Surat Hud.

The interrogative *man* (who/what) suspends the verb *ta'lamūna* ("you will know") from governing its two objects.

The disgracing punishment is the punishment of this world, and what is meant here is the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr. The lasting punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, and its lastingness is its eternity. The indefiniteness of *ʿadhāb* in both places is for magnification, and what is intended by it is to inspire awe.

The verb *ya'tīhi* is ascribed to the disgracing punishment because "coming" conveys that it will surprise them, as the night visitor comes. Likewise, the verb *yaḥillu* is ascribed to the lasting punishment because "alighting" (*ḥulūl*) conveys permanence and remaining with them, and this is the punishment of eternity. For this reason the dwelling place of a people is called *ḥilla*, and settled people who do not travel are called *ḥilāl*. Thus the verb is appropriate to describing it as "lasting" (*muqīm*).

The governing of the verb *yaḥillu* by the preposition *ʿalā* indicates its firm establishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own self; and whoever goes astray, he strays only to its detriment. And you are not a guardian over them.﴾

The sentence gives the reason for the command to say to them, ﴿Work according to your position﴾ [al-Zumar: 39], which conveys disengagement from them, belittling the firmness of their disbelief, and strengthening him in his call. The meaning: Because We have sent down the Book to you in truth for the benefit of mankind, and that is sufficient for you as an honour and as guidance, and sufficient for you is its delivery to them. So whoever among mankind is guided, his guidance is for his own self, through your means; and whoever goes astray, not being guided by it, his straying is upon himself, and you bear no responsibility for their straying, because you have delivered what you were commanded.

For this reason, what is here differs from His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 2], because that verse is for the purpose of honouring the Prophet (ﷺ), so it was appropriate that the sending down of the Book be to him. "For mankind" (lil-nas) is connected to "We have sent down," "in truth" (bil-haqq) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book," the bi' indicates accompaniment (mulabasah), and the lam in lil-nas indicates cause, i.e., for the sake of mankind. In the speech there is an implied elided element, understood from what the lam signifies of benefit and advantage, i.e., for the benefit of mankind; or from what the conditional structure in His saying "So whoever is guided" etc. indicates.

The fa' in "So whoever is guided, it is for his own self" is a fa' of consequence (tafri'), and this consequence arises from the meaning of the lam. "Man" (man) is conditional, i.e., whoever is guided in the future, his guidance is for the benefit of his own self alone, not otherwise; that is, you have no personal benefit from his guidance, because the benefit of the Messenger (ﷺ), which is his honour and reward, is established upon the delivery, whether or not those who are guided are guided and those who go astray go astray.

A parallel of this verse has already occurred in His saying, ﴿Say: O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord, so whoever is guided, he is guided only for his own self﴾ [Yunus: 108] at the end of Surat Yunus, and in His saying, ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [al-Naml: 91], ﴿and to recite the Qur'an; so whoever is guided, he is guided only for his own self﴾ [al-Naml: 92] at the end of Surat al-Naml. However, in those two verses the expression restricts guidance to the guided person's own self, whereas this is omitted in this surah. The reason is that those two verses were revealed with the command to address the polytheists, so the context there was suited to conveying that the benefit of their guidance returns only to themselves, i.e., there is no gain for me from their guidance. In contrast, this verse is an address directed by God to His Messenger (ﷺ), and it contains no reference to one who would take the position of being proud of his own guidance.

As for His saying, ﴿and whoever goes astray, he strays only to its detriment﴾, the restrictive form in it is to place the Messenger's (ﷺ) distress over their straying, which leads them to punishment, in the position of one upon whom their straying brings harm, so he is addressed with the restrictive form, which is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb) contrary to what the apparent sense requires. For this reason, the three verses are alike in including restriction regarding the side of their straying, for His saying in Surat al-Naml (﴿So say: I am only one of the warners﴾ [al-Naml: 92]). These are subtle points of the inimitability of the Qur'an.

His saying, ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾, is like the statement in ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾ [Yunus: 108] in Surat Yunus.

The clause ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ is coordinated (ataf) with the clause "So whoever is guided, it is for his own self," meaning: you are not commanded to compel them to be guided. This statement is therefore phrased as a nominal sentence to indicate the permanence of the ruling of this negation.

[Page 23]

﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. Then He withholds those for which He has decreed death, and sends the others back until a specified term. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

This may serve as a parable for the state of the misguided who go astray and the guided who are guided. It arises from His saying ﴿whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [al-Zumar: 41], up to His saying (﴿and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [al-Zumar: 41]).

The meaning is that the one who persists in misguidance may afterwards be guided, or his term may reach him while he is still in his misguidance. So He gave the parable of this with the sleep of the sleeper, who may be followed by waking, or who may die in his sleep. This is a consolation to the soul of the Prophet ﷺ, with hope for the faith of many who at that time were in error and polytheism, as that was realized. Thus the sentence is a reason (ta'lil) for the sentence before it, and it has a connection with His saying ﴿Is one whose breast God has opened to Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], up to His saying ﴿those are in clear error﴾ [al-Zumar: 22].

It is also possible that it is a transition to an argument for God's exclusive authority over the conditions of beings. He had mentioned the proof of His disposing through the creation of essences from the beginning, from His saying ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 5] up to His saying ﴿in three darknesses﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Then (He mentioned) the proof of His disposing through creating states of essences and bringing essences into being from those states, from His saying ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 21] up to His saying ﴿for people of understanding﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. He followed each proof with what shows its effect of admonition, lesson, and warning against opposing its requirement. So here He moved to argument by a wondrous condition among the conditions of created souls, which is the state of death and the state of sleep. The argument is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾, for this is a proof for people from themselves. He said ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21], and said ﴿He has set forth for you a parable from yourselves﴾. So the sentence is a resumptive beginning (istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi) for the gradual progression in argument, and it has a connection with the sentences ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 5] and ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down...﴾ [al-Zumar: 21] mentioned before.

On both views the verse conveys the making manifest of two great truths from the laws of the two lives, the psychic and the bodily. The placing of the Name of Majesty (God) before the verbal predicate is to restrict the predicate to the content of the statement, i.e., God takes, not other than Him. This is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi) to make manifest the corruption of their association of gods who do not possess any disposal over the conditions of people.

[Page 24]

Al-tawaffi means causing death. It is named tawaffi because when God causes someone to die, He has fully taken his term (tawaffahu ajalahu). So God is the One who takes (al-Mutawaffi), and the angel of death is also one who takes, since he is the direct agent of the taking.

The dead person is mutawaffa in the passive form, and this became common, so that tawaffi became synonymous with causing death, and wafat is synonymous with death, regardless of the manner of its inflection and derivation from the root w-f-y.

This was mentioned in His saying ﴿those of you who die﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying ﴿Say: the angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11] in Surat al-Sajdah.

Al-anfus is the plural of nafs, which means the person and the essence. He said ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. It is also applied to the spirit by which there is life and perception.

The meaning of tawaffi relates to the souls under both usages.

The meaning is: He takes the people who die, for what is described as dying is the essence, not the spirit, and its taking is the removal of the spirits from it.

His saying "and those that have not died" is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "the souls," considering the qualifier "at the time of their death," since it has the sense of a description. It is as if it were said: He takes the souls that die in the state of their sleep, and the souls that have not died in their sleep but then wake up. The phrase "during their sleep" is connected to "takes" (yatawaffa), meaning: and He takes souls that have not died, taking them in their sleep every day. So it is understood that the intended meaning of their taking is their sleep. This is according to the manner of comparison by the usage of the language, since the sleeper is not called dead (mayyit) or taken (mutawaffa).

This is a comparison used to draw attention to a scientific truth, for the state of sleep is a state in which the most important benefits of life are cut off from the body, namely perception, except that its principal organs have not lost their capacity to return to their functions upon waking. For this reason He said ﴿It is He who takes you at night, and knows what you have earned by day, then raises you up therein﴾ [al-An'am: 60], as was mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

[Page 25]

The fa' in (fa-yumsiku) is the eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasihah), because what precedes requires an extent that the fa' makes explicit to explain the taking of souls in the context.

Al-imsak means gripping with the hand and not releasing what is gripped.

The meaning is: He keeps back and does not return the soul for which He has decreed death, i.e., He prevents it from returning to life. The use of "holding back" for the continuation of the state of death is a figure of speech (tamthil) for the permanence of that state. Among its subtle points is that the people of the dead wish for the return of their dead if they could find a way to bring him back, but God does not allow a soul that has died to return to life.

Al-irsal means release and enabling the leaving of a place to return to what it was. The intended meaning of "the others" (al-ukhra) is "those that have not died," but God has placed them in the position of the dead. The meaning is: He returns life to them fully.

The purpose of this is to make manifest the difference between the two kinds of death.

The phrase (﴿until a specified term﴾) is connected to the verb (sends) because it contains the sense of "returns life to them," meaning: He does not deprive them of life entirely except at their appointed term, that is, the term determined for them in God's decree.

Al-tasmiyah means determination, and it was mentioned in His saying ﴿When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

This is the way to interpret the verse, free of artificial constructions, of the use of a kind of pun (shibh al-istikhdam) in His saying ﴿those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back﴾, and free of supposed omissions.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ is a new sentence, as it mentions the conclusion after the proof. That is, in the state of causing death and causing sleep there are indications that God alone has disposal, that He alone deserves worship to the exclusion of others, and that the purpose of this statement is not merely to inform about the difference between the states of death and sleep. Rather, the purpose is reflection and consideration on the subject of the parable, on the subtleties of God's craftsmanship, and reminding (people) of the subtle wisdom contained in it, which passes over every person each day in his own self, and passes over many people in their families and clans, while they turn away from the wisdoms in it and its wondrous craftsmanship.

[Page 26]

He made what these indicate "signs" (ayat) in the plural because they are two wondrous states, and within each state there is a disposal that differs from the disposal in the other. In the state of death there is the removal of life from the body, the body remaining like inanimate matter, and a prevention from life returning to it. In the state of sleep there is the removal of part of life from the body until it is like the dead, though it is not dead; then the granting that life returns to it, time after time, until the appointed time arrives for its permanent removal.

The phrase "signs for a people who reflect" applies both to the intention of the parable and to the intention of the argument for God's exclusive disposal.

The emphasis of the statement with (inna) is to treat the majority of people as if they were deniers of those signs, because they do not act in their conditions in accordance with what those signs indicate.

Al-tafakkur means the effort of thinking; it is working the mind and repeatedly pondering the indication of proofs regarding realities.

Al-Jumhur read (﴿qada 'alayha al-mawt﴾) with the verb in the active voice and "death" in the accusative. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "﴿qudiya 'alayha al-mawtu﴾" with the verb in the passive voice and "death" in the nominative. This is on the basis of omitting the preposition (naz' al-khafid). The estimated phrase is: "It was decreed against it by death." When the preposition was omitted, the noun that had been in the genitive took the place of the object and was made the deputy of the subject. Alternatively, "qudiya" is taken to include the meaning of "was written" and "was decreed."

**[Page 27]** *Am* here is *munqati‘ah* (disjunctive), indicating *al-idrab al-intiqali* (a transitional shift), a move from condemning their association of partners with God to refuting their excuses for that association. This is because, when the proofs of the Qur'an had overwhelmed them with the impossibility of God having partners, they devised an interpretation to justify their polytheism and said, ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], as was related of them at the beginning of this surah. Since the proofs against polytheism had been fully established, the discourse here turns to refuting their interpretation and their excuse.

The interrogation implied by *am* in all its positions is here one of denial (*inkar*), meaning that their interpretation and their excuse are themselves objectionable, just as the thing they offered as an excuse was objectionable. Therefore, they will not attain their purpose through this excuse.

The meaning of their calling them "intercessors" (*shufa‘a'*) was explained at the beginning of the surah.

God commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them a statement that cuts off their slander, namely: ﴿Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾

The *waw* in *awa-law kanu* (even though they were) is conjunctive, joining the speech of the respondent to their speech. This is of the kind called *ʿatf al-talqin* (conjunction of instruction), as in God's words ﴿He said, "And of my descendants?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is also possible to take the *waw* as indicating a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as is preferred in its parallel, and this was mentioned in His words ﴿even if he should offer it in ransom﴾ [Al ʿImran: 91] in Surat Al ʿImran. The subject of the circumstantial clause is implied, and what precedes it indicates it, namely His words ﴿they have taken intercessors besides Allah﴾. The implied sense is: "Would they intercede even though they possess nothing?"

The apparent view is that the rule for placing the interrogative before the *waw* of the circumstantial clause is the same as its rule when placed before the *waw* of conjunction.

The indefiniteness of *shay'an* (anything) in the context of negation conveys the generality of everything that can be possessed, so that all kinds of intercession are included in its scope. Since intercession is a non-material matter, possessing it means securing its granting. The statement is sarcastic, since how can one who does not understand intercede? For, because of his lack of understanding, it is inconceivable that the notion of intercession would occur to him, let alone that his will would turn toward seeking intercession. Therefore, taking them as intercessors is folly.

Since He negated that their idols have any share of intercession within the general negation of possessing anything of existing things, He answered it with His words: ﴿To Allah belongs intercession entirely﴾, that is, all intercession belongs to Allah. The Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say this to them so that they would know that no one possesses intercession except Allah, that is, He is the one who owns the granting of the intercession of the true intercessors.

**[Page 28]** The fronting of the prepositional phrase *li-Allahi* (to Allah), which is the predicate, before the subject is for the purpose of restriction (*hasr*). The *lam* indicates ownership, meaning the restriction of ownership of intercession to God Most High, so that no one possesses intercession with Him.

*Jami‘an* (entirely) is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "intercession," conveying comprehensiveness, meaning that no particular instance of the reality of intercession deviates from being owned by Allah. This is reinforced by the necessary implication of this restriction: that no part of intercession belongs to anyone other than Allah.

The clause ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ serves to generalize the exclusive authority of Allah over the heavens and the earth, which includes control over the holding of creatures accountable and the management of their affairs. Its position is that of a *tadhyil* (concluding generalization) that confirms and enlarges upon the preceding clause. The dominion meant is that of disposing and governing creation and the affairs of both worlds and whatever is in them. Since this dominion belongs to Him, no one can turn Him from a matter He wills to occur to its opposite during the duration of the heavens and the earth. This refutes the idea that their deities could have intercession on their behalf in their worldly affairs.

Following this is ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, to indicate the affirmation of resurrection, and that no one intercedes with Allah after the gathering (*hashr*) except one whom Allah has permitted to do so.

*Thumma* (then) indicates a rank-based sequence, as is its way in conjoining sentences. This is because the content of ﴿to Him you will be returned﴾ is that Allah possesses the dominion of the Hereafter just as He possessed the dominion of this world, and the dominion of the Hereafter is greater because of the vastness of what is possessed and its permanence.

The fronting of *ilayhi* (to Him) before *turja‘un* (you will be returned) is for emphasis and reinforcement, and for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fasila*).

**[Page 27]** *Am* here is *munqati‘ah* (disjunctive), indicating *al-idrab al-intiqali* (a transitional shift), a move from condemning their association of partners with God to refuting their excuses for that association. This is because, when the proofs of the Qur'an had overwhelmed them with the impossibility of God having partners, they devised an interpretation to justify their polytheism and said, ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], as was related of them at the beginning of this surah. Since the proofs against polytheism had been fully established, the discourse here turns to refuting their interpretation and their excuse.

The interrogation implied by *am* in all its positions is here one of denial (*inkar*), meaning that their interpretation and their excuse are themselves objectionable, just as the thing they offered as an excuse was objectionable. Therefore, they will not attain their purpose through this excuse.

The meaning of their calling them "intercessors" (*shufa‘a'*) was explained at the beginning of the surah.

God commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them a statement that cuts off their slander, namely: ﴿Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾

The *waw* in *awa-law kanu* (even though they were) is conjunctive, joining the speech of the respondent to their speech. This is of the kind called *ʿatf al-talqin* (conjunction of instruction), as in God's words ﴿He said, "And of my descendants?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is also possible to take the *waw* as indicating a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as is preferred in its parallel, and this was mentioned in His words ﴿even if he should offer it in ransom﴾ [Al ʿImran: 91] in Surat Al ʿImran. The subject of the circumstantial clause is implied, and what precedes it indicates it, namely His words ﴿they have taken intercessors besides Allah﴾. The implied sense is: "Would they intercede even though they possess nothing?"

The apparent view is that the rule for placing the interrogative before the *waw* of the circumstantial clause is the same as its rule when placed before the *waw* of conjunction.

The indefiniteness of *shay'an* (anything) in the context of negation conveys the generality of everything that can be possessed, so that all kinds of intercession are included in its scope. Since intercession is a non-material matter, possessing it means securing its granting. The statement is sarcastic, since how can one who does not understand intercede? For, because of his lack of understanding, it is inconceivable that the notion of intercession would occur to him, let alone that his will would turn toward seeking intercession. Therefore, taking them as intercessors is folly.

This is a commentary on the words "And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shudder; but when those others besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice" (﴿وإذا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وحْدَهُ اشْمَأزَّتْ قُلُوبُ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ وإذا ذُكِرَ الَّذِينَ مِن دُونِهِ إذا هم يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾).

This is a continuation of the clause "They have taken intercessors besides God" (﴿اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ شُفَعاءَ﴾ [al-Zumar: 43]). It shows their self-contradiction in their statements, which indicates that what they say are sophistic arguments (ahkam sufsata'iyya, sophistic reasoning) that they utter to escape the decisive proofs the Qur'an confronted them with. They sometimes justify their polytheism by claiming that their associates are intercessors for them with God. This implies that they acknowledge that God is their God and the God of their associates. Then

[p. 29]

when the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that God is One, or when the Muslims uttered the formula "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah), their hearts shuddered at confining the mention to God alone. They are not content to remain silent about describing their idols with divinity, and this indicates that they equate them with God, exalted is He.

So His words "alone" (wahdahu) may be taken as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala), meaning "singled out." In His words "when God is mentioned" there is an implied sense: "by the attribute of divinity," so the meaning of "when God alone is mentioned" is "when His singularity in divinity is mentioned." This is in accordance with the view of Yunus ibn Habib regarding "wahdahu." It is also permissible to take it as a verbal noun (masdar), which is the view of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad. That is, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb "was mentioned," specifying its type: a mention "alone," meaning that the names of their idols were not mentioned alongside the name of God. The verbal noun is attached to the pronoun for the Name of Majesty because the referent is well known through this singling out. This mention is what takes place in the call of the Prophet (ﷺ), in the prayers, in the recitation of the Qur'an, and in the gatherings of the Muslims.

The meaning of "when those others besides Him are mentioned" (﴿وإذا ذُكِرَ الَّذِينَ مِن دُونِهِ﴾) is: when their idols are mentioned with the attribute of divinity. This happens when they hear the statements of the polytheists in their conversations and their professions of faith in al-Lat and al-'Uzza, that is, without the name of God being mentioned alongside them. Their rejoicing at confining the mention to their idols indicates that they prefer the side of the idols over the side of God, exalted is He. "Mention" (al-dhikr) means uttering the name. The intended meaning is: when the Muslims mention the name of God, the polytheists shudder because they do not hear the mention of their gods; and when the polytheists mention the names of their idols, those among their people who hear them rejoice.

The expression for their gods as "those besides Him" (﴿الَّذِينَ مِن دُونِهِ﴾), rather than "their associates" (shuraka'ihim) or "their intercessors" (shufa'ihim), is used to imply that the reason for their rejoicing at that mention is that it is a mention of those who are besides God. That is, it is a mention appropriate to this relation, meaning it is devoid of the name of God. Thus the meaning is: "when their associates are mentioned to the exclusion of the mention of God, behold, they rejoice."

The limitation to these two kinds of mention is because they are the most evident in showing the ill intentions of the polytheists toward God, exalted is He, and in refuting their excuse that they worship idols only so that these may bring them closer to God and intercede for them with Him. As for the mention in which the name of God and the names of their gods are both mentioned, like their saying in the talbiyah (the pilgrim's call, talbiyah): "Here I am, O God, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns," that is a mention that has no relevance to the context.

Some exegetes have stated, concerning His words "when those others besides Him are mentioned," that it refers to what is narrated in the story of the Gharaniq (the "cranes"), and this interpretation has been attributed to Mujahid. But this is far from the context of the verse. Building upon the fabricated reports, "how excellent is the judgment of those who turned away from mentioning that."

Al-ishmi'zaz (shuddering): the intensity of aversion and repulsion, meaning that their hearts and perceptions disliked that.

Al-istibshar (rejoicing): the intensity of joy to the point that its effect appears on the complexion of the face. It was mentioned earlier in His words "and the people of the city came rejoicing" (﴿وجاءَ أهْلُ المَدِينَةِ يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾) in Surah al-Hijr.

The contrast between shuddering (al-ishmi'zaz) and rejoicing (al-istibshar) is a complete antithesis, because shuddering is the extreme of aversion and rejoicing is the extreme of joy.

The expression for the polytheists as "those who do not believe in the Hereafter" (﴿الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾) is used because they were known among people by this description, with the intent of reminding them again of the occurrence of the Resurrection.

The first "when" (idha) and the second "when" are temporal adverbs that carry the sense of a condition, as is usually the case. The third "when" (idha) is the "when" of sudden occurrence (lil-mufaja'a), indicating that rejoicing overtakes them at that moment because of their excessive love for their gods.

For this reason the present tense is used in "they rejoice" (yastabshirun) rather than saying "they are rejoicing" (mustabshirun), to convey the renewal of their rejoicing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 46:

﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾

When most of what preceded in the surah pointed to the disagreement between the polytheists and the believers, and to the fact that the polytheists were determined upon their falsehood despite the proofs of truth that had overwhelmed them, and despite the signs and reflection not benefiting them, the Messenger ﷺ was commanded, following that, to say this statement,

صفحة ٣١

to relieve him of the distress of grief over his people, to give them an excuse by warning them, and to make them aware that the truth lies on their side being neglected, and that the more fitting course for the Messenger ﷺ is to part ways with them and to entrust the judgment in their dispute to Allah.

In this entrusting there is an indication that the one who entrusts his affair to Allah is the one who is certain of the truth of his religion, and who is reassured that arbitration will manifest his truth and the falsehood of his opponent.

The address of the Messenger ﷺ to his Lord began with the vocative (an-nida') because the situation is one of directing and seeking judgment.

The application of the two attributes to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because of the suitability they carry: the submission of all creation to His judgment, and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of their inner dispositions, whether righteous or false.

Al-Fatir means the Creator; "Fatir of the heavens and the earth" means the One who originates what they contain.

The description "Fatir of the heavens and the earth" indicates the attribute of power, and its being placed before the attribute of knowledge is because people's awareness of His power precedes their awareness of His knowledge, and because power is more suitable for the request of judgment, since judgment is imposition and subjugation, and so it is a direct effect of power.

Al-Ghayb (the unseen) is what is hidden and has become absent from people's knowledge, and ash-shahadah (the witnessed) is what people know of what falls under perception, which is the basis of knowledge.

The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun in His words (﴿between Your servants﴾), rather than saying "between us," is because of the generality contained in "servants" (ʿibad), as it is a plural in construct form, so it encompasses the judgment between them in this their matter and the judgment between every two disputants, since generalization is more fitting for supplication and mubahala (mutual invocation).

The clause (﴿You judge between Your servants﴾) is a declarative sentence used in the sense of supplication. The meaning is: "Judge between us." In teaching this supplication to the Prophet ﷺ there is an indication that He is the true Doer.

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate in His words (﴿You judge﴾) is to convey exclusivity, meaning: You, not other than You.

Since none of the two parties believes that Allah judges between people in such a disagreement, the response to such a belief would be by the implication of restriction, so it is established that the restriction is used as an allusive metaphor (kinayah talwihiyyah)

صفحة ٣٢

for the intensity of their stubbornness in obstinacy, their lack of fairness, and their failure to submit to decisive proofs, to the extent that whoever seeks a judge among them finds no judge among them except Allah the Exalted. This also alludes to an excuse for the Messenger ﷺ in his exertion to the utmost of what he was charged with, since this statement is only issued by one who has expended his effort in what was incumbent upon him. When his Lord taught him to say it, it carried the meaning: you have conveyed and fulfilled the message, so nothing remains except what falls under the power of Allah the Exalted, which the obstinate ones like your people cannot overcome. In it there is consolation for the Messenger ﷺ and a warning to the opponents.

Judgment applies to the judgment of the Hereafter, which is the realized judgment that is not broken, and it includes the judgment of this world by the victory of the one who is right over the one who is wrong, if Allah wills to hasten part of His judgment by hastening punishment for them in this world.

The use of the verb of being (kana) as a relative clause for (ma) serves to show the realization of the disagreement, and the predicate of (kana) being in the present tense (mudari') hints that it is a renewed disagreement, since there is no hope of the polytheists desisting from their falsehood.

The placing of (fihi) before (yakhtalifun) is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah) together with the concern for the matter in dispute.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 47–48:

﴿Even if those who did wrong possessed everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the terrible torment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from Allah what they had never reckoned.﴾ ﴿And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned, and there will befall them what they used to mock.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿatf) of the statement ﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Zumar: 46] and so on, because it indicates that the truth lies with the Prophet ﷺ, who called upon his Lord for judgment, and that the judgment will be against the polytheists. Thereafter he follows this with a depiction of the magnitude of what the judgment will involve: that even if the polytheists were to possess a ransom from it, however great, they would offer it.

﴿Mā fī al-arḍ﴾ ("what is on the earth") includes every precious thing of theirs: their families, their wealth, and even their own selves, for these are less than the terrible torment on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning is: were that to be their possession on the Day of Resurrection, they would offer it as ransom on that day. The aspect of the depiction in this lies in what the possession of these things entails of stinginess toward them according to the common disposition of souls. The statement is thus an analogy (tamthīl) for their condition in the severity of their plight and misery, by the condition of one who, if he had what is mentioned, would give it as a ransom from that torment. A parallel to this has preceded in Surat al-ʿUqūd. The conditional particle implies that the possession of what is on the earth by them is negated, and so it conveys that there is no ransom for them from the terrible torment, which is a demoralization (taʾyīs) of them.

The particle (min) in ﴿min sūʾ al-ʿadhāb﴾ ("from the evil of the torment") has the sense of the causal lām, i.e., they would ransom themselves with it for the sake of the evil torment they witnessed. It may also be partitive/substitutive (li-l-badal), i.e., as a substitute for ﴿sūʾ al-ʿadhāb﴾.

Coordinated with this demoralization is another depiction of the greatness of what will befall them of torment, namely what is in the relative clause (al-mawṣūl) in the phrase ﴿mā lam yakūnū yaḥtasibūn﴾ ("what they had never reckoned"), by way of the indefiniteness in which the listener's soul goes to every image of severity.

It is permissible to make the waw (in "wa-badā") a waw of circumstance (ḥāl), i.e., they would ransom themselves with it in a state in which there appears what they had never reckoned.

﴿Min Allāh﴾ is connected to (badā), and (min) is inceptive (ibtidāʾiyya), i.e., there appeared to them from what Allah had prepared for them that which they had never supposed.

Al-iḥtisāb: an intensive form of the reckoning (ḥisāb) in the sense of supposing (ẓann), like iqtaraba in the sense of qaruba. The meaning: what they had never supposed. This is a kināya (allusive expression) for it exceeding the utmost of what the imaginer could picture when he hears its attributes. There is no regard in this kināya to their having denied resurrection, so that it did not occur to their minds. A parallel to this promise of news is His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So no soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17].

(Sayyiʾāt) is the plural of sayyiʾa, an attribute added to its qualified noun, which is the relative clause (mā kasabū), i.e., their evil acquisitions. Its feminine form is due to the prevalence of applying the term sayyiʾa to an act, even though among what they earned there are things of corrupt belief, such as believing in partners with Allah and harboring hatred toward the Messenger and the righteous, and resentments and envy. The feminine of the attribute follows the predominance of practical evils such as usurpation, killing, and immoralities, a verbal predominance owing to the frequency of usage.

The verb (kasabū) was preferred over (ʿamilū, "they did") to cut off their impatience with the torment by recording that they acquired its causes by themselves, as was mentioned earlier in His statement ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn"﴾ [al-Zumar: 24], rather than (taʿlamūn, "you know").

Al-ḥawq: encompassing, i.e., it encircled them so that they could not escape from it. The disagreement over its derivation has preceded in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but those who ridiculed them were enveloped by what they used to mock﴾ [al-Anʿām: 10] in Surat al-Anʿām.

What ﴿they used to mock﴾ [al-Anʿām: 10] refers to is the torment of the Hereafter, i.e., they would mock by mentioning it, treating the punishment as though it were something mocked, so the pronoun in the genitive is a metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya).

You may also make the bāʾ causal, and let the object of (yastahziʾūn) be omitted, i.e., they would mock the Prophet ﷺ because of his mentioning the torment.

The fronting of (bihi) before (yastahziʾūn) is for emphasis on it and for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila).

**[p. 35]**

The *fa'* (فاء, "so") here marks the sequence of this statement after His words, ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil﴾ [al-Zumar: 45], and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*) whose parts are linked to one another by their relevance.

The sequence introduced by the *fa'* is the description of one of the strange features of their conditions following another. And what is stranger than their turning to God alone in supplication when harm touches them, though they had recoiled from the mention of His name alone? This is a contradiction and an inversion in their conduct, for it is the causal connection of one event to another, not a causal connection of existence. This point distinguishes the use of *fa'* here from the use of *wa'* (واو, "and") in the parallel expression at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. The intended sequence is His words, ﴿So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us﴾, and what follows it is a completion (*tatmim*) and a digression (*istiṭrad*).

The discussion of the parallel of the opening of this verse has already been given in His words, ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He bestows upon him a blessing from Himself, he forgets﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. The meaning of "man" (*al-insān*) there is every polytheist, so the definite article is the generic definite (*ta'rīf al-jins*), and the intended meaning is a group of people, namely the people of polytheism. Hence it is the customary generalization (*istighrāq 'urfī*).

The variation between the two verses is stylistic variety (*tafannun*), and so that the repetition of the verse is not devoid of an additional benefit, as is the Qur'an's habit in repeated narratives.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, I was given it on knowledge﴾, the *innamā* (إنَّما) here is the compound word formed from *inna* (إنَّ) with the *kāffa* (the particle that "restricts" it), which becomes a single word indicating exclusivity (*ḥaṣr*), in the position of the negative *mā* followed by the exceptive *illā* (إلّا).

The meaning is: "I was not given what I was given of blessing except for knowledge from me of the ways of acquiring it." The use of the masculine third-person pronoun in (*ūtītuhu*, "I was given it") refers back to (*ni'matan*, "a blessing"), understood as a reporting of their statement as issuing from them while the various kinds of blessings were present before them. It is thus a return of the pronoun to a perceived entity, and the pronoun functions as a demonstrative, like His words, ﴿Rather, it is what you sought to hasten, a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 24].

The meaning of ﴿He said: Indeed, I was given it on knowledge﴾ is that he believed this, and so it flowed into his statements, since speech follows belief.

The (*'alā*, "on") here is causal, meaning "for the sake of knowledge," that is, "because of knowledge." A difference is drawn between this verse and the verse in the surah of al-Qaṣaṣ in His words, ﴿On knowledge with me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 78]. Here "with me" (*'indī*) is not mentioned, because the knowledge intended here is merely shrewdness and management, whereas there what is intended is the knowledge of the crafting of gold and silver and alchemy (*al-kīmiyā'*), by which Qārūn acquired great wealth through knowing their methods, **[p. 36]** which was a knowledge specific to him. As for the knowledge here, it is that which exists in all people of judgment and management.

What is meant is knowledge of the ways of gaining and of averting harm, like the stratagems of the sailor (*nūtī*) in the terror of the sea.

The meaning is that he says this when the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or one of the believers, reminds him of God's blessing upon him. By this the placement of the exclusive construction becomes clear, for he intended to reverse the speech of one who tells him that this is from God's mercy toward him.

The *bal* (بَلْ, "rather") here is for retractive transition (*iḍrāb ibṭālī*), and it is a nullification of their claim that they were given that on account of their knowledge and management. That is: "Rather, the mercy they were given was bestowed on them by God only in order to show the nations the measure of their gratitude." That is, it indicates a state in them resembling the state of testing, as to the measure of their knowledge of God and their gratitude to Him, because mercy and blessing have an effect in what is bestowed on him, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. God knows them, and He is independent of testing them.

The pronoun of (*hiya*, "it") refers to the statement implied by (*qāla*, "he said"), following the manner of returning a pronoun to a verbal noun derived from a verb, as in His words, ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 8]. Its pronoun is feminine by consideration of the predication about it with the word (*fitnatun*, "a trial"), or by interpreting the statement as a word, as in His words, ﴿No! It is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 100], after His words, ﴿He says: My Lord, return me﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 99], ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 100]. What is meant is that this statement is a cause of trial or is caused by a trial in their souls. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer back to (*ni'matan*, "a blessing").

The contrast (*istidrāk*) introduced by His words, ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, arises from the content of the clause, ﴿when We bestow upon him a blessing from Us, he says: Indeed, I was given it on knowledge.﴾ That is: "But most people do not know, and among them are those who make this statement, that they are in a trial by what they have been given of blessing, when they are like these speakers who claim that what they have of good is the result of their own efforts and stratagems."

The pronoun of (*akthарahum*, "most of them") refers to something known from the context, not mentioned in the speech, since nothing preceded it that would suit being its antecedent. What is meant by it is people: that is, "But most people do not know that some of the blessing they were given in this world will be a trial for them, according to how they receive it, through little gratitude and what leads to disbelief." Thus included in this "most" are all the polytheists, each of whom says: "Indeed, I was given it on knowledge."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 50–51:

﴿Indeed, those before them said it, but what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them. And those who wronged among these [people] — the evil consequences of what they earned will befall them, and they will not escape.﴾

The clause "qad qalaha" (they had indeed said it) explains the content of "hiya fitnah" (it is a trial), because explaining the outcome of those who spoke this statement about the blessing that reached them shows that the blessing of these people was a trial for them.

The pronoun in "qalaha" (said it) refers to the statement of the speaker, ﴿It was given to me only on the basis of knowledge﴾ [al-Zumar: 49], on the interpretation of "qawl" (saying) as the word which is a sentence, like His exalted saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, send me back"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99] ﴿so that I may do righteousness in what I left behind. No! It is only a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100].

And ﴿those before them﴾ are the non-religious ones from among those who passed away, whom God knew, and among them was Qarun, and He related in Surat al-Qasas that he said that [statement].

By ﴿what they used to earn﴾ is meant the wealth they acquired. Its not availing them means that they were unable to repel the punishment with their wealth. The "fa" (so) in ﴿so what they earned did not avail them﴾ is for the consequence of the non-availing of what they earned upon their statement, for the non-availing indicates that there befell them an evil of such a kind that its victim would seek to ransom himself from it; so if that evil was great, there was no ransom for it. Thus there is an elliptical brevity in the speech, which is made clear by His saying after it, ﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them.﴾

So the "fa" of ﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿what did not avail them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 207], meaning that the non-availing of their earnings caused the descent of punishment upon them.

The apparent order in arranging the clauses would have been for the clause ﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them﴾ to precede the clause ﴿so what they earned did not avail them﴾, because the availing is only awaited when harm befalls them; when the non-availing is established, the befalling of the calamity is mentioned after it. The order was reversed, contrary to what the apparent order requires, for the purpose of hastening the refutation of the saying of their speaker, "It was given to me only on the basis of knowledge," i.e., if their knowledge had any effect in bringing them blessing, it would have had an effect in repelling harm from them.

The indication by "these" (ha'ulaa') refers to the polytheists of Makkah. We have explained more than once that we have discovered a habit of the Qur'an: when this demonstrative is mentioned in it, what is meant by it is the polytheists of Quraysh.

The befalling of evil deeds is meant in both places as the befalling of the recompense of evil deeds, which is the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, because the recompense of an evil deed is an evil like it.

Al-mu'jiz: the one who overcomes. It was mentioned at His exalted saying ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape﴾ [al-An'am: 134] in Surat al-An'am, i.e., they are not escaping from Us, so the object of the active participle was omitted because the context indicates it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 52:

﴿Have they not known that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it? Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ [al-Zumar: 49]. Having described most of them as lacking knowledge of this, and as neglecting to reflect on the proofs that yield knowledge, and as having stopped their ears against the signs that would remind them of it, so that they remain in a compound ignorance (jahala murakkaba), the matter was that they should have known that Allah extends provision to whoever He wills and restricts it, meaning He gives good to whomever He wills and withholds it from whomever He wills.

The interrogative (istifham) is therefore a rebuke (inkar) directed at them for the absence of their knowledge of this, since they were the cause of that absence; the rebuke thus carries an admonition (tawbikh).

He limited the denial to the negation of their knowledge, namely that the extension of provision and its measure are among the acts of Allah, exalted is He, because this is closest to what they witness of the conditions of their own people: how many a person strives and is not provided for, and how many another receives provision from where he does not expect it.

He made in this many signs, because the variation in the conditions of provision, which indicate that disposal lies in the hand of Allah, exalted is He, points to the remaining conditions; thus there are many signs in it indicating that Allah, exalted is He, alone holds disposal in reality.

The signs were made for "a people who believe" because the believers have known this and adorned themselves with it, whereas there are no signs in it for the polytheists who are heedless of it.

[Page 39]

Verses of warning, with their preceding branches, extended their discourse to such a degree that it reached the souls of those who heard them with the utmost terror and fear, despite their pretending to pay little attention to them. Their impact could reach the point of despair of any effort that would save them from its threat. So God followed them with the awakening of hope in their souls, to go out to the shore of salvation if they wished it, in keeping with the custom of this glorious Book of healing souls by blending encouragement (tarhib, rather: targhib) and warning.

The statement is a *istinaf bayani* (a resumptive clause that explains what precedes it), because the preceding admonitions stir in the souls of those addressed by them the thought of inquiring about the paths to salvation. Angelic and satanic impulses then clash within them until the clash settles in favour of one of the two groups. So illuminating the way for them makes easier the steps of those bewildered in the darkness of doubt, comforts them after the wounds of rebuke, reproach and threat had weakened them, and dresses that wound. The forbearing person rebukes and then softens. It also stirs in the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ) the fear that the anger of God might encompass those he invited, who turned away, or whom he made dear to the truth yet who hated it, so that he might not open to them the door of repentance, and their return (awba) after their aversion might not be accepted. This is especially so after He commanded him to entrust the matter to His judgment, which implies anticipating the cutting off and severing of the dispute.

So He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to call to them with this summons, as a relief for him and an opening of the door of return to Him. This is a statement that resolves into two resumptions. The phrase (qul, "Say") is a resumption explaining what the best of the Prophets (ﷺ) was expecting, meaning: convey this statement from me.

The phrase (O My servants) is a fresh resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) from God's address to them.

Beginning the address with the vocative and the title "servants" indicates that what follows is preparation for acceptance and an encouragement toward salvation.

The address with the title "My servants" is primarily directed at the polytheists, as shown by His saying (﴿And submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you﴾ [Az-Zumar: 54]), His saying (﴿And indeed, I was among the mockers﴾ [Az-Zumar: 56]), and His saying (﴿Yes, My verses had come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant and became among the disbelievers﴾ [Az-Zumar: 59]). This address follows a pattern different from the usual one in the Qur'an when "servants" is mentioned in construct with the first-person pronoun of the Speaker, may He be exalted.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "Some people among the polytheists had killed many and committed fornication many times, then came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: 'What you say and call to is good, if you would only tell us that there is expiation for what we have done.'" They said this although they had heard the verses of warning for one who does those deeds; otherwise, how would they know that those deeds are crimes, while they were in the state of ignorance (jahiliyya)? Then there was revealed (﴿And those who do not invoke with God another deity, and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [Al-Furqan: 68]), meaning up to His saying (﴿except for those who repent, believe and do righteous work﴾ [Al-Furqan: 70]). And there was revealed (﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾).

Several other reports have been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, other than the hadith of al-Bukhari. They range between weak and unknown transmissions, and from their collection it is inferred that they are particular instances of the generality of the verse, and that the verse is general in addressing all polytheists. We have referred to this in the preface to the commentary of the surah.

Among the most beautiful reports narrated concerning it is what Ibn Ishaq narrated from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, from 'Umar, who said: "When we gathered for the emigration (hijra), I made an appointment with Hisham ibn al-'As al-Sahmi and 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a ibn 'Utba. We said: 'The meeting place is the pond of Banu Ghifar,' and we said: 'Whoever of us is delayed has been detained, so let his two companions proceed.' Then I and 'Ayyash ibn 'Utba arrived, and Hisham was detained from us. He had been tested, and he was tested [and turned back]. We used to say in Medina: 'These people knew God, then they were tested for a trial that befell them; we see no repentance for them.' They themselves used to say this to themselves. So God revealed (﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾) up to His saying (﴿an abode for the disbelievers﴾ [Az-Zumar: 32]). 'Umar said: 'I wrote it with my own hand, then sent it to Hisham.' Hisham said: 'When it reached me, I went out with it to Dhu Tuwa, and said: "O God, make me understand it." I understood that it had been revealed concerning us. So I turned back, sat on my camel, and caught up with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).'" End of quotation.

'Umar's saying "then God revealed" means that he heard it after he had emigrated, and that it was among what was revealed in Mecca. 'Umar did not hear it because he was busy preparing for the emigration; he heard it only while in Medina, for 'Umar emigrated to Medina before the Prophet (ﷺ).

So the address (﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾) is an introduction in general terms, whose explanation comes in the verses after it, from His saying (﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar: 54]). After this, the generality of (My servants) and the generality of the relative clause (who have transgressed) include the people of sins from among the Muslims, even though the primary intended audience of the address is the polytheists, in keeping with eloquent speech, which contains many intended purposes and meanings poured into moulds that can contain them.

al-Jumhur (the majority) read (﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾) with the *fath* (open vowel) on the ya' of the first person, while Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with *sukun* (silent ya'). Perhaps the reason for retaining the ya' in this verse, unlike its parallel in His saying (﴿O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10]), is that the address here is to those who transgressed, among whom the polytheists come first, and all of them are liable to despair of God's mercy entering their souls. So retaining the ya' of the first person in addressing them is an added explicit marker of the first person, strengthening the attribution of their servanthood to God, exalted is He, as an indication that the way of the Lord is mercy towards His servants.

*Al-israf* means excess (al-ikthar). Here it means excess in sins and transgressions. The word *israf* has already been mentioned in His saying (﴿And do not consume them extravagantly﴾ [An-Nisa: 6]) in Surat an-Nisa, and His saying (﴿So let him not commit excess in killing﴾ [Al-Isra: 33]) in Surat al-Isra.

Most commonly it is followed by its object with the preposition *min* (from), but here it is followed by *'ala* (upon), because the excess here is in deeds that the soul bears and by which it is burdened. This is customary in matters of liabilities and aggression. One says: "I have overburdened so-and-so" (akthartu 'ala fulan). So the meaning of (﴿transgressed against themselves﴾) is that they brought upon themselves what burdens them with its consequence, to include what they committed of polytheism and evil deeds.

*Al-qunut* means despair, and it has been mentioned in His saying (﴿So do not be among the despairing﴾ [Al-Hijr: 55]) in Surat al-Hijr.

The clause (﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾) is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition against despair of God's mercy.

The root *ghafr* goes back to covering (al-sitr), and this requires the existence of what is covered and its need for covering. So (﴿forgives sins﴾) indicates that sins are established, meaning that liability for them is established, and God forgives them, that is, He removes the liability for them. This forgiveness requires causes, which are stated in general terms here and detailed in other evidences from the Book and the Sunna, among them His saying (﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteous work, and then remains guided﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82]). All these evidences are gathered in that forgiveness has causes that arise in the sinner. Were it not so, liability for sins would be pointless, which the Wise, exalted is He, is far above. How could it be, since He has called them sins and threatened for them? So His saying (﴿Indeed, God forgives sins﴾) is a call to seek the causes of this forgiveness, and when the sinner seeks them, he learns their details.

(*Jami'an*, "all") is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of (sins), meaning in its entirety, i.e., in its generality, so He forgives every sin of them if the causes of that forgiveness occur in the sinner. The discussion of the word (*jami'*) will come at His saying (﴿and the earth entirely will be in His grip﴾ [Az-Zumar: 67]) in this surah.

The clause (﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾) is a reason for the clause (﴿He forgives sins entirely﴾), meaning: nothing prevents Him from forgiving all sins, however numerous they may be, because He is intensely forgiving and intensely merciful.

Thereby, by this verse, the saying of the Murji'a is refuted, that nothing harms along with faith.

[Page 43]

﴿Turn back in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped.﴾

When He opened for them the door of hope, He followed it with guidance toward the means of forgiveness, joining it with the conjunction *waw* (and). This indicates the combining of two things: the prohibition of despair from mercy, and the call to repentance (*inabah*). The combination implies haste, and the imperative form also demands haste.

*Inabah* means *tawbah* (repentance). Because it and repentance carry the sense of returning, the two verbs are followed by the preposition *ila* (to).

The meaning is: repent to God from the polytheism (*shirk*) you were engaged in, by affirming His oneness (*tawhid*).

It is followed by the command to submit to Islam, that is, to affirm belief in the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, and to follow the laws of Islam (*shara'i' al-Islam*).

In His words ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ there is a warning (*iwdhan bi-wa'id*) of a near threat if they do not repent and submit, as the verb *ya'tiyakum* (comes upon you) hints.

The definite article in *al-'adhab* (the punishment) is the article of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), and it implies that if they do not repent and submit, the punishment will come upon them.

Among punishment is what occurs in this world, if God wills it. This applies specifically to the polytheists. As for the Muslims, the Messenger (ﷺ) sought refuge from it for them when the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet﴾ [al-An'am: 65], as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am. Among punishment is also the punishment of the Hereafter, which is the recompense for disbelief and major sins.

This address takes each group according to its share. The share of the polytheists is repentance toward monotheism and following the religion of Islam. The share of the believers is repentance when they have transgressed against themselves, and increasing good deeds. As for submission to Islam, it is already attained for them.

*Al-nasr* (help) is aid in victory, such that the defeated escapes the domination of his conqueror against the conqueror's will. And there is no helper for anyone against God.

[Page 44]

As for intercession (*shafa'ah*) for the people of major sins, it is not part of the true meaning of the negated *nasr*. And in this passage, the greatest share is the share of the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 55:

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive.﴾

(Aḥsana mā unzila) is the Qur'an, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18]. The share (ḥaẓẓ) of the polytheists in this verse is that the Muslims have already followed the Qur'an, as the Exalted said: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17], ﴿those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾ [al-Zumar: 18].

And (aḥsan) is a superlative form (ism tafḍīl) used in the sense of perfect beauty, not in the sense of preferring some of it over others, because all of what is in the Qur'an is beautiful. It is thus of the same type as His saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to"﴾ [Yusuf: 33].

The idafa of (aḥsan) to (mā unzila) is an idafa of the attribute to the thing described.

The punishment mentioned in this verse is the punishment mentioned before it, in both its kinds, and all of it comes suddenly, since it is not preceded by any warning. The punishment of this world descends suddenly, and the punishment of the Hereafter is likewise, because its signs appear at the Resurrection. The punishment of the sword came upon them on the Day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter will come upon them on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 56–58:

﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for my neglect concerning God's side, though I was indeed among the mockers!"﴾ ﴿Or should say: "Had God guided me, I would certainly have been among the God-fearing!"﴾ ﴿Or should say, when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return, so that I might be among the good-doers!"﴾.

(An) here is a causative particle for the commands in His words ﴿And turn penitently to your Lord and submit to Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 54] and ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down﴾ [al-Zumar: 55], with the causative lam (lam al-ta'lil) omitted alongside (an), which is common.

Page 45
Within this is the omission of the negating (la) after (an), which is also common, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and fear God, that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 155], ﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [al-An'am: 156], ﴿Or you should say: "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they"﴾ [al-An'am: 157], and as in His words, ﴿So do not follow desire, lest you deviate﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. The habit of the author of al-Kashshaf is to estimate: "out of dislike that you should do such-and-such."
