Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 59:

[Page 48]
﴿Yes, indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.﴾

(Balā) is a particle of contradiction (ibṭāl) for a negated statement, or one that carries a trace of negation, with the purpose of affirming what was negated before it. It is therefore determined that it here serves as the answer to the soul's statement, ﴿If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing﴾ [al-Zumar: 57], in accordance with what (law) requires, since it is used to express a wish, namely the negation of what it wished for, which is that Allah should have guided it so that it would be among the God-fearing. That is, Allah did not guide me, so I did not become God-fearing. The clause ﴿My signs came to you﴾ is an elaboration of the contradiction and an explanation of it, and it is like the answer by acceptance after denial, that is: Allah did guide you.

The soul's statement has been met with an answer corresponding to it in terms of its three parts. This is in His words, ﴿My signs came to you, but you denied them﴾, which corresponds to ﴿If only Allah had guided me﴾ [al-Zumar: 57]. Then His words, (and you grew arrogant), which corresponds to its saying ﴿for what I neglected concerning Allah's side﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], meaning: the end of your affair was not mere neglect, but something greater than it, which is arrogance. Then His words, ﴿and you were among the disbelievers﴾, which corresponds to the soul's statement ﴿I would have been among the God-fearing﴾ [al-Zumar: 57]. These are three correspondences.

The meaning: Allah guided you in this world through the guidance of the verses of the Qur'an, but you met the guidance with denial, arrogance and disbelief in them, so there is no excuse for you.

The answer followed the method of disordered distribution (al-nashr al-mushawwash) after the wrapping (al-laff), in observance of what that disorder requires, namely that the distribution begins with refuting the most important of what the wrapping contained, which is what they had put forward as an excuse and apology, from their saying (﴿If only Allah had guided me﴾ [al-Zumar: 57]), with the aim of hastening to inform them of what defeats their excuse. Then it returned to refuting their saying (﴿for what I neglected concerning Allah's side﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]), which was refuted by His words (﴿but you denied them﴾), then it completed the refutation of their saying (﴿If only I had another chance, I would be among the good-doers﴾ [al-Zumar: 58]) with His words (﴿and you were among the disbelievers﴾).

No answer was given to the soul's statement (﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]), because it is an admission.

[Page 49]
Had this method not been followed in distributing this wrapping, the swift refutation of the excuse would have been lost, and the correspondence of the three parts answered by parallel parts would have been lost, since you know that the refutation was arranged to match the three parts of the soul's statements, and that the order of the soul's statements followed the natural order. So if the distribution had not been disordered, it would have been necessary to limit it to fewer than the number of parts in the wrapping, and the subtle point of correspondence, which is the nature of argument, would be lost, along with what it contains of ta-warruk (a kind of hesitation or evasion).

The construction of His words ﴿and you were among the disbelievers﴾ is like what preceded just now in its parallels, His words ﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾ [al-Zumar: 56] and what follows it, in which the verb kuntu (was) has been inserted.

The readers agreed on the vowelling of the three tā' (you) in His words (﴿but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers﴾) with fatḥa, and likewise the fatḥa of the kāf in His words (jā'atka, "came to you") refers to the nafs (soul), in the sense of the dhāt (self) taken as masculine, so that by it is meant the male, and it is understood that women are like them, like the masculine plural form used for generalization in His words (min al-sākhirīn, "among the mockers").

And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant? ﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with one of the preceding clauses concerning the punishment of the polytheists in this world and the Hereafter. It is better that it be coordinated with the clause ﴿And those who did wrong among these, the evil consequences of what they earned will strike them﴾ [az-Zumar: 51], meaning: in this world, just as it struck those before them, and on the Day of Resurrection their faces will be blackened.

It is permissible that the blackening of the faces be literal, which Allah made a sign for them, and He made the rest of the people the opposite of them.

Allah has made the blackening of the faces on the Day of Resurrection a sign of an evil destination, just as He made their whiteness a sign of a good destination. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day when faces will be whitened and faces will be blackened. As for those whose faces were blackened: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 106] ﴿And as for those whose faces were whitened, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide eternally﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 107], in the Sūrah of Āl ʿImrān.

[p. 50]
It is also permissible that the whitening of the faces be used figuratively for radiance and joy. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 22]. And Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:

White-faced, noble are their lineages...

They say to the one who possesses a quality for which his people take pride: "You have whitened our faces."

The address in His saying "you see" (tarā) is to an unspecified person.

The clause ﴿their faces are blackened﴾ is a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ and khabar), and its position is that of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to ﴿those who lied against Allah﴾, because the seeing here is visual (baṣariyyah), whose verb does not govern two objects. And it is not required that a nominal circumstantial clause be joined by the conjunction "wa".

And ﴿those who lied against Allah﴾ are those who attributed to Him what is far removed from Him, such as a partner and other than that from the lies of polytheism. So those who lied against Allah are those who did wrong, mentioned in His saying ﴿And those who did wrong among these, the evil consequences of what they earned will strike them﴾ [az-Zumar: 51]. They were described first as wrongdoers, and then described as lying against Allah in another account. So His saying ﴿those who lied against Allah﴾ is not an explicit noun in place of a pronoun.

Included among those who lied against Allah is everyone who attributes to Allah a quality for which he has no evidence, and whoever legislates something and claims that Allah legislated it, deliberately and intending to promote its acceptance without evidence. Thus included are the people of misguidance who invented attributes for Allah or attributed legislation to Him. Not included are the mujtahids who erred in their evidences, whether in the subsidiary matters by consensus, or in the fundamentals according to what we choose, when they have exhausted their efforts.

Attributing something to Allah is a grave matter. For this reason our Imams said: a deduced ruling that is not explicitly stated may be called "the religion of Allah," but it may not be said "Allah said it."

For this reason, the clause ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ stands in the position of an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) to the clause ﴿You see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾, on both meanings, because the listener asks about the cause of the blackening of the faces, so he is answered that their abode is in Hell, meaning: because blackness suits what the fire of Hell will scorch their faces with. It is answered by way of the affirmative interrogative (istifhām taqrīrī), placing the presumed questioner in the position of one who knows that their abode is Hell, so it is not fitting for him to be unaware of the correspondence between the blackening of their faces and their destination to the Fire, for the hidden things have their signs. This interrogative is like His saying ﴿so that they may say: "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of the grateful?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 53], and like the saying of Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī to al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah when he was governor of Kufa and had delayed the prayer one day: "What is this, O Mughīrah? Do you not know that Gabriel descended and prayed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed?" And like the saying of al-Ḥajjāj in his sermon to the people of Kufa: "Were you not my companions at al-Ahwāz when you intended treachery...," etc.

Al-takabbur: intensity of pride (al-kibr). Among the attributes of Allah is al-Mutakabbir. Al-kibr: a person's displaying of greatness over others, because he considers himself great.

The definite article in "al-mutakabbirīn" here is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq), and the people of arrogance have degrees, the strongest of which is polytheism. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell, humiliated﴾ [Ghāfir: 60]. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise, and no one who has in his heart an atom's weight of faith will enter the Fire." Related by Muslim from Ibn Masʿūd. Do you not see that he contrasted it with faith? Below it are many degrees, varying in the strength of the reality of the essence of arrogance, and all of them are blameworthy. As for what is commonly said, that arrogance toward the arrogant is an act of worship, it is not correct.

In describing them as "the arrogant" there is an indication that their punishment by blackening their faces was fitting to their pride, because the arrogant person, when his face is ugly, his pride is broken, since pride weakens in proportion to its possessor's awareness of people knowing his shortcomings.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 61:**

﴿And Allah will save those who were mindful of Him with their triumph; no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve.﴾

It is coordinated (*'atf*, a grammatical conjunction) with the clause ﴿On the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah with their faces blackened﴾ [Az-Zumar: 60] to its end. That is: and Allah will save those who were mindful of Him (*ittaqaw*, from *taqwa*, God-consciousness) from Hell, because they are not arrogant.

[Page 52]

This indicates that *taqwa* (God-consciousness) is incompatible with arrogance (*takabbur*), because *taqwa* is the perfection of the legal character and requires avoiding what is forbidden and carrying out the command outwardly and inwardly. Arrogance is an inward disease of the heart. If arrogance casts its bearer into the Fire, by the ruling of His saying ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 60], then the opposite of those are the ones saved from it, namely the mindful (*al-muttaqun*), since *taqwa* prevents the causes of punishment, of which arrogance is one. So "those who were mindful" are the people of *taqwa*, and it is well known. For this reason the verb (*ittaqaw*) is treated as intransitive (*munazzal manzilat al-lazim*), and no object is to be supposed for it.

*Al-mafaza* (the triumph, the place of success) may be a mimi *masdar* (a verbal noun beginning with *mim*) from *al-fawz*, which is success (*al-falah*), like *al-mata*b (the place of return). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, for the mindful is a triumph﴾ [An-Naba': 31], and the attachment of the *ta'* to it are of the same kind as the attachment of the feminine *ha'* to a verbal noun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Its occurrence will have no denier﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 2]. This was discussed at the name of the surah al-Fatihah and at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So do not think them to be in a place of triumph from the punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188] in Al 'Imran.

The *ba'* (with) indicates accompaniment (*mulabasah*), meaning: while clothed in success. Or the *ba'* indicates cause (*sababiyyah*), meaning: because of what they attained of success.

It is permissible that *al-mafaza* be a noun for a wasteland (*al-falah*), as in the verse of Labid:

*For a watering-place from which the pastures shrink, it surpasses the perfect five-day desert crossing.*

It was named *mafaza* by the name of a place of success, that is, deliverance, and its feminine form is according to the interpretation of "the tract of land." They called it *mafaza* in view of the fact that whoever lodged in it was safe from his enemy reaching him, as al-'Udayl said:

*And beyond the reach of al-Hajjaj's hand, to keep it from reaching me, is a wide spread carpet for the hands of the she-camels.*

And the saying of al-Nabighah:

*They push people away from us when we ride them, from the wrongs; she is called Umm Sabbar.*

On this meaning, the *ba'* is in the sense of *fi* (in), and *al-mafaza* is the Garden. The annexation of *mafaza* to their pronoun is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the intensity of their being clothed in success, to the point that it became known by them, as one says: "He triumphed with the triumph of so-and-so."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *bimafazatihim* in the singular form. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf read *bimafazatihim* in the plural form. Both readings fit the two meanings of *al-mafaza*, because the verbal noun may be pluralized in view of the multiplicity of what issues from it, or in view of the multiplicity of its kinds. Likewise, the multiplicity of places of success corresponds to the multiplicity of groups. On this basis, the annexation of *al-mafaza* to the pronoun of (*alladhina ittaqaw*) is to define it by them, that is: the triumph which you know to belong to them, which is the Garden. This is known from verses and reports, among them His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, for the mindful is a triumph﴾ [An-Naba': 31], ﴿gardens and vineyards﴾ [An-Naba': 32], ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾ [An-Naba': 33].

The clause (﴿no evil will touch them, nor will they grieve﴾) explains the clause ﴿Allah will save those who were mindful of Him with their triumph﴾, because the negation of the touch of evil is their deliverance, and the negation of grief from them is the negation of the effect of the touch of evil.

In the negation of evil, the verbal sentence was used, because that negates the state of the people of the Fire from them, and the touch of evil for the people of the Fire is renewed. In the negation of grief from them, the nominal sentence was used, because the people of the Fire are also in grief and distress that is fixed and constant for them.

Among the subtle features of this expression is this variation: the nature of bodily harms is the renewal of their pains, and the nature of heart-afflictions is the continuance of the feeling of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 62–63:

﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is Guardian over all things.﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah – it is they who are the losers.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), serving as a preface to His saying ﴿Say: Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], in the context of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the messengers before him holding fast to monotheism, rejecting polytheism, disassociating from it, standing firm in opposing it, and resolving to cut off its root. The three sentences from His saying ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾ up to His saying (﴿the heavens and the earth﴾) are placed as premises that support what follows them, namely His saying ﴿Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64].

This resumptive sentence and what is coordinated with it comprise three sentences and a fourth sentence:

The first sentence (﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾): this sentence includes every existent within the fact that it is created by Allah, Exalted, so He is the one with authority to dispose of it. Excluded from this generality is only the Essence of Allah, Exalted, and His attributes, which are specified from this generality by rational proof, namely that He is the Creator of all things. For if He were the creator of Himself or of His attributes, it would necessitate that a thing depends on what it itself depends upon, and this is what is called circularity (al-dawr) in logic, whose impossibility is rational. Thus reason specified this generality. The purpose of this is to establish a fact and to obligate people to His monotheism, because He is their Creator; there is in this no intent of praise or exaltation. The purpose of this premise is to remind people that they, together with all that is with them, are servants of Allah alone, and no one else has any favour upon them through bringing them into existence.

The second sentence (﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾): it is brought in coordinated because its meaning differs from the meaning of the one before it. The wakil (guardian) is one who disposes of a thing without being held to account, and since no object is attached to this attribute, it is understood that the kind of disposal is entrusted to Him, and its reality encompasses all the individuals of what is disposed of. Thus His disposal encompasses the conditions of all existents: the determination of their deeds, their terms, and their movements. This premise implies that they are in need of Him for sustenance; after He brought them into existence, they are not independent of Him for an instant.

The third sentence (﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾): it is brought in separately because it serves to explain the sentence before it, for the one who is Guardian over a thing is the one who disposes of giving and withholding.

The "maqalid" (keys) is the plural of iqlid, with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the qaf; this is a plural not following the regular pattern. Iqlid is said to be arabized from Persian, its origin being "kilid"; it is also said to be from Greek, its origin being "iqlidis"; and it is said to be a Yemeni word; and these are among the words in which languages have converged. It is a metonymy (kinaya) for the safeguarding of their treasures: the treasures of the earth are its elements, its minerals, the qualities of its atmospheres and seas; and the treasures of the heavens are the courses of its stars, and the dispositions of their spirits in their worlds and in our world, and what none knows but Allah, Exalted. Since those elements and powers are extremely beneficial to people, and people are in need of them, they are likened to precious stored goods, so it is also correct that "maqalid" be a implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya); and it is also an explicit metaphor (isti'ara musarraha) for the divine, creative and subjugating command which overflows upon people from those stored treasures, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

This premise indicates that Allah is the Giver of what He wills to whom He wills of His creation, and among the greatest of that is prophethood and the guidance of the Law. The ignorance of the polytheists about this is what emboldened them to deny that Muhammad (ﷺ) was specially chosen for the message over them, and that his followers were specially given guidance, so they said: ﴿Is it these whom Allah has favoured from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

These sentences thus contain three premises, each of which indicates the Oneness of Allah in creation, then in absolute disposal over His creatures, then in placing the natural, rational and disciplinary systems and laws into the order of the world and the order of mankind. All of that necessitates His monotheism, the confirmation of His Messenger (ﷺ), and holding firmly to His bond, as those of faith were guided by this.

As for the fourth sentence, which is ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah – it is they who are the losers﴾, it may be considered a parenthetical sentence (i'tiradh), but its coupling with the conjunction "wa" after its counterparts suggests that the "wa" in it is conjunctive, and that it is intended by coordination with what precedes it, because it contains an addition beyond the content of the sentence before it; and it is a fourth premise for the purpose, by way of declaring ignorant those who are the opposite of the intended premises, for proving the truth by refuting its opposite is a kind of argumentation.

Because the argument returns to encouragement and warning: when those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah are losers, it is inevitable that those who believe in the signs of Allah are the victorious. This sentence corresponds to the sentence ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him with their achievement﴾ [al-Zumar: 61], from which the discourse moved to these signs; and it also serves to warn them and to refute their opinions, because its placement after the proofs of the Oneness, which are signs indicating that Allah is One, requires reproach upon them for not being guided by them.

The describing of those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah as "the losers" is because they disbelieved in the signs of the One to whom belong the keys of the treasures of good, so they exposed themselves to deprivation of what is in His treasures, and the greatest of these are the treasures of the good of the Hereafter.

The signs of Allah are the indications of His existence and His Oneness, which the three preceding sentences pointed to.

The reporting about those who disbelieve by the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) is to alert that those indicated lost because of what they were described with before the demonstrative noun, namely disbelief in the signs of Allah.

The placement of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is to convey the restriction of loss to them, and it is an assumed restriction (qasr idda'i), based on not counting the loss of others in comparison with their loss, so their loss is the greatest loss.

"Say: Do you order me to worship other than Allah, O you ignorant ones?"

This is the conclusion of the premises and the matter intended to be established. The fa' in His saying ﴿Afa-ghayra Allah﴾ ("Then other than Allah?") is for the derivation (tafri') of the speech that the Messenger ﷺ is commanded to say from the speech revealed to him, so that it may strike their ears. For the truths mentioned earlier are addressed to the polytheists; after these truths have been established among them, and after they have been warned for opposing, by their conduct, what those truths require, the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to direct to them this rebuking interrogative, varied in form from what preceded it, since their souls had already been humbled by the earlier speech that struck them, despairing them of attempting to turn the Messenger ﷺ away from monotheism toward the worship of other than Allah.

The interposition of the verb (Qul, "Say") is a parenthetical insertion between the derivation and what is derived, in order to make the context one of addressing the polytheists specifically, after the context before it had been one of explanation for every hearer, whether believers or others. Thus His saying "Qul" is the means by which the derivation was made specific to them. This is among the marvels of the composition and the abundance of its meanings, and it is worthy of being called "the variation of the carpet" (talwin al-bisat).

"Ghayra Allah" (other than Allah) is in the accusative, governed by "a'budu" (I worship), which is dependent on "ta'murunni" (you order me). The preposition has been elided together with "an" (that). The elision of the preposition with "an" is common. So His saying "a'budu" is taken as "an a'buda" (that I worship). When the preposition attached to "ta'murunni" was elided, the "an" that was joined to it was elided as well, just as it is elided in the verse of Tarafa:

"Ala aiyuhadha al-za'iri ahdura al-waghā wa an ashhada al-ladhdhāti hal anta mukhlidi"

This usage is permissible according to Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, Ibn Malik, and the grammarians of Andalusia. The majority of grammarians prohibit it, and they make His saying "a'budu" (I worship) the object of the interrogation, while the verb "ta'murunni" is either a parenthetical clause or a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning is: "Shall I worship other than Allah while you order me to that?" From this is their proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aiyadi is better than seeing him," and in the hadith: "And your helping a man with his mount, by lifting him onto it or lifting his goods onto it, is charity."

Nafi' recited "ta'murunni" with a single light nun, eliding one of the two nuns, which were the nun of the nominative (nun al-raf') and the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah), according to the disagreement over which was elided. This is common in the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿Fa-bima tubashshirun﴾. Nafi' also pronounced the ya' of the speaker with a fatha for lightness and to avoid the prolongation. The majority recited "ta'murunnī" with a doubled nun, by assimilating the two nuns, with the ya' sukun for lightness. Ibn Kathir recited with a doubled nun and a fatha on the ya'. Ibn 'Amir recited "ta'murunanī" with the two nuns made distinct and the ya' with sukun.

Their address with the description "the ignorant ones" is a rebuke to them, after they were described with loss, so that it combines for them the deficiency of the Hereafter and the deficiency of this world.

Ignorance (jahl) here is the opposite of knowledge (ilm), because they were ignorant of the indication of the earlier proofs, so those proofs benefited them nothing. They were blind to the proofs of Divine Oneness, which lay before their sight and hearing, and so they were ignorant of their indication of the one Creator. This portion of ignorance did not suffice them, until they descended to the depths of worshipping bodies of silent stone.

The application of ignorance to the opposite of knowledge is an ancient Arabic usage. Al-Nabigha said:

"Yukhbirka dhu 'irdihim 'anni wa 'alimuhum / wa laysa jahilu shay'in mithla man 'alima"

And al-Samaw'al, or 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi, said:

"Sali in jahilti al-nasa 'anna wa 'anhum / fa-laysa sawa'un 'alimun wa jahulu"

The object of "al-jahiluna" (the ignorant ones) is omitted, the verb being treated as intransitive, as if ignorance had become their disposition, so that they comprehend nothing. They are ignorant of what the proofs convey of Oneness; had they known it, they would not have associated partners, nor would they have invited the Prophet ﷺ to follow their polytheism. They are also ignorant of the stations of perfected souls, with an ignorance that led them to hope they could turn the Prophet ﷺ away from monotheism and cause him to slip by their nonsense and by their urging him to worship God on condition that he join them in worshipping their idols, reckoning religion as a bargain, a haggling, and a short-weighing.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 65–66:**

﴿Indeed it has been revealed to you, and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely come to nothing, and you will surely be among the losers."﴾ ﴿Rather, worship God alone, and be among the thankful.﴾

This is a confirmation of His command to say to the polytheists that statement, the statement of rejection that they should hope to get from him (the Prophet) the worship of God. It is a saying which they deserve to be struck with its harshness, because they are ignorant of the proofs and ignorant of the Messenger's own self and its purity. It is followed by (the statement) that they are ignorant that monotheism (tawhid) is the custom (sunnah) of the prophets, and that polytheism cannot approach their hearts. Therefore the most important purpose of this report is an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists, since they tried to get the Prophet ﷺ to acknowledge the divinity of their idols.

The conjunction "wa" (waw) is coordinating, joined to the sentence "Say" (qul). The emphasis of the report by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and by the particle "qad" is for the sake of emphasizing what it contains of allusion to the polytheists.

Wahy (revelation): notification from God through an angel. "Those before him" are the prophets and messengers, so what is meant is the precedence in the attribute of prophethood. Thus "those before you" (﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾) is meant to refer to the prophets.

The clause ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely come to nothing﴾ explains the meaning of "it has been revealed" (uhiya), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120].

The "ta" in "ashraktа" (ashrakta, "you associate") is the ta of address for everyone to whom the content of this clause was revealed among the prophets, so the clause is an explanation of what was revealed to him and to those before him. It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, so the clause is an explanation of the clause "it has been revealed to you," and "and to those before you" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), because explanation follows the general sense of what it explains and its like. In either case, the address is intended as an allusion to the people of the one to whom it was revealed, because supposing that the Prophet ﷺ would associate partners is not an expected thing.

[p. 59]

The "lam" in "la'in ashrakta" (if you associate) is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the omitted oath, indicating it, and the "lam" in "la-yahbatanna" (will surely come to nothing) is the lam of the answer to the oath.

Habt (ḥabṭ): nullification and rejection. "Habita 'amaluhu" means his deed went away as vain.

What is meant here by "deed" is the righteous deed from which a good, lasting reward is hoped for.

The meaning of its ḥabṭ is that it becomes idle, not rewarded. The ruling on associating partners after faith has already been discussed, as has the ruling on the return of the reward of a deed to its doer if he returns to faith after having nullified his faith, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Then it is coordinated with it that the one who associates partners is among the losers. Its state at that time is likened to the state of a merchant who brought out wealth in order to gain an increase in wealth from it, then returned and his wealth that was in his hand had gone, or most of it. So the speech is an illustration (tamthil) of the state of one who associates partners after monotheism, for polytheism was devised by its originators seeking increased nearness to God, when they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18]. So their state was like the state of the merchant who sought an increase over what he had of wealth, but he sought profit from other than its source, so he returned with his loss and ruin. In supposing that polytheism occurs from the Messenger and those before him, while their infallibility (‘ismah) is firmly established, there is an alert to the greatness of the matter of monotheism and the danger of polytheism, so that people may know that the highest ranks in excellence, if it were supposed that polytheism came upon them, would leave no trace of them, and would utterly annihilate them.

And "bal" (rather) is for the negation of the content of the clause "la'in ashrakta" (if you associate), meaning: rather, you do not associate partners. Or it is for the negation of the content of the clause ﴿Do you order me to worship other than God, O ignorant ones?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64].

The "fa" (fa') in His saying "fa'bud" (so worship) appears to be a consequence of the warning against the nullification of deeds and against loss. Thus by the combination of "bal" and "fa" at the beginning of the clause, it gathers two purposes: the purpose of nullifying their speech, and the purpose of warning against their conditions. This is an elegant point.

The implication of Sibawayh's speech is that the "fa" is a consequence of an omitted imperative verb, estimated according to the context. Its estimate is: "Be alert, so worship God," meaning: be alert to their scheming, and do not be deceived by what they have ordered you to worship other than God. The imperative verb was omitted for brevity. When it was omitted, beginning with "fa" was deemed objectionable, so they put forward the object of the verb that follows it, so the "fa" became medial, as is its nature in the weaving of speech, and along with that fronting there resulted a restriction (hasr).

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj made the "fa" a conditional response (jazā'iyya) indicating an estimated condition, meaning one that the context indicates. Its estimate is: "If you are intelligent," in contrast to His saying "O ignorant ones," so "worship God." When the condition was omitted for brevity, He substituted for it the fronting of the object, and this is close to Sibawayh's speech.

From al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', the "fa" indicates a verb before it, which is indicated by the verb that follows it. The estimate is: "God I worship, so worship," so when the first verb was omitted, the object of the verb pronounced was omitted, being dispensed with by the object of the omitted verb.

The fronting of the complement before "fa'bud" is for the purpose of restriction (qasr), as previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Say: "It is God I worship"﴾ [al-Zumar: 14] in this surah, meaning: I worship God and not other than Him. This is in the context of refuting the polytheists, as is contained in His saying ﴿Say: "Do you order me to worship other than God, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64].

Gratitude (shukr) here is righteous deed, because it is coordinated with the singling out of God, exalted is He, for worship. So the meaning of gratitude here is purely the deed that pleases God, exalted is He. It is said that the address is general to the Prophet ﷺ and to those before him, or specific to the Prophet ﷺ, and the prophets are analogized to him, as was said regarding ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely come to nothing﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verses 65–66:**

﴿Indeed it has been revealed to you, and to those before you: "If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely come to nothing, and you will surely be among the losers."﴾ ﴿Rather, worship God alone, and be among the thankful.﴾

This is a confirmation of His command to say to the polytheists that statement, the statement of rejection that they should hope to get from him (the Prophet) the worship of God. It is a saying which they deserve to be struck with its harshness, because they are ignorant of the proofs and ignorant of the Messenger's own self and its purity. It is followed by (the statement) that they are ignorant that monotheism (tawhid) is the custom (sunnah) of the prophets, and that polytheism cannot approach their hearts. Therefore the most important purpose of this report is an indirect allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists, since they tried to get the Prophet ﷺ to acknowledge the divinity of their idols.

The conjunction "wa" (waw) is coordinating, joined to the sentence "Say" (qul). The emphasis of the report by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and by the particle "qad" is for the sake of emphasizing what it contains of allusion to the polytheists.

Wahy (revelation): notification from God through an angel. "Those before him" are the prophets and messengers, so what is meant is the precedence in the attribute of prophethood. Thus "those before you" (﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾) is meant to refer to the prophets.

The clause ﴿If you associate partners with God, your deeds will surely come to nothing﴾ explains the meaning of "it has been revealed" (uhiya), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120].

The "ta" in "ashraktа" (ashrakta, "you associate") is the ta of address for everyone to whom the content of this clause was revealed among the prophets, so the clause is an explanation of what was revealed to him and to those before him. It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, so the clause is an explanation of the clause "it has been revealed to you," and "and to those before you" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), because explanation follows the general sense of what it explains and its like. In either case, the address is intended as an allusion to the people of the one to whom it was revealed, because supposing that the Prophet ﷺ would associate partners is not an expected thing.

[p. 59]

[Page 61]

When the discourse established that God Most High created everything, that the keys of the heavens and the earth belong to Him, and that He is the King of the worlds of this present life, and concluded this by stating that those who disbelieve in the proof of His oneness are "the losers," the discourse here moved to the greatness of God's dominion in the eternal Hereafter. Those who disbelieved in God's signs, which point to the dominion (malakut) of this world, have lost by abandoning reflection. So if they had come to know the great dominion of God in the Hereafter, they would have measured Him with His true measure. Thus the waw is conjunctive, joining the clause ﴿and the earth entirely in His grip on the Day of Resurrection﴾ to the clause ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [39:63]. The statement ﴿They did not measure God﴾ and so on is then parenthetical between the two clauses, required by the coherence with the clause ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of God, they are the losers﴾ [39:63].

It is also permissible that they be conjoined to the clause ﴿God is the Creator of all things﴾ [39:62]. In that case, the clause ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ and the clause ﴿and the earth entirely in His grip﴾ are both conjoined to the clause ﴿God is the Creator of all things﴾ [39:62]. The meaning is the same, except that the state (hal) expresses it more clearly.

It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and the earth entirely in His grip﴾ is a conjunction of one purpose to another purpose, moving on to the description of the Day of Resurrection and the states of the two groups in it. The clause ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ would then be parenthetical. It is an illustration of the state of one who is ignorant of the greatness of something, likened to the state of one who did not determine the measure of a heap of grain and so diminished it from its true quantity. The meaning of ﴿They did not measure God﴾ is therefore: they did not know His greatness, since they did not exalt Him above what is unbefitting His majesty, such as a partner in His divinity.

The phrase ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ (His true measure) is an idafa (construct phrase) of the attribute to the qualified noun, meaning "they did not measure God His true measure." Thus ﴿haqqa﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) specifying the type. A parallel to this occurred in Surat al-An'am.

﴿Jami'an﴾ (entirely): its origin is a passive participle, like qatil (slain). Labid said:

"They were emptied, and the whole (jami') who had been there went out at dawn,
leaving behind their hearth-stones and their thyme."

In this way it is used as an emphatic, like kull (all) and ajma' (all together). God Most High said ﴿on the day when God raises them all together (jami'an)﴾ [58:6] in Surat al-Mujadilah. Here ﴿jami'an﴾ is in the accusative as a state (hal) of ﴿al-ard﴾ (the earth). The noun ﴿al-ard﴾ is feminine, yet ﴿jami'﴾ is stripped of the feminine marker, following the common usage of the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul when it describes its qualified noun. The feminine marker may also be attached, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"If only it were a soul that died all together (jami'ah),
but it is a soul that falls away, soul after soul."

Here ﴿jami'an﴾ is in the accusative as a state of ﴿al-ard﴾, and a parallel to it occurred earlier in His saying ﴿Say: To God belongs all intercession (al-shafa'ah jami'an)﴾ [39:44].

﴿Al-qabdhah﴾ (grip), with a fatha on the qaf, is the single instance of grasping (al-qabd). It occurred earlier in His saying ﴿So I took a handful (qabdhah) from the trace of the Messenger﴾ [20:96] in Surat Ta-Ha.

The description of the earth by this verbal noun, which has the meaning of the passive participle, is like khalq (creation) in the sense of makhluq (created thing), for the sake of emphasis on the attribute of the verbal sense. It was given the pattern of the single instance (marrah) to belittle it in comparison with the greatness of God's dominion. It was not given the form with a damma on the qaf in the sense of the thing grasped, so that the emphasis on the attribute would not be lost, nor the indication of belittling. Thus ﴿al-qabdhah﴾ is a clear metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah) for taking hold. The handful indicates complete control over what is grasped, and that what is grasped has no ability to act or move.

This is an allusion to the cessation of the earth's motion and the extinguishing of its manifestations, for in the world of the Hereafter it becomes a thing existing without any activity. This comes about through the cessation of the system of gravity and the ending of the causes of life which used to sustain living beings upon the earth's surface, both animal and plant.

﴿Tayy al-samawat﴾ (the folding up of the heavens) is a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyyah) for the disruption of their arrangement and the disturbance of the dimensions of their bodies. Folding (tayy) is the turning back and wrapping of some parts of a cloth or a paper over others, after they had been spread out and extended in an order suited to the purpose for which they were spread. When the purpose is accomplished, the spread thing is folded. God Most High said: ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings. As We originated the first creation, We will bring it back﴾ [21:104].

The attribution of folding is an imaginative representation (takhyil).

The ba' in ﴿bi-yaminihi﴾ (with His right hand) indicates the instrument and causation.

﴿Al-yamin﴾ (the right hand) is an attribute of a hand, but there is no hand here. It is rather a metonymy (kinayah) for power, because action is carried out by the right hand. A poet, whose verse al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad recited, said, as al-Qurtubi reports:

"When I saw the sun, its light had shone forth,
I took from it my need with the right hand (bi-yamin)."

That is, with power. The pronoun in ﴿minha﴾ (from it) refers to something mentioned in the verses before it.

[Page 62]

The purpose of these two clauses is to represent God's greatness through the state of one who holds the earth in his grasp, and of one for whom the heavens are folded, their spheres and horizons, in his hand. This is a representation of the intelligible by the imagined (tashbih al-ma'qul bil-mutakhayyal). It is an imaginative analogy (tamthiliyyah) whose parts dissolve into two metaphors. It also indicates that the earth and the heavens remain and do not perish, but their familiar order has been affected by suspension. In the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim), on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say:

"God will seize the earth and fold up the heavens with His right hand. Then He will say: I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth?"

On the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said:

"A rabbi (habr) from among the rabbis came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, we find that God has placed the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the trees on one finger, the water and the moist earth on one finger, and all the rest of creation on one finger. Then He says: I am the King. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed until his molar teeth showed, confirming the words of the rabbi. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure. The earth entirely in His grip on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens folded in His right hand. Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾."

The meaning of his saying "Then he recited this verse" is that it was revealed before that, because it is among what was revealed in Mecca. The rabbi (habr) is one of the rabbis of the Jews of Medina. The narrator's statement "confirming the words of the rabbi" is an interpolation into the hadith from the narrator's own understanding, as al-Qurtubi, Abu al-Abbas, firmly stated in his book al-Mufhim 'ala Sahih Muslim. Al-Khattabi said: this hadith was transmitted by more than one narrator from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud through the line of Ubaydah, but they did not mention his saying "confirming the words of the rabbi," and perhaps it was a supposition and conjecture by the narrator. End of quotation. That is, it is an insertion by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i in transmitting from Ubaydah.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) laughter was mockery of the rabbi, in view of his supposition that God does this literally and that He has hands and fingers, according to the Jewish belief in corporealism (tajsim). For this reason he followed it with the recitation of ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, because its opening includes the refutation of what the rabbi and his like imagined of corporeality. This is well known from their beliefs, and the Qur'an had refuted it against them more than once. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not need to state its refutation explicitly and was satisfied with an allusion that believers would understand. Then he indicated that what the Jew imagined, a distribution over the fingers, is only a metaphor for taking hold and disposing.

[Page 63]

In some transmissions of the hadith it says: "Then God revealed His saying ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾." This is a mistake by some of its narrators, and how could it be, since this sura is Meccan and the story of the rabbi is Medinan?

His saying ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾ is a declarative of exaltation (insha' tanzih) of God Most High above the association of the polytheists, who ascribe gods to Him. It reinforces the clause ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾.

[Page 65]

This is a transition from the general description of the majesty of Allah's power on the Day of Resurrection to its detailed description, because of the awe and vivid imagery it contains, depicting all the conditions of that Day, which warn the disbelievers and give good news to the believers. It also reminds of the establishment of justice and truth, and then depicts the driving of the polytheists to Hell and the leading of the believers to Paradise.

The sentence is a continuation of one narrative upon another, and the reason for the connection is clear. He used the past tense in His words "and the Horn was blown" and "so swooned," as a figurative usage, because the event is certain to occur, like His words "the command of Allah has come" (Qur'an 16:1). It is also possible that the waw is a waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), with an implied "qad" (already), meaning: "while the Horn has already been blown," so that the past-tense verbs "was blown" and "swooned" are used in their literal sense.

The sentence begins with the matter of the blowing of the Horn, since it is the appointed time of the Day of Resurrection and of what precedes it, namely the death of every living being on the earth. Its mention is repeated in the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

The Sur (the Horn) is a trumpet by which one calls a far-off and scattered group, such as an army, and like the call to prayer. The Jews used to call to a communal prayer with it, as is reported in the hadith about the beginning of the adhan in Islam. What is meant here is the calling of creation to attend the gathering, both the living and the dead. It was mentioned earlier at His words "the Day the Horn is blown" (Qur'an 6:73), in Al-An'am. It is a sign of the matter of creation (amr al-takwin): the living are struck with terror and die "as the one who is terrified dies" at the first blast, and the dead are struck with a shock of agitation through which life stirs in them, so that they become prepared to receive life. When the second blast is sounded, the souls will enter the bodies created for them, in the likeness of what decayed of their bodies that had decayed, or the souls will enter bodies that have not yet decayed, like the bodies of those who swooned at the first blast. It is also possible that there will be a period between the two blasts in which the bodies decay.

The exception is from the first relative pronoun, meaning: except whomever Allah wills not to swoon, namely the angels and the spirits. It was mentioned in Surat An-Naml: "The Horn is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth are terrified" (Qur'an 27:87).

The particle "thumma" (then) indicates a delay in rank, because it is a conjunction of sentences, and it may also convey, together with that, the interval appropriate to what lies between the two blasts. "Ukhra" (another) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "another blast." It is the blast whose effect differs from the effect of the first blast, because the first is a blast of destruction and swooning, and the second is a blast of giving life. This difference is due to the difference between the two sounds, or to the difference between the two modes of creation.

The second blast is mentioned in this verse but not in His words in Surat An-Naml: "The Horn is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth are terrified, except whomever Allah wills, and all come to Him humbled" (Qur'an 27:87). The reason is that the Naml verse is concerned with admonition through the passing away of this world, whereas this verse is concerned with the magnificence of Allah's majesty on the Day of Resurrection. Likewise, the description of the blast as single appears in Surat Al-Haqqah: "So when the Horn is blown with one blast" (Qur'an 69:13), "and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing" (Qur'an 69:14), "then on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur" (Qur'an 69:15). Here, however, two blasts are mentioned.

The pronoun in "hum" (they) refers to "whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth" in what remains of its meaning after the restriction by "except whomever Allah wills." They are the ones who swooned, both the swoon of death and the swoon of agitation, which prepares them to receive life at the blast.

The "idha" (behold) is for surprise, to draw attention to the swiftness with which life enters them and their standing up immediately after it. "Qiyam" is the plural of "qa'im" (standing).

The clause "yanzuruna" (looking) is a circumstantial clause (hal).

"Al-nazar" means seeing with the eyes. The purpose of this circumstantial clause is to indicate that they have been given complete life, with no veil over their sight, meaning there is no bewilderment in it, as in His words, Exalted is He: "It is but a single shout, and behold, they are looking" (Qur'an 37:19), in Surat As-Saffat. Or it is intended that they look with the look of one who turns his gaze searching. It may also be from "nazrah" (a respite) or "intizar" (waiting).

[Page 66]

“﴿And the earth shone with the light of its Lord, and the Book was placed, and the prophets and the witnesses were brought, and judgment was passed between them with truth, and they were not wronged.﴾ ﴿And every soul was paid in full for what it did, and He is most knowing of what they do.﴾”

These verses depict the majesty and beauty of that station in the most masterful portrayal. The definiteness of "the earth" (al-ard) is the implicit anaphoric definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhikri al-dimni), since His saying ﴿So behold, they are standing, looking on﴾ [39:68] implies that they are standing upon a firm ground, for standing requires a place where those creatures stand. This is the earth of the gathering (ard al-hashr), which is al-Sahirah (the wakeful plain) in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Nazi'at: ﴿It will be but a single blast﴾ [79:13], ﴿and behold, they will be upon al-Sahirah﴾ [79:14]. It has been explained as the white, pure earth. What is meant is not the earth they were upon in the world, for that has passed away, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to a different earth﴾ [14:48].

The "shining" (ishraq) of the earth is the spreading of light upon it. One says "the earth shone" (ashraqat al-ard), and one does not say "the sun shone" (ashraqat al-shams), as was mentioned earlier at His saying (﴿at evening and at sunrise﴾ [38:18]) in Surat Sad.

The attribution of the light to the Lord (idafat al-nur ila al-Rabb) is an attribution of magnification, because it emanates from the side of the Holy (al-Qudus), which is the light referred to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp﴾ [24:35], the verse from Surat al-Nur. Thus the attribution of the Lord's light is an attribution of honor to what is attributed, like His saying ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ [7:73]. Likewise, the attribution of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of "the earth" is for the honor of the one attributed to, meaning: with a special light which Allah created in it, not by the blaze of a lamp, nor by the light of a star or sun or other than them. Since the light was an inherent light of that earth, it indicates its purity from the darknesses of deeds. Thus it shows that what takes place upon that earth of deeds and events is truth and perfection in its own domain, because the world of lights is not tainted by anything of the darknesses of deeds. Do you not see that the earthly world, since it is not luminous in itself, but its light is borrowed from the rising of the sun and the stars at night, what is upon the face of the earth of deeds and creatures is

[Page 67]
a mixture of good and evil. This makes it unnecessary to take the light as a metaphor for justice, since that meaning is achieved by necessary implication (dalalat al-iltizam) as a kinayah (implicature). These verses depict the majesty and beauty of that station in the most masterful portrayal. The definiteness of "the earth" (al-ard) is the implicit anaphoric definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhikri al-dimni), since His saying ﴿So behold, they are standing, looking on﴾ [39:68] implies that they are standing upon a firm ground, for standing requires a place where those creatures stand. This is the earth of the gathering (ard al-hashr), which is al-Sahirah (the wakeful plain) in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Nazi'at: ﴿It will be but a single blast﴾ [79:13], ﴿and behold, they will be upon al-Sahirah﴾ [79:14]. It has been explained as the white, pure earth. What is meant is not the earth they were upon in the world, for that has passed away, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to a different earth﴾ [14:48].

The "shining" (ishraq) of the earth is the spreading of light upon it. One says "the earth shone" (ashraqat al-ard), and one does not say "the sun shone" (ashraqat al-shams), as was mentioned earlier at His saying (﴿at evening and at sunrise﴾ [38:18]) in Surat Sad.

The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp﴾ [24:35], the verse from Surat al-Nur. Thus the attribution of the Lord's light is an attribution of honor to what is attributed, like His saying ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ [7:73]. Likewise, the attribution of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of "the earth" is for the honor of the one attributed to, meaning: with a special light which Allah created in it, not by the blaze of a lamp, nor by the light of a star or sun or other than them. Since the light was an inherent light of that earth, it indicates its purity from the darknesses of deeds. Thus it shows that what takes place upon that earth of deeds and events is truth and perfection in its own domain, because the world of lights is not tainted by anything of the darknesses of deeds. Do you not see that the earthly world, since it is not luminous in itself, but its light is borrowed from the rising of the sun and the stars at night, what is upon the face of the earth of deeds and creatures is

The Tafsir of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 39, verses 71–72:

"﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them, 'Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?' They will say, 'Yes, but the word of punishment has come due upon the disbelievers.'﴾ ﴿It will be said, 'Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein; and wretched is the abode of the arrogant.'﴾"

This is the execution of the judgment that came in His saying, ﴿And it will be judged between them with truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 69], and His saying, ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did﴾ [al-Zumar: 70]. The outcome and result of that is the placing of the criminals in punishment

Page 69

and the placing of the righteous in the abode of reward.

The report began with mention of those deserving punishment because that is the more important matter in this context, since this is a context of repeating admonition and warning for those who did not take heed from the many similar admonitions repeated in the Qur'an. As for the people of reward, the purpose has already been achieved concerning them, so what is mentioned of them is only a repetition of glad tidings and praise.

Al-sawq (driving): that a walker makes another walker walk ahead of him and keep close to him. Its opposite is al-qawd (leading). Al-sawq implies hustling and humiliation. The Exalted said, ﴿As if they were being driven to death﴾ [al-Anfāl: 6].

Al-zumar is the plural of zumrah, which is a company of people followed by another company, so one does not say "a zumrah of people passed" unless it is followed by another. This is one of the words whose meaning is restricted.

They were made into zumar because of the differences in their degrees of disbelief. If the intended "those who disbelieved" are the polytheists of Quraysh targeted by this threat, their differences correspond to the degree of their obstinacy in disbelief and what mixes with it of hostility toward the Muslims or harshness, and of neutrality toward the Prophet ﷺ or harm. If the intended are all the people of polytheism, as the narration of the scene with His saying (Did there not come to you messengers) suggests, then the multiplicity of their groups corresponds to the kinds of their polytheism.

(Ḥattā) is inceptive, and (idhā) is an adverb of future time that generally takes on the meaning of a conditional, i.e., they will be driven with a driving that clings to them in its harshness, connected to the time of their arrival at the Fire.

The clause (futtiḥat) is the answer of (idhā), because it is given the meaning of a conditional, and the mention of (idhā) dispenses with using the temporal (lammā). The implied sense is: "When they came to it, its gates were opened," i.e., they had been closed, so that they would be opened in their faces at the moment of their arrival suddenly, as awe and terror.

Al-Jumhūr read "futtiḥat" with a doubled tāʾ for emphasis in the opening. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a single tāʾ according to the original form of the verb.

Al-khazaná (the keepers) is the plural of khāzin, who is the agent and gatekeeper; the name khāzin came to predominate because he is sought for guarding wealth.

Page 70

The interrogation addressed to the people of the Fire is a confirmatory interrogation used for reproach and rebuke, as indicated by their words after it, ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein; and wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾

(Min-kum) is a qualifier of (rusul). The purpose of the qualifier is to express disdain toward them, for they used to say, ﴿A single human being from among us that we should follow?﴾ [al-Qamar: 24]. Al-tilāwah is the recitation of the message and the Book, because the reciter follows some speech with other speech. The original meaning of āyāt is signs, like the signs of a road. It was applied to statements indicating the truth, and what is meant here is the statements revealed to the messengers, such as the scrolls of Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, and the Qur'an. The term āyāt is most specifically applied to the verses of the Qur'an, because they have completed the essence of signs by including great indication of the truth, and since they are miraculous in their composition and wording. Whatever else is called āyāt is so called by way of mushākalah (analogy), as in the hadith of stoning, "that the Jew who brought the Torah placed his hand on the verse of stoning," and because in the meanings of much of the Qur'an and the heavenly books there are theoretical proofs of the Oneness of God, the Resurrection, and similar matters of reasoning.

The recitation is attributed to all the messengers, although some of them had no scripture, according to the manner of taghlīb (predominance of the majority).

The idafah of (yawm) to the pronoun of the addressees is in view of their being in it, like the words of the Prophet ﷺ in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "As the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours." So the idafah stands in place of definition by the definite article al-ʿahdiyyah.

Their answer with the particle (balā) is an affirmation of the negation of what was negated, namely the coming of the messengers and their delivery. Its meaning is the affirmation of the coming of the messengers and their delivery.

(Kalimat al-ʿadhāb) is the threat of punishment through the tongues of the messengers, as in the words of one of them in another verse, ﴿So the word of our Lord has come due upon us; indeed we are to taste [it]﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 31], meaning it was realized in us. The definiteness in (kalimat al-ʿadhāb) is generic definiteness, since it is idafah to a noun defined by the generic al-, meaning the words [of punishment].

Page 71

The place of the istidrāk (contrast) is what was omitted in the speech, which required that the words of threat come due upon them, namely their turning away from listening to the command of the messengers. The implied sense is: "But we were arrogant and opposed, so the word of punishment came due upon the disbelievers." This answer is of the kind of answer of one who is remorseful and distressed, who briefly answers his questioner or blamer with, "The matter is as you see."

The verb (qālū) is not conjoined to what precedes it, because it came in the context of dialogue, as was mentioned more than once before; see His saying, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] up to His saying, ﴿He said, "Indeed I know what you do not know."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].
