Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 39, verse 73:

﴿And those who had feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups, until, when they reach it and its gates have been opened, its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it to abide eternally."﴾

The verb "driven" (suq) is applied to the advance of the God-fearing toward Paradise by way of mushakalah (paronomastic correspondence) with the first "driven" (siq). Mushakalah is among the embellishments (muhassinat) of speech, and on close examination it belongs to the category of metaphor (isti'arah), whose only connection is the general resemblance that is brought about by the similarity of wording (mujanasat al-lafz).

Their being in groups accords with the degrees of God-consciousness (taqwa).

The waw in the clause ﴿and its gates have been opened﴾ is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal), meaning: when they reach it, and its gates have already been opened, so they find the gates open, as is the custom in the welcoming of the people of honour.

Some grammarians erred concerning this waw, such as Ibn Khalawayh and al-Hariri, and al-Tha'labi followed them in his tafsir. They claimed that it is a waw that enters upon the eighth item, either because it contains the root of "eight" (thamaniyah), as in His saying ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], so they said that in ﴿and its gates have been opened﴾ the waw was brought because the gates of Paradise are eight; or because it is the eighth in an enumeration, as in the Exalted's saying ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112] up to His saying ﴿and those who forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], for it is the eighth attribute in the enumeration. The occurrence of these waws is a strange coincidence, and the attention of those people to this coincidence is a subtle observation, but it has no benefit in the meanings of the Qur'an, let alone its eloquence. Ibn Hisham embellished it in Mughni al-Labib. The discussion of these waws has preceded at His saying ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112] in Surah al-Tawbah, and at His saying ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] in Surah al-Kahf.

Here "idha" (when) is merely temporal, not carrying the meaning of a conditional. The sense is: "until the time of their arrival at the gates of Paradise." That is, the angels who are assigned to surround them at the gates of Paradise escort them, like the case of one who leads a bride to her house: when he brings her to its door, he leaves her between herself and her home, as if they were saying, "This is your dwelling, so take it." Then the keepers of Paradise receive them with peace.

"Tibtum" (you have been good) is a supplication for their good, that is, for purification and goodness of state, and the clause is an expressive utterance of honour and supplication.

The difference among the readers concerning "futtihat" (have been opened) here is like the difference concerning its counterpart mentioned just above.

And the phrase "they said" in this statement indicates that their saying that is not a reply to the angels' words. Rather, they praised God for the bliss He had granted them, which He had promised them, and He promised it to them under the heading of righteous deeds. Since they were people of righteous deeds, they treated the promise to those who do righteous deeds as a promise to themselves, because the condition attached to the promise was fulfilled in them.

The meaning of (*ṣadaqanā*, "He has fulfilled for us") is: He made His promise to us come true.

[Page 73]

His words ﴿and has caused us to inherit the earth﴾ are a statement that works as a proverb for one who inherits sovereignty. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 105]. So the Qur'an expressed the intended meaning of the people of Paradise, who speak different languages, through this Arabic construction, which conveys the meanings of what they uttered in their various languages.

It is also possible that the people of Paradise spoke in Arabic, a speech that God inspired in them. Reports have indeed come that the speech of the people of Paradise is in classical Arabic. The word "earth" is used in consideration of the figurative construction, since the earth has either perished or been replaced.

It is also possible that the word "earth" is used metaphorically for Paradise, because it is their abode, just as the earth is the dwelling place of people in the first life.

The use of "inherit" is a metaphor (*istiʿāra*), by likening giving to inheritance in its freedom from the toil of acquisition.

*Al-tabawwuʾ* means to dwell and to settle. The meaning is that they move freely among the chambers and gardens, delighting in bliss.

By "those who do" (*al-ʿāmilīn*) they meant themselves, that is, those who do good. This is a plain statement of realities, and there is no fault in it as self-praise, because that world is the world of perfect realities, free from any admixture of deficiency.

Know that these verses described the fate of the disbelievers and the fate of the God-fearing on the Day of Gathering, and they were silent about the fate of the people of sins who did not join the God-fearing through repentance from major sins and the forgiveness of minor sins through avoiding major sins. This is the Qur'an's habit of not describing men of the Islamic community as disobedient to their Lord, except where a ruling requires explanation. Major sins belong to the affairs of the age of ignorance, and it was not fitting for the people of Islam to fall into them. If they do fall into them, they must repent. If they die without repenting, God, exalted is He, counts for them the good deeds of their actions and the pure intentions of their hearts, and He settles their accounts with these if He wills. Then, in what is below that, they draw near to punishment in proportion to their approach to the state of the disbelievers in the abundance of sins, so they are commanded to the Fire or to Paradise. Among them are the people of the *A'raf*. A portion of this matter has already been discussed in the commentary on Surat al-A'raf.

[Page 74]

﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) to what precedes it, namely the mention of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, some of which are conjoined to others, beginning with His words, exalted is He, ﴿And the Horn will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. Among those conditions is the encircling of the Throne by the angels.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), so it indicates that this is a sight of closeness to the Throne and its angels, and that this is an honour for him, in that he is surrounded by the procession of the angels who are around the Throne.

Al-ḥaff (encircling) means to surround a thing and be on all its sides.

The clause ﴿glorifying the praise of their Lord﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that they utter statements which indicate the transcendence and magnification of God, accompanied by their praise of Him. Thus the bāʾ in "bi-ḥamdi rabbihim" expresses accompaniment and is connected to "yusabbiḥūna."

In mentioning God through the description "their Lord," there is an allusion that their nearness to the Throne is an elevation in the station of servanthood, which is constant for all creatures.

* * *

﴿And it will be judged between them with truth.﴾

This is an emphasis of the preceding clause, ﴿And it will be judged between them with truth, while they will not be wronged﴾ [al-Zumar: 69].

* * *

﴿And it will be said: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

This may be an emphasis of ﴿And they will say: Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. It may also be the report of another saying, uttered by speakers among the angels, the messengers and the people of Paradise. It is then more general than the preceding saying, which is the saying of those driven to Paradise from among the righteous. This is their saying, praising God for the justice of His judgment and for all His attributes of perfection.

* * *

[Page 75]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Sūrat al-Mu'min.

The name of this sūrah is attested in the Sunnah as "Ḥā Mīm al-Mu'min." al-Tirmidhī narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites (Ḥā Mīm al-Mu'min) up to (ilayhi al-maṣīr), and the Verse of the Throne in the morning, will be protected by them," and the hadith continues. By this name it became well known in the codices of the East, and by it al-Bukhārī titled it in his Ṣaḥīḥ and al-Tirmidhī in his al-Jāmiʿ. The reason for the name is that the story of the believer from the household of Pharaoh is mentioned in it, and it is not mentioned in any other sūrah explicitly.

The grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of this name is that the letters "Ḥā Mīm" are cited with the letter Mīm quiescent, in the form in which they are pronounced. It is also construed as an idafah (annexation) to the word "al-Mu'min," with the implied meaning: the sūrah of Ḥā Mīm, the mention of the believer, or the word "al-Mu'min." It is also called Sūrat al-Ṭawl, because of the words in its beginning, ﴿the Possessor of Bounty﴾, though this name has fallen into disuse. It is called Sūrat Ghāfir, because of the description of Him, exalted is He, as ﴿Forgiver of sin﴾ at its beginning. By this name it became well known in the codices of the Maghrib.

It is a Meccan sūrah by consensus. However, al-Ḥasan made an exception of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And glorify the praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning﴾ [Ghāfir: 55], because he held that it was revealed concerning the obligation of the five prayers and their times. He held that the obligation of five prayers and their times occurred only in Medina, and that what was obligatory in Mecca was two rak'ahs each day without specified times. This is a weak position built upon another weak one, for the majority hold that the five prayers were enjoined in Mecca at their times. Moreover, it is not necessary that "glorification" in that verse means the prayers; rather it is to be taken in its apparent sense as any utterance by which God is declared free from imperfection.

Stranger than this is what is narrated from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, that the words of God, exalted is He,

* * *

[Page 76]

﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of God without authority having come to them—there is in their breasts nothing but pride, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghāfir: 56], were revealed concerning Jews of Medina who disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) about the matter of the Dajjāl and claimed that he was one of them. At the beginning of the sūrah there is ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾ [Ghāfir: 4], and by these are meant the polytheists.

This sūrah is numbered sixtieth in the chronological order of the revelation of the sūrahs. It was revealed after Sūrat al-Zumar and before Sūrat Fuṣṣilat, and it is the first of the Ḥā Mīm sūrahs in revelation.

This sūrah was recited following the death of Abū Ṭālib, that is, in the third year before the Hijrah, because it will be mentioned later that Abū Bakr recited the verse ﴿Will you kill a man because he says, "My Lord is God"?﴾ [Ghāfir: 28] when a group of Quraysh harmed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) around the Kaʿbah. The harm of Quraysh to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became severe only after the death of Abū Ṭālib.

The sūrahs that begin with the letters "Ḥā Mīm" are seven sūrahs, arranged in the codices according to their order of revelation, and their collective name is "Āl Ḥā Mīm." They were given the name "Āl" because of their similarity in their openings, so they are as if they were one family. The word āl is attached to someone of honour, and it is said of one whose honour is not intended: "the people of so-and-so." al-Kumayt said:

"We have read for you in the Āl Ḥā Mīm a verse,
whose interpretation (taʾwīl) was given by a jurist and a grammarian among us."

He means the words of God, exalted is He, in the sūrah ﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ [al-Shūrā: 1], ﴿ʿAyn Sīn Qāf﴾ [al-Shūrā: 2], ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward, except affection for relatives﴾ [al-Shūrā: 23], according to an interpretation other than that of Ibn ʿAbbās. Therefore he strengthened it with his words: "whose interpretation was given by a jurist and a grammarian among us."

Sometimes the sūrahs beginning with "Ḥā Mīm" are collectively called "al-Ḥawāmīm," a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr) on the pattern fawāʿīl. Its singular is on the pattern fāʿīl, a form that arose from combining the names of the two letters, Ḥā and Mīm, so it became like foreign patterns such as Qābīl and Rāḥīl. It is not foreign, because it is an accidental pattern that is not taken into account. The broken plural on the pattern fawāʿīl is regular for this type of word.

It is established that they pluralized "Ḥā Mīm" as "al-Ḥawāmīm" in many reports from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and Samurah ibn Jundab. In some reports it is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is not established by a sound chain.

* * *

[Page 77]

Similar to this are the sūrahs beginning with "Ṭā Sīn" or "Ṭā Sīn Mīm," which they pluralized as "ṭawāsīn" with the nūn, by way of prevalence (taghlīb). Abū ʿUbaydah recited verses without naming their composer:

"I swear by the seven that were lengthened,
and by the hundreds that come after them,
and by the eight that were doubled and repeated,
and by the ṭawāsīn that were tripled,
and by the ḥawāmīm that were made seven,
and by the mufaṣṣal that was made distinct."

It is reported from Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Farrāʾ that the common people's saying "al-Ḥawāmīm" is not from the speech of the Arabs, and Abū Manṣūr al-Jawāliqī followed them in this.

Its verses are counted as eighty-four according to the count of the people of Medina and Mecca, eighty-five according to the count of the people of Syria and Kufa, and eighty-two according to the count of the people of Basra.

* * *

The Purposes of This Sūrah

This sūrah contains purposes from the foundations of the call to faith. It begins with what requires challenging the obstinate concerning the truthfulness of the Qur'an, as the two disjoined letters at its opening require, as was explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah.

The attributes of God, exalted is He, that are attached to His name contain an implicit call to them to abandon what they are engaged in. Thus the opening of the sūrahs is like the preface of a sermon, pointing to the purpose of the revelation of this sūrah.

It then follows this with the proof that the revelation of this Book is from God, a clear proof which none deny except the disbelievers, out of envy in acknowledging it, and that their disputation is mere confusion. The mention of those who dispute concerning the signs of God is repeated five times in this sūrah. There is the depiction of their condition through the condition of the nations who denied the messengers of God, mentioned in general terms; then the warning concerning the traces of their destruction; and the striking of an example through the people of Pharaoh.

The admonition of the believer of the household of Pharaoh to his people, with admonitions resembling the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) to his people.

* * *

[Page 78]

The indication, in general terms, of the signs of God's sole divinity.

The nullification of the worship of what they worship besides God.

The reminder of God's blessings upon people, so that those who turned away from giving thanks to Him may thank Him.

The argument for the possibility of resurrection.

The warning to them of the terror they will encounter and the punishment that awaits them, and the threat that they will have no helper on that day, and that their leaders will disown them.

The affirmation of God's Messenger (ﷺ) through the establishment of the victory of this religion during his lifetime and after his death.

Interwoven with all this is the praise of the believers, the description of their honour, and the praise of the angels for them.

The hadith that al-Tirmidhī narrated from Abū Hurayrah concerning the virtue of this sūrah has come down: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ḥā Mīm al-Mu'min up to (ilayhi al-maṣīr) and the Verse of the Throne in the morning will be protected by them until evening, and whoever recites them in the evening will be protected by them until morning."
